equal the trust-ir reference interpreter's, and the interpreter is itself
pinned to closed forms. An admitted program only transports poison, so no
native run observes the NoUndef zero; the zero constant of each scalar
carrier is pinned at LIR level by the conformance manifest instead. The
stage and its lowering are target-independent, so x86-64 (ELF and Mach-O)
and aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu (ELF) now compile these constructs too, with
no native or emulated run on any host. There is no ELF/Linux twin. This is
test evidence, not proof.

A niche-encoded `Ty::Enum` (rustc's `Option<&T>`, `Option<NonZero*>`,
`Option<bool>`, `Option<char>` and multi-variant niche layouts) lowers to the
payload struct its producer descriptor states. Its discriminant is read
(`ExtractField` element 0: one lane load, wrapping subtraction of
`niche_start`, unsigned range test) and constructed (`Constant::Aggregate`)
through a codec that first checks the
producer's niche parameters against trust-cg's own layout. Incoherent
parameters, a lane that is not exactly one integer, `bool`, `char`, pointer,
fat-pointer word, nested Direct-enum tag or nested niche lane of the untagged
payload, reserved values that a `bool`, `char`, reference, `Rc`, function
pointer or nested enum treats as valid, niche-tagged fields overlapping the
lane, niche-range discriminants that do not step by one, and untagged
constants whose lane holds a reserved value fail closed with
`[TCG-NICHE-ENUM]`. Integer and raw-pointer lanes state no validity range, so
their reserved range is the producer's invariant, as trust-ir defines it.
Lanes are the 8/16/32/64-bit `EnumTagRepr` widths. The codec emits existing
LIR opcodes; there is no niche-specific proof obligation. The native corpus
reads `Ref`-typed payloads and constructs `Ptr`-typed payloads; it does not
qualify general reference-valued enum construction. An untagged constant
whose niche lane holds a relocated address is refused by name
(`[TCG-NICHE-ENUM]`, "does not determine the value its payload puts in the
niche lane"). The codec classifies a lane constant only when it is an integer,
`bool` or `u128` literal, and it cannot show that a link-time address avoids
the reserved values. This is not limited to references: a `SymbolAddr` at a
`Ref`, `PtrConst` or bare `Ptr` lane (`Some(&STATIC)`), an `FnDef` at a
function-pointer lane (`Some(f)` as an `Option<fn()>`) and the data word of a
`&str` constant (`Some("abc")`) are all refused, though TrustIR admits each.
A separate rule covers every function-body struct, tuple or array constant,
a splat included, whether or not an enum holds it. Such a constant may place
a `SymbolAddr` only at a `Ptr` or `Func` field, although TrustIR also admits
one at `Ref`, `PtrConst` and `PtrMut`. A symbol address at one of those
typed-pointer fields is refused by name ("requires a Ty::Ptr or Ty::Func
field"). The object writer's global initializers apply the same rule, and
every niche payload field, the lane included, is written through that walk,
so a typed-pointer lane would stay refused here once the codec classified its
address. A niche
or untagged enum whose payload is a TUPLE lowers only under a declared tuple
layout that agrees with this backend's. TrustIR bounds a descriptor's fields
by their layout, and only a declared tuple layout gives a tuple one. Since
WS7.7 this backend consumes a declared row that EQUALS the declaration-order
layout its byte path emits and refuses one that differs
(`DeclaredTupleLayoutDisagrees`), so a reordered tuple payload stays refused.
A struct payload with declared offsets carries the same lanes. Of these three
refusals, only the tuple payload removed a lowering that worked before typed
admission, and WS7.7 restores it for agreeing layouts.
`tests/niche_enum_codec.rs` pins the lane refusal and the tuple rule, and
`tests/aggregate_constants.rs` pins the field rule.
OD-TYPED-ADMISSION-GAPS-20261010 in `docs/decision-record.md` rules on each
one and states what would reverse it.
Enum-typed globals and DWARF for niche layouts (every enum is still
described as a four-byte C enum) remain open. TrustIR `GEP` strides the
whole pointee image for every index; it does not project enum fields. The
[flat GEP regression record](reports/perf/2026-09-24-flat-gep/README.md) retains
528 native O0–O3 calls and 85 WebAssembly calls; record/closure cases have
closed-form layout oracles because the reference interpreter lacks their byte layouts.
The [Linux regression repair](reports/perf/2026-09-20-linux-floor-repairs/README.md)
executes the twenty-function corpus at O0-O3, with 882 C-oracle checks per level.
Canonical `InsertField` cannot rewrite an enum discriminant: the adapter now
refuses that operation for niche encodings as well as direct-tag encodings.
The corpus selects and stores complete variants. This is execution and
canonical-admission evidence, not a proof of general enum semantics.

A direct-tag `Ty::Enum` (no descriptor, or a `Direct` v31 descriptor) is
projected by value with `ExtractField` through one image authority
(`trust_cg_lower::direct_enum`): element 0 loads the tag word at the image's
tag offset at the enum's canonical tag type (`EnumDef::canonical_tag_repr`:
the explicit repr, else the narrowest type that fits every effective
discriminant, signed when one is negative), and element `i > 0` loads payload
field `i - 1` at one static offset. The stored tag word is the discriminant
VALUE, never the variant index, so `Switch` cases and signed compares consume
it as any integer. A `Direct` descriptor is read verbatim for the tag offset
and every field offset; the canonical `Type::Enum` is emitted only where it
reproduces the declared bytes, and otherwise the enum lowers to a byte-image
carrier of exactly the declared size and alignment. A descriptor-less enum is
projected only when trust-cg's canonical layout equals trust-ir's
`enum_layout_shape` on tag width, size, alignment, payload offset and every
variant field's offset and size (`EnumCanonicalLayoutDisagrees` otherwise); a
packed or declared-padding payload without a descriptor therefore stays
refused. The instruction names no variant, so every variant with a field of
the projected type there must place it at the same offset; otherwise the
projection is refused (`EnumProjectionOffsetAmbiguous`) rather than dispatched
on the tag. A projection whose active variant is not such a candidate reads
another variant's bytes, which trust-ir defines as undefined behaviour.
Refused by name (`[TCG-DIRECT-ENUM]`): duplicate or overflowing discriminants,
a repr too narrow for its values, 128-bit tag lanes, and a descriptor whose
tag or fields overlap, misalign or leave the image. `InsertField` on a
direct-tag enum is refused: element 0 would re-tag the value, which trust-ir
makes undefined behaviour (`EnumTagWriteUnsupported`), and a payload element
stays refused (`EnumPayloadInsertUnsupported`) because the value-semantic
insert that struct, array and sequence values use is not wired to the
direct-tag carrier. Flat `GEP` indices stride the whole enum image without selecting a
variant or payload field. Native evidence is `e2e_aarch64_direct_enums.rs` on
aarch64-apple-darwin at O0-O3 against a C driver and the trust-ir reference
interpreter; it is execution evidence for those shapes, not a proof of enum
semantics, and the 68-module corpus counts quoted in older comments have not
been re-measured in this repository.

`InsertField` and `InsertElement` on an aggregate value give their result
storage of its own. The adapter copies the source into a fresh stack slot
and writes the member there. It reuses the source's slot only when a
`Const`, `Load` or insert allocated that slot for the source alone and the
insert, in the same block, is the source's only use. Aggregate block
parameters own their storage, and every edge copies the argument's bytes
into it, so a loop-carried value never names a slot that a later iteration
rewrites. A zero-sized value (`()`, an empty struct) owns its slot but has
no bytes to copy, and none of these paths emits a copy for it. An
`InsertField` whose operand is not a value of the aggregate type, such as
a pointer to it (the "store form", which trust-ir's validator and
interpreter reject), is refused as `AggregateInsertNotValueForm`; the rustc
bridge writes a field as `GEP` + `Store` instead. Until 2026-09-23 every
insert stored into its source's storage, so
`swap(s) = insert(insert(s, 0, s.1), 1, s.0)` returned `{s.1, s.1}`, and an
aggregate `Load` re-executed in a loop overwrote the value its block
parameter still held. `e2e_aarch64_aggregate_insert_linux.rs` executes 27
such shapes against a C oracle at O0-O3 on aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu; that
is execution evidence for those shapes, not a proof.

A composite argument larger than 16 bytes that is not an HFA/HVA is passed
by reference (AAPCS64 B.4; DarwinPCS keeps the rule), and the callee may
write the memory it receives. On AArch64 the trust-ir adapter passes every
such argument of a direct, variadic, invoke or indirect call, fixed or
anonymous, as a pointer to storage the callee may own: the value's own slot
when a `Const`, `Load` or insert made that slot for it alone, the call is
its only use and it is defined in the same block; otherwise a fresh frame
slot, aligned to the type (at least 8), filled by a `Memcpy`. The argument's
type is its parameter's for a fixed argument and its own trust-ir type
otherwise (a function or block parameter forwarded as an anonymous argument
has no other). Selection inlines a copy of at most 32 bytes and calls
`memcpy` above that, so code size and compile time do not grow with the
aggregate. Every copy site has a slot of its own (64 calls in a block
passing a 1 KiB value use 64 KiB of frame), and the frame epilogue still
releases a large frame in 4,080-byte steps. An invoke with such an argument
moves into a block of its own after the copy, because its protected block
may hold only one call; the landing pad cannot observe a partial copy. A
call that passes a caller-frame slot in tail position keeps its `BL`.
Instruction selection copies an aggregate-typed by-reference argument only
when it reaches selection unconverted: from another LIR producer, or an
argument whose type the adapter cannot determine. It copies inline up to 256
bytes and refuses a larger one (`[TCG-BYREF-COPY]`). DarwinPCS anonymous
by-reference arguments stay refused (`[TCG-VARARG-ABI]`), and so does an
invoke of a variadic callee under any convention but base AAPCS64: an
invoke carries no fixed-argument count or variadic flag, so its anonymous
arguments would be placed as named ones, in registers where DarwinPCS puts
them on the stack, and on x86-64 without the `AL` count SysV requires (base
AAPCS64 places both kinds alike, so Linux variadic invokes are lowered). The
adapter admits such an invoke only when its TLS dialect names AAPCS64 and the
module's declared triple, when it has one, selects AAPCS64 too (OD-56). A
trust-cg callee uses the caller's
copy as its parameter's storage and never writes it. Until 2026-09-23 the
caller passed the address of the value's own storage; the first repair
copied inline in selection without a size limit (a 72,000-byte argument took
47 s to compile at O1), and its replacement at first refused a function or
block parameter over 256 bytes forwarded as an anonymous argument.
`e2e_aarch64_large_aggregate_args_linux.rs` executes 23 such shapes against
C callees, and 6 invoke shapes (2 of them variadic) against C++ callees that
also throw, all of which write every by-reference parameter, at O0-O3 on
aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu. On Darwin, named by-reference arguments execute in
both directions against Apple clang in `e2e_aarch64_aggregate_stack_darwin`,
but only with callees that read them; callees that write their parameter,
the invoke shapes and the copy decisions are covered by object, refusal,
tail-branch, code-size and selection-level rows, not by execution.

Compile time grows faster than linearly with the number of calls in one
block at O1-O3 (1,000 scalar calls in one block: 14.2 s and 495 MB at O2;
500 calls in one block each copying a 40-byte argument with `memcpy`: 18.2
s, measured by an independent verifier on 2026-09-23). This predates the
by-reference copies, which add one call per copied argument; it is not
fixed.

A homogeneous floating-point or short-vector aggregate is recognized over its
flattened members, at most four. A zero-sized member (an empty struct, `()`
or a non-empty array of them) contributes no member, and a zero-length array
member makes the aggregate non-homogeneous, which is how GCC 13 on Linux
AArch64 and clang classify them. Until 2026-09-23 a struct with more than
four declared fields was never homogeneous, so `struct { double a; struct {}
z; double b, c, d; }` went by reference where GCC uses d0-d3, and a
zero-length array member was ignored. rustc ignores a Rust `[T; 0]` field
instead of disqualifying the aggregate; trust-cg follows the C ABI there, so
such a Rust type is classified differently from rustc's own placement.
`e2e_aarch64_hfa_zero_sized_linux.rs` checks nine such shapes in both
directions, as arguments and returns, against GCC at O0-O3 on Linux; Darwin
is covered by object and classification rows only.

Module-scoped `Ty::Refine` inputs are validated with trust-ir's refinement
rules. trust-cg lowers the representation-identical base carrier only for the
identity/signature pass-through subset; most ordinary operations that consume
refined values still fail closed. The predicate is not optimization authority,
including with `lattice-guard-elision`: the shared replay gate rejects
declarations, and no RefinementType rechecker exists yet. Declared external
and loaded indices keep their bounds guards; see the
authority regression record.
Narrow signed/unsigned call and return extensions now use the representation,
including direct/indirect register arguments and Darwin's recorded FFI extension
refusal. Refined GEP indices retain the pinned TrustIR `GepIndexNotInteger`
verdict; refined volatile I128/U128 accesses retain the bare adapter refusal.
The erasure hazard record
records failing-first cases and the remaining C-04 steps.
Table-only type helpers reject refinements because they lack the containing
module needed for validation. Recursive type-table expansion is capped at 128
levels and fails closed beyond that limit.

The v41 input schema carries codegen requirements that this backend cannot yet
honor everywhere. AOT, JIT, Wasm and public lowering entry points reject module
assembly and naked function bodies. Function-specific target features are
refused on the Wasm lane and outside each target's modeled vocabulary; on
AArch64 a modeled list is admitted for that function alone (see Targets and
object formats, AArch64). Global
symbol facts depend on the object path. A global definition's hidden or
protected visibility is consumed, not rejected: the AArch64 ELF emitters spell
it `STV_HIDDEN`/`STV_PROTECTED` on strong, weak and COMDAT (`LinkOnce`,
`LinkOnceOdr`, `WeakOdr`) definitions, data and thread-local alike (object
rows under every relocation model, and native rows for `pic` shared
objects), and the Mach-O emitters spell hidden as `N_PEXT` (Mach-O has no
protected visibility). An `Internal`/`Private` global with a stated hidden
or protected visibility is emitted `STB_LOCAL` `STV_DEFAULT`, which binds
no differently. A data import's hidden or protected visibility is spelled
on its undefined symbol by the AArch64 ELF module path only, which addresses it through the GOT like every undefined
reference; every other entry refuses it (`ImportVisibilityUnsupported`), as
the AArch64 ELF path does for an `Internal`/`Private` thread-local import. An
explicit section is placed or refused by name by the AArch64 object emitters
and refused on every other architecture, and retention is honored on a
definition (ELF: the definition alone in a section of its own flagged
`SHF_GNU_RETAIN`, as llc places an `@llvm.used` global; Mach-O
`N_NO_DEAD_STRIP`). On an import (a declaration LLVM lists in
`@llvm.used`) the AArch64 and x86-64 ELF emitters write nothing for it, as
llc's ELF writer does. The RISC-V path, which emits no module data, compiles
an unreferenced one and writes nothing for it either (a referenced one fails
at its instruction selection, as every data reference there does). The
AArch64 and x86-64 Mach-O emitters, the x86-64 COFF emitter, the JIT data
image and the Wasm lane refuse it: llc's Mach-O writer gives such a
declaration an `N_NO_DEAD_STRIP` undefined symbol and its COFF writer a
`/INCLUDE:` linker directive (`.drectve`), even when nothing references it
(before the L02-P13 second closure-audit repair's verifier round every
object path refused it, where llc compiles it). Bodies
marked `BodyGate::Ungated` are rejected. A `BodyGate::Gated` body is admitted
only when its authority is recognized AND trust-ir's own license layer finds
its evidence (roadmap WS7.5): the one default-recognized authority,
`clean-kernel-tv`, is evidence-bound and needs exactly one `Certified`
TranslationValidation row whose kernel certificate replays against the current
body (a missing, pending, ambiguous, corrupted or stale certificate is refused
as `GatedWithoutEvidence`; a `Failed` row about the body as
`GatedFunctionRefuted`). Any other authority is rejected unless the caller
names it (`--recognize-authority`), and such a name-only authority carries no
evidence rule here: an authority string alone never licenses a body by
default. Legacy bodies with no body-gate metadata are REFUSED by default; the
CLI compiles them only under the explicit `--permit-unlicensed`, which prints
the admitted bodies, and the in-process producers (the rustc MIR lane, the JIT
kernel matrix, the LLVM importer, the fuzz harness) and the bench tools that
replay claim-less corpora do so under named, counted exceptions until they
stamp a license of their own. A license binds to the
module's certificate, not yet to a body digest carried in the gate itself
(trust-ir WS1.12(c) is not on the wire). Bodyless
declarations have no local body to consume. These checks also run when a caller
supplies a previously complete IR validation report, and before AOT/JIT cache
use. Refusals carry the diagnostic marker `[TCG-CODEGEN-METADATA]`.

Dialect legalization (`L05-P11`): every `Compiler` entry (AOT `compile`,
`compile_module_to_jit`) legalizes trust-ir dialect constructs before the
adapter, through a `DialectLegalizationRegistry`
(`crates/trust-cg-codegen/src/dialect_legalization.rs`;
`Compiler::with_dialect_legalization_registry` replaces the default). A
registration names a namespace, its schema version, who defines its semantics,
its payload grammar (trust-ir's exact `OperationSchema`s, checked against the
module's SSA types by trust-ir-build, or a dialect-owned validator), one rule per
declared op and one carrier rule per nominal type. A malformed registration is
refused when the registry is built (`[TCG-DIALECT-REGISTRATION]`), including an
evidence class its lowering cannot rest on. A `DialectOp` or `Ty::Dialect` whose
namespace, op, or type name and version no registration declares is refused by
exact name (`[TCG-DIALECT-UNREGISTERED]`); a payload that violates its grammar
is refused as `[TCG-DIALECT-GRAMMAR]`. Op rules keep the op for the adapter's
typed arm, rewrite it through trust-ir's own `lower_module` driver (which
refuses a node carrying an unmapped semantic marker or call contract), call a
named runtime entry with the op's whole payload as a read-only descriptor, or
refuse with a stated reason (`[TCG-DIALECT-UNBOUND]`). A nominal type is
replaced by the core integer or pointer carrier its registration declares,
which is also its native ABI; the substitution is admitted only when
trust-ir's nominal rule holds (no `InvalidDialectType`: only exact-typed
transport and dialect ops touch the value), no dialect op spells or consumes a
nominal type of another namespace (this backend is stricter than trust-ir
there; `[TCG-DIALECT-NOMINAL]` for either), and no `Ty::Dialect` survives. A
runtime call passes a nominal operand or result as its carrier: the
declaration the legalization adds is spelled in carriers, and an existing
declaration of the symbol is reused only when its signature, with carriers
substituted, is exactly the binding's. The legalized
module is re-validated by trust-ir-build (a finding the source did not have
refuses it) and then takes exactly the core path: the same adapter,
instruction evidence, proof promotion and object or JIT emission.

Each applied rule leaves a receipt on `CompilationResult::dialect_legalization`
and `JitCompilationResult::dialect_legalization` (and in the CLI's metrics
JSON): the dialect, its version, the owner statement, the op (with its payload
version) or type (with its carrier), the rule id, the rule's evidence class,
the source site (for a type, its number of occurrences in the source module),
and digests of what was replaced and what replaced it (the replacement nodes
exactly as they sit in the legalized module, diagnostic span and scope
included), with the registry's digest. That digest covers the registrations'
declared content but identifies validators, guards and rewrite functions only
by name: it cannot see their code, so an equal digest does not show that the
same rules ran. `verify_legalization` replays a legalization under a registry
and names any edited, dropped, added or reordered field, and a module the
replay does not reproduce; the replay is what compares the rules' effect. A
receipt records which rule ran and what that rule rests on; it is not a
proof.

A proof-required compile (`emit_proofs`, or on its own a verifying JIT
validation mode, `CachedVerified` or `AlwaysVerify`, which is x86-64's JIT
default) admits only the two evidence classes the compile itself checks: an op kept
for the adapter (it then carries the same instruction evidence as any core
instruction) and the checked carrier substitution. Every other rule is refused
by name before anything is rewritten (`[TCG-DIALECT-PROOF]`): a rewrite through
trust-ir's `VectorLoweringPass` (its Lean refinement theorem is cited by name
and not replayed here, and the correspondence of the Rust pass to the
modelled one is not checked), the per-lane `vector.fma` rule (tested only),
and a runtime call (the runtime owns the meaning).

The default registry declares trust-ir's `vector` dialect, trust-cg's typed
`trust-cg` bitfield/mask-extract and `trust-cg-aarch64-fp` ops, and the `verif`
v1 payload contract. `vector.pack_lanes`/`extract_lane`/`insert_lane`, the
typed ops, and `vector.mask_to_bits` of a compare result or canonical constant
stay with the adapter exactly as before (such a module reaches the adapter
unchanged, so its bytes are unchanged). `vector.reduce` and `vector.shuffle`
on the 128-bit integer lane vectors are rewritten by trust-ir's
`VectorLoweringPass`, and `vector.fma` on `<4 x f32>`/`<2 x f64>` becomes one
`trust-cg-aarch64-fp.fmadd` per lane. All three rewrites are admitted for
AArch64 only and refused by name on any other target (`[TCG-DIALECT-TARGET]`):
`fma` emits AArch64 typed ops, and the target-independent `reduce`/`shuffle`
output has been executed only on AArch64, so x86-64 and RISC-V keep the
refusal the adapter gave these ops before the registry existed. Refused by
name: `mask_to_bits` of any other mask (a bool-lane vector
crosses parameters, returns and block parameters only as an opaque register
value and never reaches memory, so this backend has no lane image to read;
`AdapterError::BoolLaneLayoutNotAdmitted`), `reduce`/`shuffle` of the 64-bit
`<8 x i8>` (the adapter lowers no single-lane extract or insert there), and
every `verif` op. `verif` v1 names no runtime symbol and trust-ir's reference
lowering calls a hard-coded function id, so the default registry no longer
applies that illustrative lowering (which erased `frontier_drain` and called
function 0 for `bfs_step`); a caller binds a runtime with
`DialectRegistration::bind_runtime_call`. No nominal type is registered by
default.

The pinned corpus's four dialect rows are executed natively on this host
(`crates/trust-cg-codegen/tests/dialect_legalization_corpus.rs`: AOT objects
linked with a C driver and in-process JIT, O0-O3), each against an
interpretation that does not go through the legalization. `inst_vector_crosslane`
and a per-op sweep of every rewritten op and admitted shape (fma cases chosen to
tell one rounding from two and `a*b+c` from a permutation) run against
trust-ir's reference interpreter. `inst_vector_dialect` is refused by name for
its two `<8 x bool>`/`<16 x bool>` parameter masks; the same row without those
two sites runs against the interpreter. `inst_dialect` (an opaque `verif.bfs_step`
payload with every attribute kind) fails the default registry's `verif` v1
grammar; bound to a test runtime, it runs against a reading of the source
payload. `ty_dialect_v39` runs under a test registration that gives
`example.value@1` an `i64` carrier, and its object is byte-identical to the
hand-written core twin's at every level, with an identical proof-required
verdict. A test dialect's runtime call over a nominal `ptr`-carried operand
runs AOT and JIT against the cell's contents and a descriptor length counted
by hand. This is native differential testing on one host; the Linux arm of
the target has not run. Registrations other than the default one are the
caller's claims about their dialects: the backend checks their grammar,
naming and evidence class, not their meaning. The adapter's own refusals of
`Ty::Dialect` and of an unhandled `DialectOp` remain as the backstop for
paths that skip this stage (for example a direct `trust_cg_lower` call).

The `DialectModule` machine-emission hook is a small facade, separate from the
main trust-ir compiler path. Its four-op I64 `machir` subset accepts a single
block, I64 parameters and a void or I64 return; block arguments/references,
multiple blocks and other ABI parameter types are rejected. Conversion preserves
multi-block layout but does not schedule forward operation-result uses.
Full-width constants now expand into MOVZ/MOVK, and explicit transfers implement
register/stack arguments and the X0 result convention. Focused tests run emitted
bytes through allocation, frame lowering and encoding, under an interpreter and
natively on macOS ARM64. These bounded fixtures do not cover arbitrary register
pressure, every target ABI, or complete dialect semantics. The sample fingerprint
and BFS conversions implement their documented PoC formulas, not real hashing or
graph traversal algorithms.

`Constant::Bytes` requires an exact `[u8; N]` type, matching length, and a
valid optional UTF-8 claim. Body lowering supports it at the top level and
nested inside the already admitted struct, tuple, array, record and direct-tag
enum constants, using the parent's existing layout and stack allocation.
Typed global initialization supports byte-array leaves within its existing
struct, tuple and array layouts, preserving padding and relocation offsets.
Module batching checks byte leaves against their resolved types; this is
capability admission, not proof authority. A byte-string payload of a niche
enum body constant goes through the niche encoder above. Direct-tag
enum-typed globals are rendered from the same `DirectEnumImage` the code path
addresses (the tag word as the discriminant value, each field of the named
variant at the image's offset, nested aggregates, byte strings and symbol
addresses included) and record-typed globals at the natural-C layout the byte
path emits for records, from a positional aggregate or a `Constant::Record`;
niche- and untagged-enum globals and untyped Bytes switch cases remain outside
this extension. The trust-ir reference interpreter has no byte layout for
records, so a record global is checked natively against its closed form only.
The legacy direct-object top-level Bytes path still accepts raw images for
some non-array carriers; that compatibility route does not gain typed batching
admission or establish canonical TrustIR validity.

The imported global-address compatibility ABI reserves the positive bit-pattern
interval `0xFADE_0000_0000_0000..0xFADF_0000_0000_0000` only in top-level
function-body `Constant::Int` values declared as a supported thin
pointer/reference carrier (`Ty::Ptr`, `Ty::Ref`, `Ty::RefMut`, `Ty::PtrConst`,
or `Ty::PtrMut`) or the legacy `Ty::I64` address carrier. In `Ty::U64`,
`Ty::U128`, `Ty::Usize`, and other declared types, the same bit patterns remain
ordinary numeric data. `Ty::Rc` and `Ty::Func` are not stub carriers. Nested
constants and switch cases are never decoded as address stubs; module batching
fails closed on tag-shaped values in those untyped positions rather than
guessing.

The text and JSON formats are review/debug surfaces in this release. Binary
tMBC is the canonical tool-to-tool input, but none of these formats has a
promised long-term compatibility window yet. Round-trip evidence is test-rung,
never proof: `trust_ir_corpus_roundtrip` drives every module of the pinned
trust-ir conformance corpus (live goldens, `compat/`, `v41-reader-compat/`
and the must-refuse rows, in tMBC, JSON, text and MessagePack) through
trust-cg's readers and writers against trust-ir's reader and the independent
MessagePack codec, and `tmbc_roundtrip_prop` generates aggregates, enums,
records, closures, collections, globals/TLS, handles, refinements, dialect
constructs, proof/lineage tables and v41-v50 metadata. Named residuals there:
trust-cg admits no MessagePack input; the pinned writer has no tMBC image for
`MakeAggregate`, `MemCopy`/`MemSet`, the `CtLz`/`CtTz`/`BSwap`/`BitReverse`
and `RotL`/`RotR`/`FCopySign` ops, an inlining-chain scope link or a
completeness claim (`encode_tmbc` refuses them, `NoTmbcWireImage`); a zero- or
one-copy `Constant::Splat` is written by every writer and refused by every
reader; text refuses by its `#lossy` marker whatever `text_losses` reports
(function summaries, clause bindings, spec carriers, custom obligation kinds,
kernel rechecks, enum field names, contradicting enum layouts, record field
offsets, `global_asm`, trailing parameter attributes); and JSON and text carry
no wire version, so a module whose tMBC form the reader refuses as a producer
omission (a v41+ header with an unstamped body) decodes from JSON or text,
where only the codegen license stands before code: the default refuses it
(`UnlicensedBodyPolicy::Refuse`), and an explicit `Permit` admits it.

Volatile scalar loads and stores use distinct side-effecting machine opcodes on
the AArch64 and x86-64 paths for the supported integer, floating-point, and
128-bit vector widths. Volatile `I128`/`U128` is deliberately rejected: those
values use two 64-bit GPR limbs, and splitting one source-level volatile event
into two architectural accesses would be observably wrong for MMIO. This
restriction is separate from atomicity; the broader atomic and memory-ordering
surface remains incomplete.

`Inst::Switch` over `I128`/`U128` selectors lowers by splitting the selector
into its 64-bit halves: a compare tree over the distinct high halves of the
case constants guards one 64-bit `Switch` per high half, so a case dispatches
only when both halves match. The dispatch is built from already-lowered
primitives (i128 truncation and constant shift, 64-bit compare/branch, the
64-bit switch strategies) and carries no new proof form of its own; its
evidence is the macOS-native clang differential
(`e2e_aarch64_i128_switch`), whose Linux arm has not yet executed. The i128
and u128 checked multiply does not compute a 256-bit product: it emits the low
product and, on AArch64, the guarded `__udivti3`/`__divti3` division identity,
on x86-64 the division-free limb check (OD-224: two `I64` `CheckedUmul`s, a
carry compare and a both-high-limbs test, on the magnitudes plus a sign check
for `i128`). The registered `checked_mul_i128_proofs` family states both flag
idioms and the `MUL; UMULH; MADD; MADD` low-product chain against the exact
256-bit product reconstructed from 64-bit limbs, discharged by the sampling
evaluator plus a native-oracle boundary battery with every negative control
refuted (the limb check's controls are the OD-224 design's mutants); that is
regression evidence, not a formal proof. The limb check's scaled analogs (8
bits with 4-bit limbs, 16 bits with 8-bit limbs) are swept exhaustively over
the adapter's actual output, evidence for those widths only. The family does
not state the Arm ARM semantics of decoded captured encoder words, does not
cover the runtime division library of the AArch64 form, and the per-compile
verifier still binds an emitted UMULH to the 64-bit `CheckedUmul_I64`
obligation. AArch64 keeps the division form until an AArch64 host runs the
OD-224 controls there (OD-224 names them).

Every AArch64 function compiled from a lowered source (each preparation and
the one-shot `compile_to_object` route) checks that its final machine stream
performs the lowered source's volatile loads and stores on every path, in the
same order and number, by direction and size
(`volatile_access_preservation`), and fails closed otherwise. Prebuilt-MachIR
routes have no lowered source and are not checked, and the machine control
flow is read from successor metadata rather than from the resolved branch
words. The check does
not compare addresses or values, so exchanging two volatile accesses of the
same direction and size is not detected, and it assumes every source CFG edge
can be taken: a transformation that removes a path around a volatile access
(a resolved constant branch or constant trip count) is refused rather than
accepted. The optimizer observed today keeps such paths. The six AArch64
volatile rows of the opcode inventory remain RED because the dereferenced
value and store effect share the plain load/store rows' missing memory model;
the x86-64 volatile rows are not wired to this check.

x86-64 128-bit atomic loads (`AtomicU128`/`AtomicI128::load`, core's
`atomic_load::<u128/i128>`) lower to one pseudo-instruction,
`AtomicLoadCmpxchg16b`, which the encoder expands to `XOR EAX,EAX; XOR EDX,EDX;
XOR EBX,EBX; XOR ECX,ECX; LOCK CMPXCHG16B m128` — LLVM's own lowering on a
CX16 target. The zeroing is part of the pseudo rather than separate
instructions, so no pass can delete or rewrite one of the zeros apart from the
compare-exchange; the reconstruction models the whole expansion over arbitrary
incoming register values (a model missing any one XOR, or clearing only the
low 32, 16 or 8 bits of one, refutes), and ENC-3 decodes all five emitted
instructions per compile. The reconstruction is keyed on the opcode and never
sees a byte, so that the emitted zeroing is four bare zero-extending
`XOR r32,r32` rests on that decode check alone; `x86_encoding_gate` and
`reconstruction_x86` exercise it in the pre-push gate. The reconstruction's
source side is fixed to the trust-ir `AtomicLoad`; what ties the pseudo to that
LIR instruction is TV-2's shared atomic op class plus the selector refusing
every other 128-bit atomic, not an operand binding. The instruction writes the
value back, so the load writes memory and faults on a read-only mapping or on
an address that is not 16-byte aligned, exactly as the LLVM-compiled load does.
It is admitted only in a trust-ir function that claims the `cmpxchg16b` target
feature; the rustc bridge states that claim only where rustc's target spec
guarantees CX16 (x86_64-apple-darwin's `penryn` baseline, the Windows and
Fuchsia specs' `+cmpxchg16b`) and neither a `-C target-cpu` override nor a
feature entry removes it: `-cmpxchg16b`, the LLVM names `-cx16` and `-cx8`
(LLVM's `cx16` implies `cx8`, so `-cx8` alone makes LLVM emit the
`__atomic_load_16` libcall), and any negative entry rustc does not recognize
(it reaches LLVM verbatim) are refused, in `-C target-feature` and in a custom
target spec's features alike. That
admission is deliberately narrower than LLVM (`-C target-cpu=native` or
`haswell` is refused although LLVM has CX16 there); the bridge's
`cfg(target_feature = "cmpxchg16b")` is computed separately, to match LLVM's.
Every other x86-64 function with a 128-bit atomic is refused before selection
(`[TCG-ATOMIC128-CX16]`), and a 128-bit atomic store, swap, read-modify-write
or compare-exchange is refused by name. The frame saves the callee-saved RBX
the pseudo clobbers. Since slice 21 (OD-201) the x86-64 source-bound body
theorem binds the pseudo row as the load's two halves, so a function
containing it can earn Formal credit through that lane (the trust it adds is
stated there). Outside a bound body the row is credited jointly: its address by the
byte-level address lane, its value by a sampled reconstruction (the
zero-comparand load over incoming registers, plus the bare CMPXCHG16B
transcription against the trust-ir compare-exchange; eleven facets). Under the
x86-64 E0.2 rule sampled evidence earns no per-compile credit, so a
proof-required compile of a function containing it is still refused
(`[TCG-PROOF-465]`) like every other x86-64 function without a source-bound
lane. Atomicity and ordering rest on the Intel SDM LOCK axiom like every other
x86-64 atomic row, and the binding of the two read-back copies to RAX and RDX
is the post-allocation dataflow model's, not an obligation.

The x86-64 reconstruction address-teeth audit is semantic: an obligation
rebuilt at a perturbed address operand must evaluate `Invalid` to count as
address evidence. No memory reconstruction does, because every one derives
both of its addresses from the emitted operand. The narrow `Cmpxchg8` and
`Cmpxchg16` rows had been recorded as having address teeth by a structural
test (their two sides are different expressions at every operand); their
address is now carried by the byte-level lane, like the other 53 memory rows.

On an LSE profile every atomic load narrower than 128 bits lowers to `LDAR*`
and every atomic store to `STLR*` whatever the requested ordering (`Relaxed` is
strengthened, never weakened), and RMW and compare-exchange use the LSE forms;
a profile without LSE uses the LL/SC loops described below.
`e2e_aarch64_concurrency` runs contended multi-thread controls on macOS arm64
and, registered in the Linux floor, on Linux GNU: eight threads on every RMW
op at 8/16/32/64 bits and a CAS-loop counter, checked for linearizable old
values and exact finals against a C `__atomic` lane and a Rust
`std::sync::atomic` oracle; a CAS/store-release spinlock; a message-passing
litmus (CG release/acquire and seq-cst around plain data accesses) and
perpetual store-buffering (CG seq-cst) and load-buffering (CG release/acquire
and seq-cst) litmus runs that never showed their forbidden outcome over 2^20
and 2^18 iterations per run, beside C relaxed controls that did show the
weak store-buffering outcome; and three waves of eight threads checking TLS
initialization, identity and isolation. On Apple M-series hardware the
message-passing and load-buffering relaxed controls almost never show their
weak outcome, and no native workload observes RMW or compare-exchange
ordering bits, so the same test decodes every executed atomic function and
pins its LSE op, access size and ordering form (`AL` RMW, `CASAL`, `LDAR`,
`STLR`), with mutation controls that strip one ordering at a time. The litmus
runs are testing evidence on one host, not a memory-model proof, and the Linux
arm has not run on a Linux host. Which C11/Rust ordering each selected form
implements is checked by the memory-order mapping below.

Memory-order mapping (L03-P3). `trust_cg_verify::aarch64_memory_order` states
the C11/Rust -> AArch64 mapping as requirements on decoded words: an acquiring
read is a load-acquire or is followed by a barrier ordering R->R and R->W; a
releasing write is a store-release or follows a barrier ordering R->W and
W->W; a SeqCst read is an RCsc load-acquire (`LDAR`, never `LDAPR`) or follows
a full barrier, and a SeqCst write is a store-release or is followed by a full
barrier; a fence's barriers order every access pair the fence orders (Acquire
R->R and R->W; Release R->W and W->W; AcqRel those three; SeqCst all four) in
a domain that reaches other threads. Its inverse table
(`orderings_implemented`) lists the orderings each decoded form implements:
`LDAR` every load ordering, `LDAPR` Relaxed and Acquire but not SeqCst,
`LD<op>`/`LD<op>A`/`LD<op>L`/`LD<op>AL` and the exclusive loops by their
`A`/`L` bits, `CASA` every compare-exchange pair without a release, `DMB ISHLD`
the Acquire fence, `DMB ISH` every fence, and `DMB ISHST` none.
`aarch64_memory_order_obligations`
compiles every request the selector admits (load, store, the ten RMW ops,
compare-exchange at all 15 valid (success, failure) pairs, fences; Bool
through 128 bits) on the Darwin AOT (LSE, LSE2), LSE and baseline (LL/SC)
profiles at O0-O3, decodes each function with the module's own decoder, and
requires the form to conform and to equal the pinned selection (4,800 rows).
It refuses by name the words a selector defect would emit (the old `DMB ISHST`
release fence, `LDAR` -> `LDAPR` for SeqCst, a dropped `A` or `L` bit, an
`LD<op>A` whose destination is `XZR`, LLVM's FEAT_LSE2 `ldp; dmb ish` SeqCst
load), checks the compare-exchange failure-ordering lift over all 25 pairs
(covering and minimal), and compares the fence and 128-bit load barriers with
Apple clang's. It found two selector defects, both fixed: a Release fence was
`DMB ISHST`, which orders only W->W, so an earlier load could be satisfied
after a later store (now `DMB ISH`, LLVM's choice); and the FEAT_LSE2 SeqCst
128-bit load was `LDP; DMB ISH`, which is not ordered after this backend's
SeqCst store-releases (`STLR`, the 128-bit `STLXP` loop), so the
store-buffering outcome SeqCst forbids was allowed (now
`DMB ISH; LDP; DMB ISH`, one barrier more than LLVM, whose same form has the
same exposure to an earlier `STLR`). Orderings without a mapping row (Release
and AcqRel loads, Acquire and AcqRel stores and failure orderings, a Relaxed
fence) are refused before any word is emitted. trust-ir has no single-thread
fence, so `compiler_fence` gets the hardware barrier of `fence`: stronger than
it needs, never weaker.

What the mapping check establishes is mapping conformance, exhaustive over the
selector's request space on those profiles and decided from the emitted words.
The ordering contribution of each instruction (ARM DDI 0487, B2.3) is
delegated, as it is for the value obligations, and the soundness of the
mapping for whole C11/Rust programs is the published compilation-correctness
result for it (for example IMM, POPL 2019), not re-checked here. It is not a
formal axiomatic memory-model proof, and no Clean certificate covers it. It
does not cover the optimizer moving plain accesses across ordered ones; that
rests on the effects model (load-acquires, `Call`-class barriers and
exclusives) and on the litmus runs.

`e2e_aarch64_memory_order_litmus` runs MP, SB, LB, IRIW and 2+2W litmus tests
natively on macOS arm64 at O0-O3, every thread body a trust-cg function:
release/acquire, SeqCst, Acquire/Release/AcqRel/SeqCst fences around plain
accesses, release/acquire and SeqCst RMWs, a release compare-exchange read
back through an acquire failure ordering, 128-bit and mixed 64/128-bit SeqCst,
and LL/SC. None showed a forbidden outcome. On this M4 the plain MP and SB
controls showed their weak outcomes in roughly 16% and 5% of rounds, the plain
IRIW and 2+2W controls showed theirs, and an inline-assembly replica of the
pre-fix SeqCst 128-bit pair showed the SB outcome SeqCst forbids in three of
four runs (0, 1, 4,501 and 8,512 of 2^20 rounds; the rate varies with load). No load-buffering outcome appeared, even for a
replica of the old `DMB ISHST` release fence, so that fix rests on the
word-level check. Testing evidence on one host; the native runs are
macOS-only.

## Targets and object formats

### AArch64

AArch64 has active AOT and JIT paths with Mach-O and ELF support. Coverage is
incomplete for platform ABI differences, aggregates, relocations and their
proof authority, TLS models, unwind/exception handling, debug info, atomics,
SIMD/NEON, target features, and full instruction selection.

NEON (ledger L04-P6). The `neon_semantics` models every NEON obligation's
machine side uses are checked against the CPU by
`trust-cg-verify/tests/aarch64_neon_silicon_differential.rs`: every form the
encoder admits that has a value model, for each of the 60 NEON value opcodes
the coverage gate audits (1,294 modeled forms: every arrangement, lane,
element size, immediate, shift amount and destination class), runs on this
CPU and is compared with its model, exhaustively for byte lanes and over
edge-value triples plus random vectors otherwise (about 3.3 million vectors).
Integer lanes and non-NaN FP lanes match bit for bit. An FP lane where both
the model and the CPU produce a NaN counts as a match by class, because the
model returns the default NaN and the CPU propagates payloads. 5,936 such
lanes, all in FP ops, are counted this way. No model disagreed otherwise. The
encoder admits 29 more forms that have no value model and no emitter: REV64
`.8B`, and DUP element into a `D` register at 8-, 16- and 32-bit lanes. They
are pinned, and their lane-effect decompositions are run on the CPU too. This
is testing evidence on one macOS arm64 host; the Linux floor registers the
target but it has not run on a Linux host. ADDP (scalar, `.2D`) has a model, a
faithful cross-lane obligation and coverage-gate credit (one of the 267
accepted rows of 302). No
lowering selects it yet, so it is the one row of the 302 audited value rows
that nothing emits today. The horizontal reductions and permutes (DUP, INS,
UMOV, DUP `Dd`, UMAXV, ADDP, REV32, REV64, RBIT, EXT, MOVI) and the four
post-index transfers (LD1/ST1, LDP/STP Q) carry word-bound decompositions
(`aarch64_neon_lane_effect`, `aarch64_memory_effect`) over the word ENC-5
binds. They are decided exactly in process: a refuted part fails the row;
otherwise the row is annotated, never credited. The lane-effect parts have no
live replay lane, so none is Clean-checked. Under the Formal-only
bound-memory rule the four post-index rows are credited by form-theorem
certificates (L04-P1): the LDP/STP `Q` rows by their pair forms, and the
LD1/ST1 rows by the fourteen `aarch64_neon_structure_forms` theorems
(LD1/ST1 x `8B`, `16B`, `4H`, `8H`, `2S`, `4S`, `2D`: the element loop of the
encoded fields against the operands' `LDR`/`STR Dt|Qt` intent, every
register byte or every memory byte around the transfer, and the writeback),
each with a committed DRAT certificate in its own set
(`verdict_db/neon_memory_certs/`) that the vendored `drat-trim` replays. The
walk credits an `LD1`/`ST1` instruction only when its memory-effect
decomposition held exactly (clause 2) and its word decodes to the bound form
(clause 3); the gate credits each opcode only when all seven arrangements
carry that authority and every machine defect (element order, big-endian
elements, the zeroed upper half, missing or wrong writeback, pre-index
access, an extra stored byte) refutes on a structured grid. Both sides of
every theorem were compared with this Apple M4
(`aarch64_neon_structure_silicon_differential`). The NEON set authorizes
only this host's checker, so no `LD1`/`ST1` row is credited on Linux until
that host replays the set.

The lowering front end now admits unsigned integer-lane vectors (`<16 x u8>`,
`<8 x u16>`, `<4 x u32>`, `<2 x u64>`) for wrapping Add/Sub/Mul, And/Or/Xor,
Neg/Not, compares feeding selects and, on `<4 x u32>`, shifts by a uniform
constant. It also admits `<8 x u8>` for the V64 And/Or/Xor and compares,
integer-lane constants of every 64-bit shape, and vector OR-NOT, which lowers
to NOT then ORR. Each constant lane is checked against its own lane type's
range, so a negative unsigned lane is refused. `e2e_aarch64_neon_admission`
runs all of these against clang -O3 NEON intrinsics at O0-O3, except the
`<8 x u8>` compare. That compare lowers to the `<8 x i8>` compare's typed op,
but nothing in TrustIR consumes its V64 mask in a way a native test can
observe, so only adapter tests cover it. Still refused by name: shifts on 8-,
16- and 64-bit lanes, V64 arithmetic, the operations of the other 64-bit
shapes, vector division and remainder, CtPop and lane extract/insert on
unsigned lanes, a select whose condition no same-shape compare produced, and
every vector conversion outside the vectorizers.

Variadic function definitions are refused on every lowering entry with
`[TCG-VARIADIC-DEFINITION]`. No `va_start`/`va_arg` lowering exists, neither the
AAPCS64 `va_list` record with its register save areas nor the DarwinPCS
`char *` cursor. Variadic calls remain supported when the callee declaration
states its fixed prefix. A call through a declaration that states none
(`params: []` with `is_vararg`, the `(...)` a producer writes for a C callee it
could not sign, or any variadic Rust-convention signature) is refused with
`[TCG-UNSIGNED-VARIADIC]`: DarwinPCS passes anonymous arguments on the stack
and fixed ones in registers, so no placement of its arguments is known. The
refusal also covers a genuine zero-fixed C23 `f(...)` call, which trust-ir
cannot tell apart from that placeholder (OD-55, OD-56). A non-variadic
`CallIndirect` whose callee pointer visibly names a variadic declaration (a
`FnDef` or `SymbolAddr` reached through copies and pointer casts) is refused
too: with `[TCG-UNSIGNED-VARIADIC]` for an unsigned declaration and
`[TCG-VARARG-ABI]` otherwise, because the edge places every argument as a
named one. A pointer that arrives through memory or a block parameter is not
traced. The LLVM importer carries each direct call's own function type: an
unprototyped `declare R @f(...)` takes the type its calls state when they all
state one, and a call whose fixed prefix or variadic tail differs from its
callee's signature is refused at import.
`byval` parameters are refused with `[TCG-BYVAL-ABI]` because no caller-copy
lowering exists. The sret, Swift-preparation and typed-install refusals keep
their own diagnostics.

Hidden-result (`sret`) results through X8 have two TrustIR shapes. A
structural `returns: [Struct]` that AAPCS64 classifies indirect is carried by
the function type itself, so direct, variadic and indirect calls (including a
pointer received from C) stage X8 and a CG callee saves X8 in its prologue. The
pre-lowered shape (`params: [Ptr sret, ...], returns: []`) exists only as
`ParamAttrs::sret` on a declared function in the pinned trust-ir; a `FuncTy`
and a `CallIndirect` carry no attribute. A direct call reads the callee's
declaration; an indirect call gets its identity only when trust-ir's typed
provenance (`Const FnDef` through `Copy` / `ReifyFnPointer`) resolves the
callee to such a declaration, and an edge that disagrees with it is refused
with `[TCG-SRET-ABI]`. A pre-lowered pointer that flows dynamically (a
parameter, a load) has no expressible identity and is lowered as the ordinary
call its signature declares; producers must use the structural shape for it.
Only a leading hidden parameter with an empty return list is admitted. Variadic
sret CALLS compose X8 with the fixed/anonymous rules; indirect calls over a
variadic signature and variadic definitions stay refused. Native evidence is
`e2e_aarch64_sret` (macOS, both directions, O0–O3); the Linux AAPCS64 arm has
no such target.
DarwinPCS anonymous `__int128`, 128-bit vector and 16-aligned non-homogeneous
aggregate arguments of up to 16 bytes use 16-aligned stack slots. A native clang
oracle checks this, and the tail's start after packed narrow fixed stack
arguments, at O0–O3 on macOS. Darwin anonymous aggregates that clang
passes by reference are refused with `[TCG-VARARG-ABI]`, as are short-vector
HVAs, because clang's own caller and `va_arg` disagree for them.

DarwinPCS named by-value composites on the stack follow clang's coercion: a
non-homogeneous composite of at most 16 bytes takes an 8-aligned slot (16 for
a 16-aligned one) of whole 8-byte words whatever its members' alignment, and
an HFA/HVA packs its members at their own alignment with no size rounding.
Until 2026-09-27 both took the composite's natural alignment and a size
rounded to 8, which disagreed with Apple clang behind packed narrow stack
arguments, and `Trunc` to `Bool` was a register move on AArch64 (ELF and
Mach-O), so `trunc(2)` was a true Bool holding 2 wherever it was branched on,
extended or passed. `e2e_aarch64_aggregate_stack_darwin`,
`e2e_aarch64_variadic_darwin` and `e2e_aarch64_bool_abi_darwin` execute the
Linux L01 aggregate-stack, variadic and Bool corpora with the DarwinPCS
packing, extension, odd-register, HFA and anonymous-argument rules against
Apple clang at O0-O3 on macOS, in both directions except where TrustCG would
be a variadic callee. That is execution evidence on one host.
`e2e_aarch64_large_aggregate_args_linux`, `e2e_aarch64_hfa_zero_sized_linux`
and `e2e_aarch64_f16_abi_linux` have no Darwin execution twin.

AArch64 atomics on a target profile without FEAT_LSE, including the generic
Linux AOT profile, lower through LL/SC retry loops. `AtomicRmw` (add, sub,
and, or, xor, xchg and signed/unsigned min/max at 8/16/32/64 bits) and
`CmpXchg` (Bool and 8/16/32/64 bits) select opaque pseudos that register
allocation treats as one instruction. They expand after allocation, spill
materialization and frame lowering into `LD{A}XR{B,H}` / ALU /
`ST{L}XR{B,H}` / `CBNZ` loops, so no spill or reload lands inside an
exclusive window. A compare-exchange failure exits through `CLREX`. Acquire
selects the load-acquire exclusive and release the store-release exclusive;
AcqRel and SeqCst use both, the armv8.0 mapping LLVM and GCC use, and a
compare-exchange lifts its success ordering to cover its failure ordering.
128-bit atomic store, read-modify-write and compare-exchange use
`LD{A}XP`/`ST{L}XP` pair loops on every profile, and so does a 128-bit load
except on a FEAT_LSE2 profile (Apple arm64), where it is one `LDP` with the
barriers of the memory-order mapping above; CASP is not used. An LL/SC 128-bit
load and a failed 128-bit compare-exchange store the loaded pair back, as the
armv8.0 single-copy-atomicity rule requires, so they write memory and fault on
read-only mappings. Bool read-modify-write admits
exchange, and, or and xor as byte atomics. Arithmetic and min/max on Bool
stay refused, as do atomics on vectors, floats and aggregates.

Single-instruction atomics (ledger `L04-P1`, `X-OPCODES-P2`). Every emitted
width of the 46 LSE and ordered atomic opcodes (`LDAR{,B,H}`, `STLR{,B,H}`,
`CAS*`, `SWP*`, `LD{ADD,CLR,EOR,SET,SMAX,SMIN,UMAX,UMIN}*`) has a form
theorem (`aarch64_atomic_forms`: 12 operations x 4 widths) stating the
returned old value at every register byte and the memory left at every query
address, over a chain-of-points memory, against the machine-IR intent. Each
of the 48 has a committed DRAT certificate in a separate set
(`verdict_db/atomic_memory_certs/`, produced by the Trust 9192 AY build 9624)
that the vendored `drat-trim` replays. Per instruction, the word the
verify-side encoder re-derives (which ENC-5 requires the emitted word to equal)
is decomposed into fields (the `A`/`R` ordering bits included), the returned
value and the 8-byte memory window it leaves (`aarch64_atomic_effect`), every
part decided exactly in process; the Formal-only rule credits the row only
when that held, the word decodes to the form, and the form's certificate
replays on a host whose checker the atomic manifest authorizes (this Darwin
host's only). The coverage gate credits each opcode only when every width's
form carries that authority, every machine defect of the form theorem
(wrong operation, swapped operands, signedness, max/min, short or extra
access, big-endian, displaced address, sign-extended or new returned value,
missing write, CAS writing on failure or comparing the whole register) is
refuted in process, and the word's ordering class is the opcode's own under
the `L03-P3` decoder. What is not claimed: single-copy atomicity and the
ordering against other threads (the architecture's guarantee and the `L03-P3`
mapping table, which is mapping conformance, not a memory-model proof);
alignment faults; the `ST<op>` aliases and a CAS whose compare register is
the zero register, which are refused (no credit); and any binding of the
instruction to a source atomic operation. The model was checked against an
Apple M4 by `aarch64_atomic_silicon_differential` (312 words, 124,800
executions, every byte of both theorem sides at sampled inputs; testing
evidence). The Linux checker is not authorized for the atomic set, so no
atomic row is credited on Linux until that host replays the set.

The backend neither emits nor requires the `__aarch64_*` outline-atomics
helpers (`__aarch64_ldadd8_relax`, `__aarch64_cas16_acq_rel`, ...) or
`__aarch64_have_lse_atomics`. A CG object has no link-time dependency on those
libgcc/compiler_builtins symbols and does no run-time LSE dispatch. LSE is
emitted only where the profile admits it (the Apple arm64 profile, an explicit
profile, or JIT host detection) or the function states `lse`. Architecturally an LSE atomic write clears
other observers' exclusive monitors like any store, so CG loops and
C-compiler outline-helper or LSE code on the same location remain mutually
atomic. On Darwin, a contention test races CG LL/SC fetch_add and CAS loops
against clang's inline LSE atomics on the same words and gets exact counts.
Its Linux leg links the C side with `-moutline-atomics` against libgcc's
`__aarch64_*` helpers and has not run. Compiling the helpers themselves
still needs module/naked assembly, which remains refused (audit C-03).

The LL/SC evidence is native C11 differential testing, multi-threaded
contention, independent decoding of every emitted exclusive window, and
decode checks of the exclusive encodings. It ran on an Apple M4 (an LSE CPU
running forced-baseline code). No Linux host and no non-LSE CPU has executed
it. It is not an exclusive-monitor, memory-model, linearizability or
forward-progress proof. The LL/SC pseudos, exclusives and `CLREX` are RED rows
in the opcode evidence inventory, and a proof-required compilation refuses
them. An allocation that would alias a loop-written register fails closed
(`[TCG-LLSC-EXPAND]`).

AArch64 target features are a closed vocabulary of 23 rustc spellings
(`AArch64IsaFeature`), each tied to the Darwin `hw.optional.arm.FEAT_*` keys
that report it; every one is present on the qualifying Apple M4 Max
(`docs/darwin-aarch64-completion.md`). A profile admits features for every
function; a function's own `FuncAttrs.target_features` admits more for that
function alone, within every modeled feature, as rustc's
`#[target_feature(enable = ...)]` does: the caller guarantees the CPU, and
nothing in an AOT object checks it. An unmodeled name is refused by name.
Only LSE, LSE2, FP16, DotProd and the `llvm.aarch64.crc32*` intrinsics change
selection; the other modeled features are admitted but nothing selects their
instructions, and other `llvm.aarch64.*` intrinsics are ordinary external
calls that fail at link. Without `crc` the CRC32 intrinsics lower to a
bit-serial shift/XOR expansion (about four words per data bit); without
`fp16` half-precision arithmetic is refused. A callee that states features is
never inlined. The rustc bridge does not yet state `#[target_feature]` into
trust-ir. Runtime dispatch (`trust_cg_codegen::aarch64_dispatch`) chooses
among compiled variants from the kernel's sysctl report and proves nothing
about their agreement. The raw JIT refuses a function stating a feature the
executing CPU lacks, which also refuses a module holding such a variant
beside its fallback. A JIT buffer records its functions' stated features:
`ExecutableBuffer::serialized_target_contract` adds them to the host-JIT
contract, and `publish_serialized_buffer_for_target` replays extra names only
for modeled features this CPU implements; the contract is the caller's
authenticated claim (the bytes are not decoded), so a caller that persists
such a buffer under the plain host-JIT contract loses the requirement. The
jit-matrix TCJ1 cache and the relocatable-image capture refuse such a buffer.
The CRC32 forms have decoded-word value obligations (ledger `L04-P1`,
`aarch64_crc32_proofs`): for each of the eight forms, the 64-bit value the
word re-derived from the operands leaves in `Xd` (its Arm ARM pseudocode:
`BitReverse`, `Poly32Mod2` by 0x04C11DB7 or 0x1EDC6F41, `BitReverse`;
`Xd[63:32]` cleared; register 31 reads as zero) equals the reflected,
least-significant-bit-first shift register the intrinsic specifies, written
with the literal reflected polynomials, for every register value. Both sides
are affine over GF(2), and `gf2_affine_decide` decides the equality exactly
in process (each result bit as an XOR of input bits, the unrolled division
shared by reference; a refutation's witness is confirmed by a separate
concrete evaluator). Every single-bit word flip, the neighbouring widths, the
other polynomial, swapped registers, a wrong destination or `sf`, and wrong
intents (MSB-first, unreflected constant, high byte first, dropped or
truncated data, the zlib complement, exchanged operands) refute: 368
controls. The decision also showed that `CRC32W`/`CRC32CW` are symmetric in
their two registers (both are padded identically before the XOR), so
exchanged operands are no defect for them. ENC-5 requires the emitted word to
be the re-derived one, and `aarch64_crc32_silicon_differential` runs every
form at seven register assignments on this Apple M4 (56 words, 30,464
executions) against both sides and a host reference, with neighbouring
models required to disagree; it is registered on the Linux floor but has not
run there. This is testing-grade evidence, not a certificate: no solver lane
checks these obligations, the coverage gate counts the rows as accepted
regression evidence, the function verifier reports a holding CRC32
instruction unverified, and a proof-required compilation refuses it. Not
claimed: that selection chose the right intrinsic or registers, or that the
CPU implements FEAT_CRC32 (the function's feature admission is trusted).

Spilled pseudo operands follow a whole-window strategy. Each gets its own
register for the whole loop: X16/X17 for uses first, then an allocatable
register that is not an operand of the pseudo. A register dead after the
pseudo is borrowed as is; a live one is saved to an emergency slot before the
pseudo and restored after it. Reloads, spill stores, saves and restores all
sit before or after the pseudo. Running out of registers fails closed
(`[TCG-LLSC-SPILL-SCRATCH]`). No defined pseudo layout can reach that refusal:
it has at most eight register operands against 27 candidates. After expansion
and again at encoding, a check refuses any spill access
(`[TCG-LLSC-SPILL-WINDOW]`) and any other memory access or call
(`[TCG-LLSC-WINDOW]`) between a load-exclusive and the next store-exclusive or
`CLREX` on any path. On the Apple M4 Max host, `e2e_aarch64_vector_spills` ran
a BASELINE fetch-add and compare-exchange at O0-O3 with 28 vectors and 24
scalars live, checked against a C model, with every exclusive window decoded
spill-free. Three of its eight windows needed a third register for spilled
operands, which the earlier two-scratch rule refused, and two windows saved
and restored a live borrowed register. A second BASELINE program branches on
the compare-exchange outcome and reads its 28 live scalars only in the two
successor blocks. At O2 and O3 it saves and restores a borrowed register that
the rest of the pseudo's block never names. In a manual mutation run that
removed the successor half of the borrow liveness, its O2 result diverged from
the C model. Moving a spill
reload or a plain load inside a window is refused by name. This is structural
and differential testing; it is not an exclusive-monitor or forward-progress
proof.

The AArch64 `Pipeline` has no default target. An empty or unrecognized
`PipelineConfig::target_triple` is refused with `[TCG-TARGET-ABI]` and does not
select DarwinPCS or Mach-O. `Compiler::new` still derives the OS/ABI from the
host; `CompilationResult::target_selection` records it as `HostDerived`. A
spelled-out triple never takes anything from the host: explicit
`aarch64-unknown-unknown` and `x86_64-unknown-unknown` name no OS and are
refused on every host.

The TrustIR adapter classifies its caller-side narrow-integer extension under
the target's convention: the compiler, JIT and strict Core entries pass the
variant resolved from the triple, the compatibility entries that take only a
TLS dialect use that object format's convention (Mach-O: DarwinPCS, ELF:
AAPCS64), and an unresolved convention refuses a call with a narrow integer
argument (`[TCG-TARGET-ABI]`). A direct `InstructionSelector` refuses ABI
classification until `set_abi_variant` is called. For x86-64 and RISC-V the
adapter still decides which narrow arguments to extend by the historical rule
(the first eight integer-class positions, as the AArch64 classifier counts
them); that is not an x86-64 or RISC-V ABI classification. Swift aggregate
scalarization runs only for DarwinPCS (Mach-O) targets, the contract that clang
`swiftcall` execution on macOS witnesses. No swiftcall aggregate layout has been
witnessed under AAPCS64 (the Linux AArch64 host has no clang or Swift compiler),
so there a Swift signature with an aggregate parameter or return is refused as
an unsupported calling convention that names the function and its first
non-scalar parameter or its return; `e2e_aarch64_swift_aggregate` pins that
refusal for every shape the Darwin run covers. The scalar Swift subset is still
admitted under AAPCS64. The rustc bridge's placement comparison
(`abi_reg_lanes.rs`) still classifies AArch64 with DarwinPCS; the bridge is a
separate workspace and was not rebuilt with this change.

Mach-O objects record `LC_BUILD_VERSION` for the macOS platform with the
minimum OS taken from the target triple (`aarch64-apple-macos12.0`) or from
`MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET` captured by the `trust-cg` CLI, and 14.0 when
neither is given. The SDK field is the minimum OS raised to 14.0 and names no
real SDK. iOS, tvOS, watchOS and visionOS triples, Darwin kernel versions
(`darwin23`), malformed versions and arm64 versions below 11.0 are refused
(`[TCG-MACHO-DEPLOYMENT]`). The library never reads the environment: other
library callers get 14.0 unless their triple names a version, and the rustc
bridge does not yet forward rustc's deployment target. The standalone Mach-O
linker still stamps linked images with 14.0 whatever its inputs record, and
host-JIT entries require the unversioned host triple. ld64 acceptance is
checked natively on macOS for 11.0 through 15.0.

Sibling tail calls (O2/O3) are admitted only from the ABI facts instruction
selection recorded for the call: no hidden result pointer, the AAPCS64
callee-saved set, and stack arguments that fit the caller's own incoming
argument area, whose stores are then redirected into that area. A call without
recorded facts (created or cloned by a later pass, or `_Unwind_Resume`),
an indirect call, an `sret` call (including one that forwards the caller's own
result pointer), variadic or aggregate stack arguments, and a caller that
takes the address of its incoming area keep their `BL`/`BLR`. When it was
measured the AOT compiler refused direct calls to module-local functions on
Darwin, so native tail-call evidence covers calls into clang-compiled callees; it ran on macOS and is registered but
has not run on a Linux host. A clang caller tail-calling a CG function is not
tested separately.

On AArch64 ELF, immutable non-TLS globals containing symbol-address slots
use `.data.rel.ro`, preserving their alignment and relocation addends. Native
PIE/shared-library tests link with `-z text -z relro -z now`, inspect the slots
inside `PT_GNU_RELRO`, and exercise data/function pointers and unwinding at
O0–O3. Final read-only protection depends on the linker's RELRO policy; an
object file alone does not enforce runtime permissions. Plain immutable bytes
remain in `.rodata`. A thread-local whose initial-value template embeds symbol
addresses (`__thread void *p = &x;`) keeps the template in `.tdata` (never
`.tbss`, even when its bytes are all zero) with one `R_AARCH64_ABS64` per slot
in `.rela.tdata`, the rows gcc emits for the same C; explicit `.tdata.*` and
COMDAT templates relocate through their own sections.
`e2e_aarch64_globals_linux` runs a pthread C driver against a `static __thread` C oracle at O0–O3 in
static and PIE executables (local-exec and initial-exec) and in a `dlopen`ed
`pic` shared object (TLSDESC, including a thread that predates the `dlopen`);
dropping one `.rela.tdata` record fails both its readelf row and the driver.
That the TLS runtime copies the relocated template into every thread is
loader behavior observed there, not proved. A pointer slot whose target is
itself a thread-local (from data or from a template, naming a definition or
an import) has no link-time address and is refused by name
(`[TCG-TLS-SLOT-TARGET]`) on every AArch64 object format, the relocation
inventory and the JIT data image; a function body naming one through
`SymbolAddr` is refused separately (see the Mach-O paragraph below).
The layout-less `Pipeline` APIs also emit pointer slots with
`R_AARCH64_ABS64`, including objects without text relocations. Their relocation
inventory includes those slots, TLS template slots included; omitting frame
layouts still omits unwind tables and cannot support unwinding through those
functions.

No certified (proof-required) object contains exception tables. The LSDA,
the personality reference and the unwind tables that register them carry
structural checks and native tests but no proof obligation (trusted base
TB-12), so a proof-required compile of a module whose object would carry any
is refused by name (`[TCG-EH-UNPROVED]`, "exception tables carry no proof
obligation"; the bridge reports it as `[TCG-PROOF-465]`) on AArch64 and
x86-64, before the relocation inventory, the certificates and any promotion,
whatever the frame opcodes' proof status. That covers a function's own
exception-handling structure and the walk-through tables an x86-64 emitter
adds under whole-program `panic=unwind`: the Mach-O filler LSDA of every framed
function and, on ELF, an LSDA for every function of the module. The x86-64
object pipeline lowers every function with a frame, so under `panic=unwind`
every non-empty x86-64 object carries exception tables — a leaf `x + 1`
included. (Before this gate a certified x86-64 Mach-O compile of an EH module
promoted its tables, and so did any `panic=unwind` module.) The proof-grade
JIT routes refuse the same functions through the same decision
(`ExceptionTableCensus`).

So, with proof certificates on, x86-64 requires `-Cpanic=abort`. This is a
behaviour change for users of the rustc bridge's default configuration
(certificates on, and Rust's default `-Cpanic=unwind`): on x86-64 targets
(`x86_64-apple-darwin`, `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu`) it refuses EVERY codegen
unit with `[TCG-EH-UNPROVED]`, as it refuses every AArch64 unit whose object
carries exception tables. Compile such programs with `-Cpanic=abort`, or
without certificates (`-Ztrust-ir-cg-args=no-proof-certs`). The bridge's
x86-64 execution differentials that build `panic=unwind` programs
(`panic_unwind_raise_x86`, `m134_x86_needs_drop_elem_x86`, the unwind leg of
`m139_flatmap_bounded_x86`) now compile without certificates and run on
x86-64 hosts (macOS and Linux). `m139`'s five lowering canaries also compile
without certificates, for whatever host runs them; they require their
specific lowering refusal and skip, stating why, when their same-host
positive control (`sum_basic`) does not compile, as on AArch64 Linux today.
A certified x86-64 COFF compile is refused either way, by its relocation
inventory, which has no proof lane for COFF relocations. On AArch64 the object emitters do not read
`panic_unwind` (no walk-through filler tables); a test pins that the objects
are byte-identical with and without it.

On AArch64 Darwin the exception tables now carry obligations, decided over
the emitted bytes but not certified (ledger row L03-P14). Every Mach-O
object the module and single-function emitters write with exception tables,
and every unchecked JIT image that publishes them (before it is mapped; the
JIT gate is host-independent, but its AArch64 Linux arm has not yet run on a
Linux host), is emitted only after `trust_cg_verify::eh_obligations` re-parses it with its
own Mach-O, LSDA, `__eh_frame`/CFA-program and A64 decoders (none shared
with the emitters) and decides, against the machine function's EH metadata
and the frame owner's layout: every `BL`/`BLR` the function's own control
flow reaches that can unwind lies in exactly one call-site record, read as
the personalities read the table (sorted, disjoint, at the return address
minus one; dead calls keep their record check); the record's landing pad
is the IR's landing block for that invoke, or none for any other call, and
no record names another; every landing pad's action chain is the IR's
clause list under the selector contract (typed index `k` is filter `k`
over a slot GOT-relocated to the IR's typeinfo, the catch-all is filter
`N + 1` over a NULL slot, Rust's empty filter is `-1`, a cleanup ends the
chain); the compact-unwind entry, or the FDE and its CIE, names the
function's personality and LSDA (a function without EH structure carries
none, or a filler LSDA naming no landing pad); and the compact encoding or
FDE rows describe exactly the frame owner's frame and, at every call, the
frame the function's words built: a forward data-flow over the decoded
words (direct branches, call fallthroughs, jump tables read from the
function's own appended bytes, and the exceptional edge of each reached
call) tracks SP, FP, every general register, D8-D15 and the stack slots at
known CFA offsets, and the description's CFA rule must give the entry SP,
each slot it names must hold that register's entry value, the return
address must come from a slot, and every callee-saved register it does not
name must still hold its entry value. A violation fails the emission by
name (`[TCG-EH-OBLIGATION]`, the bridge's `[TCG-EH-UNWIND]`). These are
exact decisions made in process by trusted Rust: testing-grade evidence,
not a certificate. Under the evidence policy (decision record OD-139: an
in-process decision is never credit) they are not admissible for
promotion, and no Clean-checked certificate of them exists, so the
`[TCG-EH-UNPROVED]` refusal stands for these objects too. Their boundary:
the personality routines and unwinder are assumed to read the tables as
the Itanium ABI and DWARF specify (TB-21); the IR side is the machine
function's EH metadata and frame layout, not trust-ir directly (TB-13);
every store at a known constant CFA offset is applied to the slots it
covers, whatever its form (`STR`/`STP` record the value; release,
exclusive, compare-and-swap, atomic, unprivileged, RCpc and SIMD structure
stores forget the slots they overlap), but a store whose address is not a
known constant CFA offset (a computed pointer, a register-offset address,
SP after a runtime-sized allocation) is assumed not to write the
callee-saved area; a word outside the classified A64 subset (including
`DC ZVA`) or an unresolvable `BR` is refused rather than modeled; a CIE
marking signal frames (`S`) is refused, as is a CIE or FDE pointer whose
`DW_EH_PE_indirect` bit disagrees with a GOT relocation; and synchronous
unwinding only (calls are the unwind points; prologue and epilogue rows
between calls are not judged). AArch64 ELF objects and objects without
exception tables are not gated: their unwind CFI stays trusted, not proven.
The Darwin RAII campaign (`e2e_aarch64_eh_raii_darwin`) pins the exact
report of every campaign object at O0-O3 (C++: 36 functions, 32 with EH,
212 unwind points, 209 of them covered, none unreached; Rust: 14, 12, 75
and 74; the JIT images 28/24/150 and 14/12/75) and checks the unwind
points against its own count of the call words, and refuses seventeen
corruptions per level (O0, O2) of the C++ object or its IR side (a call
outside every record, a wrong landing pad, a wrong compact or CIE
personality, an FDE CFA offset off by 16, a frame pointer set 16 bytes off,
a compact encoding without its X19/X20 pair, that pair missing on both
sides, a prologue storing X21 in X20's slot, a typed slot naming the wrong
typeinfo, swapped invoke bindings, a foreign LSDA, a pad-free frame's filler
LSDA stopping before a call, a CIE personality encoding without
`DW_EH_PE_indirect` over its GOT relocation, and the frame record
overwritten by `STLR`, `ST1` or `STXR` before a call) and three per JIT
image, each by the obligation it breaks; its native rows execute the gated
objects.

The relocation inventory itself enumerates the unwind-table rows of an
AArch64 ELF object with exception-handling structure (ledger row L03-P13):
the zPLR CIE's `R_AARCH64_PREL32` to the `DW.ref.<personality>` slot, one FDE
pc-begin and one FDE LSDA `R_AARCH64_PREL32` per function, and the slot's
`R_AARCH64_ABS64` to the personality; `.gcc_except_table` carries none. It
still refuses by name (`EhSidecarUnsupported`, the bridge's
`[TCG-EH-UNWIND]`) Mach-O EH objects, a typed catch or exception
specification, a second personality, an LSDA or CIE whose pointer encodings
it does not enumerate, and an EH module without a frame layout for every
function; a certified compile never reaches those refusals, because the
census refuses it first. Every relocation inventory report — AArch64 and
x86-64 — marks the exception-table rows `Unverified` (AArch64: the CIE
personality, FDE LSDA and `DW.ref` slot rows; x86-64: the whole EH surface —
Mach-O compact unwind and personality GOT, ELF CIE personality, FDE pc-begin
and LSDA pointers and `DW.ref` slot), so a report of an object with exception
tables is never promotable. The record-by-record comparison
`Compiler::compile` runs after emission (by section and symbol index, AArch64
ELF only) has checked EH objects only in tests, since certified EH compiles
stop before emission.

AArch64 Mach-O objects get a coarser artifact check. `Compiler::compile`
reparses their relocation records and requires the kind multiset to equal the
inventory rows, each lane-covered record to have the `r_pcrel`/`r_length`
shape its lane models, every `ARM64_RELOC_SUBTRACTOR` to be followed by its
`ARM64_RELOC_UNSIGNED` minuend, and every `ARM64_RELOC_ADDEND` to prefix a
same-address BRANCH26/PAGE21/PAGEOFF12 record. It does not compare records
one by one: a record moved to another section or address, retargeted, or
flipped in `r_extern` with its kind and shape kept is not detected, nor is an
`ARM64_RELOC_ADDEND` prefix's value, nor the placement of compact-unwind
entries and DWARF-fallback FDE pc-begin pairs against their functions.

Unwind tables of frames without exception handling are different: every
AArch64 object emitted with frame layouts carries an ELF `.eh_frame` FDE or a
Mach-O compact-unwind entry (and, for some frames, a DWARF-fallback FDE) per
function, and once the frame opcodes gain proofs (L07-P2) such objects can
promote. Their content (which frame state each PC range restores) is trusted
base TB-12 — encoder checks and native unwinding tests, no proof — and the
AArch64 relocation-inventory certificate says so ("trusted, not proven:
unwind CFI of N .eh_frame FDE(s)" on ELF, "trusted, not proven: compact
unwind of N function(s), M with a DWARF-fallback __eh_frame FDE" on Mach-O).
