functions come from more than 254 source files cannot be one DWARF compile
unit (`DW_AT_decl_file` is one byte), so with `-g` its batched compile is
refused and the bridge falls back to per-function objects: the program is
the same, its object partitioning and layout are not. On AArch64 Linux and
Darwin rustc's linkage is carried onto symbols (hidden CGU-local copies,
`N_PEXT`, weak/link-once definitions, no definition for
`available_externally`); `common`, extern-weak definitions, weak
thread-locals and, on the other targets, every weak or link-once definition
are refused as `[TCG-LINKAGE]` (wasm32 keeps its own placement table). Since
2026-10-24 the other native targets (x86-64 ELF and COFF) also refuse by
name every function definition rustc binds `Internal` (`[TCG-LINKAGE]`) or
hidden or protected (`[TCG-VISIBILITY]`), and a session default visibility
or hidden `__rdl_*` declaration the bridge would have to synthesize there
(ruling OD-BRIDGE-UNSPELLED-BINDING-20261024): those objects would bind the
function as a default-visible global, exported from a shared object and
preemptible. rustc binds most functions of an ordinary crate `Internal` (one
codegen unit) or hidden (called from another codegen unit), so the bridge
now refuses almost every ordinary crate for `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu`
(including the `scripts/check_linux_x86_64_bridge.py` diagnostic corpus and
an x86-64 Linux `core` census) until the x86-64 ELF writer spells local and
hidden/protected function definitions and hidden undefined references and
the bridge admits that target's private namespace with x86-64 native
controls; the x86-64 evidence for the refusal was link-level only when the
ruling landed (no x86-64 sysroot or executor on the measuring host) and was
then measured on an x86-64 Linux host as 18 of 18 benchmark programs refused
in both lanes, 12 `[TCG-VISIBILITY]` and 6 `[TCG-LINKAGE]`
(DR-X86-LINUX-MAP-20261027). All four of those conditions now have an
implementation: the x86-64 ELF writer spells a local function definition
(OD-X86-ELF-LOCAL-BINDING-20261027), hidden/protected FUNCTION DEFINITIONS
(OD-X86-ELF-DEFINITION-VISIBILITY-20261027) and an undefined symbol's weakness
and visibility (OD-X86-ELF-UNDEFINED-REFERENCE-20261106), and the bridge
admits this target's private namespace while the adapter admits a codegen
DECLARATION's visibility (OD-X86-BRIDGE-ELF-PRIVATE-ROUTE-20261106). Measured
on an x86-64 Linux host, **17 of those 18 benchmark programs now compile and
exit-match the LLVM arm**; the one holdout, `h3_box_leak`, refuses on
`[TCG-BOX-DEREF]`, a MIR lowering gap of a different class. The route flip
alone lifts nothing — it relocates the refusal to the adapter on the allocator
shim's hidden `__rdl_*` declaration, which every `std` binary links.
**The fourth condition's native-control requirement is not yet met**: both
`multi_cgu_link_*` targets are `#![cfg(target_os = "macos")]`, so the x86-64
ELF symbol read-back behind that measurement is a session result, not a
committed gate, and no `core` census or
`scripts/check_linux_x86_64_bridge.py` run was made. Those results are also
the DIAGNOSTIC lane only: the PROOF lane still refuses every one of them with
`[TCG-EH-UNPROVED]`, because whole-program `panic=unwind` gives each function
walk-through exception tables that are trusted base TB-12 and carry no proof
obligation. The private copies are spelled `__trust_cg_private.{cgu}.{index}`
bound `GLOBAL`+`STV_HIDDEN`, not `STB_LOCAL` under the rustc name as LLVM
spells them; both keep the copy out of a linked image's `.dynsym`, and
equality with LLVM is not claimed. A foreign `#[thread_local]`
static declared with `#[linkage]` (`extern_weak` or any other import
linkage) is refused by name (`[TCG-EXTERN-STATIC-LINKAGE]`, ruling
OD-BRIDGE-TLS-IMPORT-LINKAGE-20261024; L02-P4): rustc reads it through a
thread-local cell holding the address of a non-TLS weak symbol, and the
bridge's thread-local import is a strong TLS reference (before, it compiled
silently to a strong `STT_TLS` undefined reference that fails to link, or
binds, where LLVM reads null). Non-TLS `extern_weak` foreign statics are
emitted on AArch64 Linux only. Only
Darwin AArch64 is measured: weak and link-once statics on AArch64 Linux and
the carried function linkage on x86_64-apple-darwin share the code path but
have not been run. A `linkonce_odr` function is bound plain `weak external`,
where LLVM binds it `weak external automatically hidden`, so the linked
image keeps exporting it (the program is unaffected).
On Mach-O the adapter admits only hidden visibility on an `External`
definition, so a hidden weak or link-once definition and protected visibility
are refused by name there. A Mach-O weak undefined reference (`N_WEAK_REF`)
is still refused by the object writer, so `extern_weak` imports stay
unsupported on Darwin.

**The strict `p3c-refine` lane refuses a translation-validation job it
cannot state** (measured 2026-10-07 on aarch64-apple-darwin, `targo
--unverified`, no proof claim). A queued job fails the strict compile with
`[TCG-REFINE-SHAPE]` (lane, symbol, job and reason) when its emission is
outside the lane's fold, when the obligation builder refuses the
reconstructed store set, when the scalar encoder or the memory verifier
cannot state it, or when the session's pointer width is outside the 64-bit
word model. The default lanes still skip such a job and credit nothing.
Six temporary real-emission mutants (never committed, measured on the
strict branch before it merged here) compile in the default lane and print
wrong values, each an extra store into a cell of a lane's captured window:
`StepBy` `step_minus_one` (lane 11), the packed `StepBy` state word (lane
12a, since replaced by the countdown lowering of lane 12c), `Range::next`
`end`, slice `Iter::next` `end`, a rewritten `split_at` left half and a
rewritten `chunks` cursor end. Strict refuses each one with
`[TCG-REFINE-SHAPE]` naming its lane. On this tree (2026-10-08) the lane-12c
review's mutant, an extra store into the countdown's `step_minus_one` cell,
compiles in the default lane, which skips its jobs, and prints wrong values
for 5 of 6 probe cases; strict refuses the three probe functions that reach
the lane with `[TCG-REFINE-SHAPE]` (`countdown StepBy::next`), and the
fourth on an `INCONCLUSIVE` memory verdict, as it does without the mutant.
With the previous builders, which read the first store of a cell, the
rewritten `split_at` half still reaches the solver. On
correct code only TV lane 14 (the slice `to_vec` header) misses. Its fold
pins an older 11-node header window, while `lower_slice_to_vec` emits std's
exact-capacity header with its guards across blocks. All 402 lane-14 jobs
measured missed, so strict refuses every function in which it lowers a
scalar `to_vec`, as it did before under `[TCG-SLICE-HEADER-REFINEMENT]`.
The measurement queued about 78,900 jobs in the 2,995 compiles that reached
the bridge: 2,281 compiled, and 714 were refused partway with
`[TCG-MIR-UNSUPPORTED]`. They come from the bridge's test programs and
corpus, the real-program guests and 224 hunt probes. Another 896 extracted
test fragments failed rustc's front end and measured nothing. No other lane
missed. On this host the solver limits strict further. Of 2,128 compiles of
the guests, the probes and 295 bridge test and corpus programs at O0-O3,
the default lane accepts 1,291; strict refuses 503 of those, 403 of them
only on `INCONCLUSIVE` verdicts (AY `incomplete self-check-rejected`, or an
incomplete proof certificate). A 4-byte-pointer session has no word model
for the pointer-word lanes, so strict refuses every one of their jobs there.
That case was not measured: the host has no Trust wasm32 sysroot. The rule
covers queued jobs only. A construct the capture step excludes is never
queued, only the first capture under a dedup key is queued, and the strict
loop-threading check (`trust_ir_interp`) still skips a loop outside its
slice, or one its verifier rejects structurally, without refusing.

**MIR families (ledger L06-P8, 2026-10-07).** `SetDiscriminant` is lowered
for every layout (Direct, explicit and fieldless `repr` discriminants, niche,
single variant) on `(*r)`, `(*r).f…`, a variant field and a memory-backed
local or its fields; a scalarized local (a bare fieldless enum local
included), a slot-backed DST base or an unbound pointer is refused.
`Rvalue::Discriminant` reads through a pointer at a runtime index; other
projected reads keep the paths and refusals they had. A `Box<T>` whose
payload has drop glue is dropped through rustc's own glue, on AArch64 Darwin
only, when every part of `T` is kept at rustc's layout (an intercepted
collection, a union, a trait object, a closure or a coroutine anywhere in `T`
keeps the refusal), and `Vec<Box<T>>` with a droppable `T` is refused; x86-64
and AArch64 Linux keep their earlier refusals. The cleanup-loop homes and the
landing-pad parameter filter run on AArch64 Darwin only: they cover a landing
pad that is itself a loop header and a loop's carried scalars live into a pad
entered from inside and outside the loop (a pad that needs no SSA input gets
none), and other landing-pad state on Darwin is still threaded through SSA
(Linux AArch64 homes all cleanup state; other targets keep their refusals).
That a body which compiled before keeps its code is a design argument
checked on probes, not proved. Indirect calls keep a live unwind edge on
Darwin through the same typed thunk as on Linux, but the `Box<dyn Fn*>`
blanket `call*` lane does so on Darwin only (Linux keeps its refusal).
`#[link_section]` is placed only for statics on AArch64 Mach-O and ELF; a
function's or a thread-local's section is refused. Inline assembly lowers only
for the bounded scalar FP grammar (now on Darwin as well as Linux). Not
implemented and refused by name: guaranteed tail calls (`become`,
`[TCG-TAIL-CALL]`), every other `asm!` block and every naked function
(`[TCG-INLINE-ASM]`), `global_asm!` (`[TCG-GLOBAL-ASM]`), unsafe binders
(`[TCG-UNSAFE-BINDER]`). The Darwin evidence (`mir_families_aarch64`) is
native differential testing against LLVM with proofs off; nothing here was
run on Linux.

**Multi-CGU link identity.** rustc gives every codegen unit that uses an
`#[inline]` item its own `Internal` copy, all under one mangled name. The
bridge emits every `Internal` function under a CGU-qualified hidden symbol
(`src/function_linkage.rs`): `__trust_cg_private.<cgu>.<index>` on AArch64
Linux ELF, and since 2026-10-01 `__trust_cg_private.<cgu>.<index>.<rustc
symbol>` on Apple Mach-O, AArch64 and x86-64 alike (`N_EXT | N_PEXT`, demoted
to a local by the final link; the x86-64 Mach-O writer spells it since the
same day). Crates built with several codegen units therefore link
(`tests/multi_cgu_link_aarch64.rs`: executables, an rlib with its downstream
binary, and a staticlib, -O0 to -O3 at 2, 4 and 16 codegen units, run against
LLVM; `tests/multi_cgu_link_x86_64.rs`: the same rows for
`x86_64-apple-darwin`). Costs that remain: such a symbol is not a
demangleable rustc name (on Mach-O it contains one; on Linux it carries none),
so backtraces, profilers and backend diagnostics show the private spelling.
The x86-64 evidence is LINK-ONLY on Apple silicon: the objects link and read
back as intended (every private copy a private extern defined once per CGU,
none exported), but no x86-64 binary was executed on the measuring host (no
Rosetta), so the x86-64 rows make no runtime claim there; they run against
LLVM only on an x86-64 host. That test's `std` rows need an
`x86_64-apple-darwin` `rust-std` in the build compiler's sysroot (the installed
Darwin Trust package ships the host's only, so they skip there; they were
measured with a stage1 `trustc`); its `#![no_std]` rows link against a `core`
built from the compiler's library source on every macOS host. x86-64 ELF
(Linux) and COFF objects bind every function definition global under
rustc's name and spell no function visibility, so since 2026-10-24 the
bridge refuses by name, before lowering, every crate with an `Internal`,
hidden or protected function for those targets (ruling
OD-BRIDGE-UNSPELLED-BINDING-20261024) rather than emit the CGU-private copy
as an exported global. (That was the writers' state when the ruling was
taken. The x86-64 ELF writer has since spelled a local definition and a
hidden or protected one (OD-X86-ELF-LOCAL-BINDING-20261027,
OD-X86-ELF-DEFINITION-VISIBILITY-20261027) and the COFF writer binds an
unreferenced module-local definition static
(OD-X86-BINDING-ONE-CARRIER-20261105); the bridge's refusal is unchanged.)

**Cross-crate local copies (AArch64 Linux).** rustc also gives each crate
that instantiates a non-generic `#[inline]` core function its own `Internal`
copy, under a name that names no instantiating crate. From O2 the same holds
for a cross-crate-inlinable method. The Linux private names are qualified by
the CGU, whose name carries the crate's disambiguator, so these copies stay
apart. Consider a bridge-built library and a bridge-built `std` binary that
both copy `<u64 as From<u16>>::from`, `<i128>::wrapping_mul` and a
trait-object method. They link and print the expected result in every
LLVM/bridge pairing at O0–O3 (`tests/support/cross_crate_definitions.rs`, in
the required `aarch64_c_fnabi_aggregate_linux` target). That test also
compares each crate's defined ELF symbols with rustc's LLVM objects. The
check was a 2026-10-02 cross-crate matrix at `13a7b0ad9`: 66 library/binary
programs at O0, O2 and O3 with one codegen unit, then again with 16 for the
38 that compile in some bridge pairing. No pairing failed with a duplicate
definition. Programs that the bridge refuses were not exercised. Three
spellings still differ from rustc's objects. None duplicates a definition
in an ordinary rustc link:

- An `Internal` static is a non-local, default-visibility definition under
  its rustc name, which names its crate. An immutable pointer-free static is
  weak, in a COMDAT group; any other static is global. LLVM binds the same
  static local.
- The allocation a pointer-bearing static points at (the bytes of `static
  PTR: &[u8] = b"..."`) is a weak, hidden object named
  `tcg.static.alloc<N>.tcg.crate.<id>`, where `<id>` is the crate's
  `StableCrateId`; LLVM emits it as a private local allocation
  (`.Lanon.<hash>.<n>`, a section symbol only). The name is private to the
  crate, so another crate's allocation never shares it (`readelf` of a
  library rlib at O0 and O2, 2026-10-02).
- Each bridge-built crate that uses a `__trustcg_*` runtime helper (such as
  `__trustcg_slice_eq_i64` for slice equality) defines it in its own object as
  a strong default-visibility symbol. rustc's archive link of a library loads
  only the copy it needs. Linking the library's helper object explicitly
  beside a binary that defines the same helper fails with `multiple
  definition` (measured with the former `print!` helper, `__trustcg_write_all`;
  a decoded `print!` now calls std's own `_print` and has no helper).

Some function definitions have no counterpart in rustc's LLVM objects at all.
An intrinsic the bridge does not lower directly has its fallback body
collected by rustc. At O0, in a probe library calling `u64::rotate_left`
among other integer operations, rustc's mono-item placement for a bridge
build adds `core::intrinsics::disjoint_bitor::<u64>` and
`core::intrinsics::unchecked_funnel_shl::<u64>` as `External` items. Their
`DisjointBitOr` / `FunnelShift` trait bodies are added as `Internal` items.
The LLVM placement has neither, because LLVM lowers those intrinsics
directly. The bridge defines the two `External` instances as global,
default-visibility functions, as placed. Their v0 names end in the
instantiating crate's tag (`...ECs<hash>_7fixture`), so another crate's
instances do not share the names. The `Internal` bodies take CGU-private
names (`-Zprint-mono-items=yes` and `readelf` at O0, 2026-10-02).

The bridge's modeled `StepBy` iterator surface is limited to
`-Copt-level=0` with the default MIR-inlining settings. Codegen optimization
levels O1–O3, or nightly flags that enable normal MIR inlining at O0, reject
`StepBy` before lowering because an inlined standard-library method can observe
state the bridge represents differently. At supported O0 settings, modeled
consumers and `next` remain available; unmodeled methods such as `size_hint`
still fail closed.

At O1--O3 the admission check conservatively traverses each monomorphized
local type graph to find `StepBy` values hidden inside aggregates and closure
state. That traversal has fixed depth and unique-type budgets. A legal
expanding recursive generic can exceed a budget even when it contains no
`StepBy`; the bridge then rejects the program with
`TCG-STEPBY-TYPE-SCAN` instead of risking an unbounded compiler scan. This is a
known false-positive, fail-closed boundary.

**MIR assertion panic runtime (2026-10-01).** The historical canonical bounds
trap shortcut is removed. Bounds/misalignment pass their exact dynamic operands
to rustc's actual panic lang item; arithmetic, zero-divisor and null forms
select their distinct entries. The hidden caller location comes from MIR scope
authority, including tracked forwarding and real inlined scopes. ARM64/macOS
O0–O3 controls match LLVM for a returning hook followed by SIGABRT, or unwind
with exactly one source Guard Drop and an exact caught payload. This is native
diagnostic coverage with certificates off, not a panic-runtime theorem.
Immediate-abort refuses until its distinct runtime policy is qualified.
Darwin termination has separate reason-call and empty-filter controls. Under
`panic=abort` every bridge frame is `nounwind`
(`CompilerConfig::eh_frames_cannot_unwind`, each EH frame's own FnAbi
re-queried), and its AArch64 LSDA applies the region rule of LLVM's call-site
table for such a function to trust-cg's own calls: the explicit Invoke
handlers, plus a keep-unwinding entry for each region between them that holds
an indirect call or a direct call to a callee the bridge did not record as
`nounwind` the way LLVM would treat it (`CompilerConfig::eh_nounwind_callees`:
rustc's FnAbi, and `memcmp` only above O0, where LLVM infers the attribute). A
region of recorded direct calls only is a gap, where the search fails (`failed
to initiate panic, error 3`). The terminate fixture checks this against LLVM at
O0–O3: its 80 original native runs, including the nested foreign panic, and 26
call-site-region rows (direct, Rust and `extern "C"` function-pointer, `&dyn`,
mixed, per-region and `memcmp` shapes; 208 runs).
This is the region rule, not LLVM's coverage. On a 56-program variant corpus
(O0–O3, 1076 runs against LLVM; trust-cg main `7546b6109` as the baseline,
and identically on `100773852`),
the policy newly diverges from LLVM on 22 programs (186 runs) that the
full-coverage filler matched. Every one aborts earlier, never later: trust-cg
fails phase one where LLVM reaches the termination pad (123 runs) or keeps
unwinding through the abort frame (63 runs: 21 caught, 21 uncaught, 21
nested-cleanup terminations). The cause is a call LLVM has in a region and
trust-cg does not (one exception below): LLVM inlines a helper that holds an indirect call
(`#[inline(always)]` at O0–O1, small helpers, `iter().for_each`, `Option::map`,
a cross-crate `#[inline]` function; 10 programs, 81 runs), places a cold,
noreturn or branch call in another region (5 programs, 51 runs), calls
`memcpy`/`memcmp` for a copy or compare trust-cg expands inline (64- and
256-byte arrays, a 128-byte struct and `raw_eq` at O0, a 1 KiB array at every
level; 6 programs, 36 runs), or turns self-recursion into a loop at O1–O3
(1 program, 18 runs). The same corpus has 27 programs (234 runs) where the
filler diverged and the policy matches, including 75 runs where the filler
kept unwinding through the abort frame (25 of them caught by the driver) while
LLVM fails phase one. Eight programs (78 runs) diverge identically under both:
in 66 runs LLVM devirtualises an indirect call to a direct `nounwind` one or
lays a loop, cold or tail region out differently, so LLVM fails phase one where
trust-cg reaches the termination pad; in 12 an unrelated `unwrap` message
differs. The fixture's rows cannot see this class: their regions hold the same
calls under both backends. Closing it needs either a model of LLVM's inlining,
libcall and block-placement decisions, or a per-call unwind contract in
TrustIR (the v53 `Inst::CallCannotUnwind` / `Inst::CallIndirectCannotUnwind`
boundary, refused by every lane today) that each call site enforces instead of
its region's calls. The exception: a user-declared `extern "C" fn memcmp` is
recorded as `nounwind` from its FnAbi, but in a crate that also calls
`compare_bytes` at O0 LLVM can keep rustc's attribute-less declaration of the
same symbol (declaration order decides) and cover the region (3 runs; also an
earlier abort).
A call trust-cg creates itself, with no MIR call behind it, is recorded per
callee and per level as LLVM's table has the same point: `nounwind` wherever
LLVM may inline, expand, fold, narrow or delete the operation (a gap), left out
only where LLVM certainly emits a libcall for it, which its call-site rule
treats as may-unwind (covered). The `__trustcg_*` helpers other than the array
fill (`slice_eq`/`cmp`/`contains`/`reverse`/`repeat`, `vec_sort`/`dedup` and the
`Vec` shifts, the `BTreeMap` helpers) stand for a std call rustc declares
`nounwind` or its inlined loop, recorded at every level; a decoded `print!`
calls std's own `_print`, as LLVM does, and is recorded from rustc's FnAbi at
every level;
libm `fma`/`fmaf` is `fmadd` (recorded); a `memset`/`memcpy`/`memmove`
intrinsic is a libcall at O0 above 32 constant bytes (left out) and recorded
otherwise, since above O0 LLVM can delete or forward it; `__trustcg_array_fill_*`
for a byte-uniform `[v; N]` is left out at O0 above 32 bytes and above O0 only
above 512 bytes when the array's address reaches a `black_box` right after the
fill (LLVM deletes or folds a fill whose few reads it sees, measured on
`[5u8; 2048]` summed over four elements and 600- and 700-byte fills read
through a helper), recorded otherwise. The libm calls (`sin`, `cos`, `exp`,
`exp2`, `log`, `log2`, `log10`, `pow`, `__powidf2`, `+f` forms) and the routines
the backend calls for a 128-bit division or remainder (`__udivti3`, `__divti3`,
`__umodti3`, `__modti3`), a float remainder (`fmod`/`fmodf`) and a 128-bit
integer <-> float conversion (`__fix*ti`, `__float*ti*`) are covered at O0
unless nothing reads the result through copies and arithmetic (LLVM deletes
such an operation even at O0) or, for a division, remainder or conversion,
no operand is certainly a runtime value (LLVM's IRBuilder folds an operation
of constants as it builds the IR; an `#[inline(always)]` call's result and a
pointer's metadata are never taken as one, so `u128::from(x) / 3` aborts
earlier than LLVM at O0), and above O0 only where every operand comes
from a different `black_box` result (InstSimplify folds `X / X` and `X % X`)
and the result reaches a `black_box` in the same invoke-free stretch with no
call LLVM could inline; LLVM folds constants it
derives itself (`sin(two())`, a value propagated through an `#[inline(never)]`
helper, a fully unrolled loop, `log10(a * 0.0 + 100.0)` of a non-negative
`a`), expands a 128-bit division by a constant, narrows zero-extended operands
(`(x as u128) / (y as u128)` is one `udiv`) and deletes dead results, none of
which trust-cg can see in general. A thread-local access's resolver call (the
Darwin TLV thunk, the ELF TLS descriptor call) never unwinds and is `nounwind`
at every level (above O0 LLVM folds a read of a thread-local nothing writes;
at O0, and for one the crate writes, LLVM's own thunk call covers its region,
so trust-cg aborts earlier there). A call through a `fn` pointer or a vtable
whose target the MIR states (never through an argument, a raw-borrowed local
or a `Pin`/`Cell` wrapper: a reified fn item or closure in a local, a field
of a struct the frame built, an immutable `static` or an element of one above
O0, a `&dyn`/`Box<dyn>` unsized from a known type above O0, a `Box<dyn Fn>`
of a known type at every level) is lowered as the direct call LLVM makes, and
a `Box<dyn Fn>` call of an unknown type at O0 goes through a `nounwind` thunk
standing for LLVM's direct call to `<Box<F> as Fn>::call`. A frame with no
foreign edge of its own gets a table where LLVM may inline into it a callee
whose foreign call has a terminate pad (`#[inline(always)]` at every level,
any inlinable local, cross-crate `#[inline]` or generic function above O0,
through up to three levels and `fn` pointer arguments): that call becomes an
invoke with a terminate pad, when it returns `()`, a primitive scalar or a
thin pointer. The backend adds its own `__divti3`/`__udivti3`
for an `i128` checked multiply (AArch64's expansion; x86-64's calls nothing
since OD-224, and non-unwinding frames are AArch64-only) and
`__sincos_stret` when both `sin` and `cos` are recorded. No call of a non-unwinding frame with an exception table becomes
a tail call. Measured against LLVM at O0–O3 (stage-1 trustc), trust-cg base
`f6a258444` vs this rule: on the round-4 review's 177-program corpus (2124
runs) the 288 runs that kept unwinding where LLVM fails phase one now match
(228 from created calls, 60 from calls MIR names), and 80 runs in 15 programs
newly fail phase one earlier than LLVM (a runtime `sin`, `powf` or `sin`/`cos`
pair whose result does not reach a `black_box`, an `i128` division LLVM keeps
as a call: a runtime divisor, sign-extended operands, a signed division by 7;
600-byte and 1 KiB fills whose region LLVM covers with a `memset` or `memcpy`
call; the thread-local thunk at O0 and a thread-local the crate writes); on
the round-3 and round-4
corpora (44, 16, 56 and 35 programs; 704, 64, 1076 and 140 runs) no run keeps
unwinding where LLVM fails phase one, 33 runs of the 56-program corpus that
reached a termination pad where LLVM fails phase one now match (a `Box<dyn>`
method call, a closure `fn` pointer at O0, a reified fn item, a `&dyn` of a
promoted constant), and 81 runs newly fail phase one earlier (2 programs of
the 44-program corpus, 7 of the 56-program corpus, where LLVM keeps the libcall
or reaches a termination pad). On 50 further probe programs (600 runs) the 176
keep-unwinding runs of the base drop to 36, all present before: a `fn` pointer,
`&dyn` or `Box<dyn Fn>` a helper returns, which LLVM resolves by inlining the
helper (O1, and O1–O3 for the box; 10 runs); a directly called closure whose
terminate pad LLVM inlines at O1 (2); and a wrapper whose terminate pad LLVM
inlines but whose call returns a tuple, a by-value struct, a `&str` or an
`Option` (O1–O3, 24: such a call's lowering lane carries no terminate edge, so
the frame keeps no table); 66 runs there newly fail phase one earlier.
Not modeled either: LLVM's block placement moving a call across an invoke, and
a frame whose inlinable callees exceed the walk's budget (256 bodies) or depth
(three levels).
LLVM's merge of adjacent same-pad invokes is not modeled
(rustc gives each foreign call in a nounwind body its own pad). A
non-unwinding frame of an unwinding crate (an `extern "C"` body under
`panic=unwind`) still keeps the propagation filler at its nounwind call sites
until source-owned call unwind boundaries are transported through final
layout.
The October 4 combined-source integration
merges this policy with the local scalar-storage and constant-Chain repairs.
On Linux AArch64 its full ten-test allocation target retains 704 LLVM matches
and 72 declared StepBy refusals over 776 rows, with no unexpected refusals.
Scalar-field and Rust unwind-cleanup targets pass, as do 51 selected root
methods, the bridge driver-classification method, fresh five-package root
Tippy and 128 Python gate/census controls. Two O0 native C++ catch/resume
drivers and sixteen native C refinement drivers also execute in that root
scope. Linux foreign-abort admission remains refused. These diagnostics do
not rerun Darwin termination, close the helper/tail-call divergences above,
or supply a complete platform gate, certified EH, canonical proof replay,
std/sysroot or verified-default package.
Coroutine-resumption entries and other targets have no new execution
qualification from the fourteen-form ARM64/macOS rows. Incoming wasm32 abort
bounds support retains its genuine `panic_bounds_check(index, len)` entry and
caller location; the merged source needs its own target-specific qualification,
not credit from an earlier native checkpoint.
Interception-generated checks and general formatted panic substitutions remain
separate legacy routes: some synthesize messages or use internal trap edges,
which are not covered by the MIR assertion differential. The O(1) `Range`
count (`emit_range_run_count_closed_form`) raises its two overflow panics
through std's own route (OD-170): core's `expect("count overflowed usize")`
past `usize::MAX` items, and `Chain::count`'s overflow-checked add. The no_std
panic-handler reachability lane does not qualify every allocation helper or
OOM shim, and the shared general-IR source-Assert refusal floor remains.
The earlier canonical bounds trap omitted the message and hook. Do not restore
that shortcut when merging loop or target work. Some legacy substitutions use
libc `abort` followed by `Unreachable`; the raw abort-intrinsic trap is a
separate route. Their coverage does not establish complete panic fidelity.
The shared general-IR adapter remains fail-closed for source `Inst::Assert`, and
certificates-on native EH remains TB-12 until actual source-bound proof
obligations qualify.

**Decoded `print!` (std's own sink, one write per call).** The bridge formats
a `print!`/`eprint!` it can decode into a heap buffer and passes the text to
std's own `_print`/`_eprint` as one string-literal `fmt::Arguments`
(`lower_print`), so std's buffered stdout, its lock, libtest's output capture
and the write-error panic apply, and on a normal exit each stream receives
LLVM's bytes in LLVM's order. Three differences remain (measured on
ARM64/macOS at O0–O3, 2026-10-05). The heap buffer is an allocation LLVM's
print does not make: a counting `#[global_allocator]` sees one more request per
call, and one that fails it aborts with std's allocation-error message where
LLVM's print succeeds. std receives the text as one `write_all` where LLVM's
`fmt::write` hands it over in pieces, so when the text crosses the free space
of std's 1024-byte stdout buffer a different prefix is already written: an
`abort()` or signal before the next flush keeps a different prefix, and an
`eprint!` while stdout and stderr share one terminal, pipe or file (`2>&1`)
lands at a different point of the stdout text. After a failed write (EPIPE)
LLVM keeps the failed line buffered and the next stdout write panics again;
the bridge keeps nothing, so a print after that panic is caught, or in a
destructor during its unwind, does not panic (exit 0 or 101 where LLVM exits
101 or aborts with "panic in a destructor during cleanup").

**Cross-backend `Memory`-argument ABI (lowered on x86-64 and AArch64,
2026-09-28).** rustc's Rust ABI passes every sized `BackendRepr::Memory` value larger
than a pointer — a non-`ScalarPair` struct, array or enum (`struct T12 { u32, u32,
u32 }`, `[u32; 3]`), and also an over-aligned single-scalar newtype
(`#[repr(C, align(16))] struct A16 { a: u64 }`, the `#[repr(align(128))]`
`CachePadded` shape) — as `PassMode::Indirect { on_stack: false }`: a POINTER to
a caller-made copy. The bridge used to pass the bytes (System V lanes, a `byval`
stack copy over 16 bytes, or the newtype's one scalar). Both sides of an
all-bridge program used the bridge's convention, so single-crate differentials and
the `core` census did not see it; across a real boundary they disagreed (measured
on x86-64 Darwin, rlib x bin: `T12` by value — LLVM rlib + bridge bin SIGSEGV,
bridge rlib + LLVM bin 197 at O0 and 71 at O2 against 237; `A16` by value — SIGSEGV
at O0 and O2, and 220 / 75 against 67). **On x86-64 (System V and Darwin) the
bridge now passes these as rustc does**: the indirect argument lane — trust-ir
`docs/SPEC_RATIFICATIONS.md` §17's pre-lowered crossing — declares the argument as
one pointer, passes the address of a fresh copy at every call site and copies the
pointee into the callee's slot (for a padded scalar: stores the scalar at offset 0
of a copy of rustc's size and alignment, and loads it back in the callee); the
argument gate (`check_param_abi_lanes`) compares that pointer against rustc's
placement and refuses a by-value declaration left over (`m145_x86_indirect_arg_xback`,
driven by `tests/tools/m145_xback.py`: every rlib x bin cell agrees with LLVM x
LLVM). What remains on x86-64:

- REFUSED BY NAME, not lowered: an over-aligned single-scalar newtype RETURNED by
  value — over a pointer too (`#[repr(C, align(16))] struct AP { p: *const u64 }`,
  `#[repr(align(16))] struct AR(&'static u64)`) — (rustc returns it through the
  hidden buffer; `[TCG-RET-ABI]` — this includes `core::hint::black_box::<A16>`;
  before: `-> CachePadded`-shaped `CP` SIGSEGV / 0 against 16, `-> AP` / `-> AR`
  a bus error / 0 against 30), a padded `f32` rustc casts to an integer register
  (`#[repr(align(8))] struct F8(f32)`; `[TCG-ARG-ABI]`; before: 3 against 13), an
  over-aligned UNION passed or returned by value, whatever its carrier
  (`#[repr(C, align(16))] union UP { p: *const u64 }` / `union UI { i: u64 }`;
  before, for the pointer carrier: SIGSEGV / 112 against 40 as an argument, a bus
  error / 3 against 33 as a return), such a newtype or union as an element of a
  `dyn Fn*` call's arguments (before, for `&dyn Fn(AP)` built by LLVM and called
  from a bridge bin: SIGSEGV against 41), and such a newtype passed to a closure
  through a lane that builds no padded copy (the iterator and collection
  interception lanes, a constant argument tuple; `[TCG-ARG-ABI]` from the
  call-argument check). Only the intercepted collections below keep their
  historical pointer, and they are recognised by identity, not by the bridge
  declaring a pointer.
- `extern "rust-call"` callables (round 10, F2): a `Fn*::call*` shim over a fn
  item or fn pointer (`FnPtrShim`), `FnOnce::call_once` over a closure
  (`ClosureOnceShim`), the `VTableShim` every `dyn Fn*` vtable carries for
  `call_once`, a `Fn*` impl method (`<&F as Fn<A>>::call`,
  `<Box<F> as Fn<A>>::call`) and a user `extern "rust-call"` fn are declared
  with the argument tuple's ELEMENTS, as rustc's `FnAbi` lists them
  (`rust_call_spread::abi_inputs`). The body binds them as ordinary arguments
  and rebuilds the tuple at entry, as `rustc_codegen_ssa` rebuilds
  `spread_arg` (`rust_call_spread::body`), and every call spreads its tuple
  operand through one reader (`spread_fn_call_tuple_untupled`). Until then the
  bridge declared the tuple as ONE parameter, which is consistent only among
  the bridge's own static calls: code reaching such a callable through its
  ADDRESS (a vtable slot, a `fn` pointer) or BY SYMBOL (`-Zshare-generics`, an
  exported or upstream item) passes the elements untupled (measured
  2026-09-27/28: `&dyn Fn(T12)` over a fn item 176 or 80 against 151; `&dyn
  Fn(u64, u64, u64)` 218 or 99 against 195; an exported `<&fn-item as Fn<(u64,
  u64, u64)>>::call` 190 / 220 against 231; a non-generic `pub extern
  "rust-call" fn` SIGSEGV / 162 against 117), and the bridge refused every such
  callable by name wherever the other backend could reach it
  (`refuse_tupled_rust_call_escape`, `refuse_tupled_rust_call_shared_symbol`,
  both deleted). Those shapes now compile and agree with LLVM x LLVM in every
  rlib x bin cell (`m145`'s `w2_*` / `w1_padded_pointer_dyn_fn` controls, the
  family matrix's `rc_p7` / `rc_p5` / `rc_i128` / `dyn_i128` / `dyn_fn_pair`
  rows; measured 2026-09-30, aarch64-apple-darwin natively and
  x86_64-apple-darwin under Rosetta, O0 and O2; on the pre-F2 build the same
  rows were refused by name in 17 cells per target, none wrong).
  Dynamic `FnOnce` dispatch is still refused, by name: a bridge-compiled
  `Box<dyn FnOnce>` call (and a `Box<dyn Fn>` or `Box<dyn FnMut>` consumed
  as `FnOnce`) moves an unsized receiver and is refused with
  `[TCG-DYN-FNONCE]`, and a bridge crate that boxes a capturing `FnOnce`
  closure is refused because the `FnOnce::call_once` vtable shim has an
  unlowerable body. A `Box<dyn Fn>` blanket call with a cleanup unwind edge
  at `-O0`/`-O1` under `panic=unwind`, and `static`/`const` `dyn Fn` vtables
  in bridge libraries, are refused under the generic `[TCG-MIR-UNSUPPORTED]`
  tag. LLVM compiles all of these (L06-P16 first closure audit,
  2026-10-16, Linux AArch64).
- By-value (`FnOnce`) closure ENVIRONMENTS (round 10): a closure body that
  takes its environment by value declares it as argument 0 of rustc's own
  `FnAbi` (`closure_body_env_by_value`), by rustc's mode, like any by-value
  argument: a pointer to a copy, the two `Pair` scalars, the one integer of a
  narrow `Cast`, or the slot. Until round 10 the bridge declared every closure
  environment as a pointer to the closure, which disagreed with rustc wherever
  rustc passes a by-value environment of at most 16 bytes of scalars in
  registers (measured 2026-09-28, `make(v) -> impl FnOnce(u64) -> u64` moving an
  8-byte `NC(u64)` in, oracle 57: LLVM rlib + bridge bin 176 / 209 / 235 across
  runs, bridge rlib + LLVM bin SIGSEGV at O0), and such a body was refused by
  name where another crate reached it by symbol
  (`refuse_by_value_closure_env_shared_symbol`, deleted). The family matrix's
  `env_pair` / `env_scalar` / `env_slice` / `env_c3` / `env_t12` / `env_refs`
  rows hold the by-mode declaration in every rlib x bin cell. `Fn` / `FnMut`
  bodies take `&self` / `&mut self`, a pointer on both sides.

- `dyn Fn*` over a fn ITEM or fn POINTER: the vtable slot holds the
  `FnPtrShim` itself, declared with the argument tuple's elements like every
  `rust-call` shim (above). While the shim was declared TUPLED, the slot held
  a module-local spread entry instead (`fn_ptr_shim_dyn_entry`), admitted only
  for scalar and thin-pointer elements and returns and refused otherwise
  (`[TCG-FN-DYN-ENTRY]`; measured 2026-10-02 on Linux AArch64 at `13a7b0ad9`
  for `&dyn Fn(u64) -> (f64, f64)` over a fn item, which LLVM compiles). The
  entry is deleted with the tupled declaration. Re-measured 2026-10-08 on
  aarch64-apple-darwin with this merge's backend, the same fixture and driver
  (`rust_call_shims_linux`'s `fn_item_float_pair_vtable`, `-Cpanic=abort`, one
  codegen unit): every library x binary pairing prints LLVM's bits at O0, O2
  and O3, so the Linux test holds it as a row that must agree; it was not run
  on Linux AArch64 for this merge.
- CLOSURE calls returning a float pair (Linux AArch64, measured 2026-10-02 at
  `13a7b0ad9`; native executions against LLVM, not an ABI proof). An
  env-gated trace of the bridge shows every one-argument closure call of the
  test taking the closure `PassMode::Pair` return, and every capturing
  zero-argument one taking the float-carrier (`hfa_return`) return.
  `rust_call_shims_linux` runs both across an rlib boundary: `move`,
  by-reference, float-environment, `FnMut` and `FnOnce` closures returning
  `(f64, f64)`, `(f32, f32)`, a `#[repr(C)]` `{f64, f64}` or a Rust
  `{f32, f32}`, called directly, through a generic, a `&dyn Fn`, an `impl Fn`
  or a borrowed library `Box<dyn Fn>`. Every bridge/LLVM pairing prints LLVM's
  bits at O0, O2 and O3 (`-Cpanic=abort`, one codegen unit). A scratch
  differential of the same fixture also matches at O0, O1, O2, O3 and Os under
  `-Cpanic=abort` and `-Cpanic=unwind`, with 1 and 16 codegen units (60 of 60
  pairings). The float-environment closures measured there capture two
  floats (a pair, `[f32; 2]` or a two-float struct); a closure capturing one
  float is below. Over the same five levels and both panic strategies, with one
  codegen unit (30 pairings each), these also match: `(f32, f64)` returns called directly, through a
  generic or through a `&dyn Fn`; `[f64; 2]` returns called directly, through
  a generic or through an `impl Fn`; `&mut dyn FnMut` over closures with
  integer environments; and a borrowed `Box<dyn Fn>` returning `(f32, f32)`.
  These shapes are REFUSED by name, although LLVM compiles them:
  - `[f64; 2]` (rustc's `PassMode::Indirect`) through a dynamic call (a
    `&dyn Fn` or a `Box<dyn Fn>`) is `[TCG-SRET-ABI]` in the crate where the
    bridge compiles that call, at O0 to Os (`closure_array_pair_dyn` pins O0,
    O2 and O3).
  - A non-capturing closure coerced to `fn(u64) -> (f64, f64)` or
    `fn(u64) -> (f32, f32)` is `[TCG-CLOSURE-FNPTR]`: its fn-pointer entry does
    not forward a float-pair carrier plan. The bridge-built crate that performs
    the coercion is refused at O0 to Os. From O1, rustc may inline a small
    coercing function into its caller's crate, and that crate is then the
    refused one (`closure_float_pair_fn_pointer` pins O0, O2 and O3).
    `fn(u64) -> u64` and `fn(u64) -> f64` compile and match. Declaring the
    closure's `FnOnce::call_once` shim untupled (F2, round 10) did not change
    this: the pointer still lands on the module-local entry
    (`closure_fn_pointer_entry`), and re-measured 2026-10-08 on
    aarch64-apple-darwin with the same fixture, the bridge-built rlib is still
    refused `[TCG-CLOSURE-FNPTR]` at O0, O2 and O3 (an LLVM-built rlib with a
    bridge-built binary compiles and matches). So is `closure_array_pair_dyn`
    above (`[TCG-SRET-ABI]`, the same three levels).
  - A closure whose whole environment is one `f32` or one `f64` (rustc's
    `Scalar(Float)`, passed `Direct` in a floating-point register) was refused
    at every by-value crossing, measured there: behind a `&dyn Fn` or `&mut dyn
    FnMut`, or passed BY VALUE to a generic `F: Fn`, `[TCG-ARG-ABI]` at O0 to
    Os; returned as an `impl Fn`, `[TCG-RET-ABI]`; the bridge declared that
    environment's slot as an INTEGER lane. Since the round-10 review (F1) the
    slot is a one-lane FLOAT aggregate (`closure_slot_ty`), which trust-cg's
    classifiers place in a floating-point register like rustc's scalar, and
    the whole-signature check compares it with rustc's placement at every
    declaration. The family matrix's `env_f64` / `env_f32` (an `impl FnOnce`
    maker), `fn_env_f64` / `fn_env_f32` (a generic `F: Fn` argument),
    `fn_env_f32_stack` (that argument on the stack after eight `f64`s),
    `dyn_env_f64` / `dyn_env_f32` and `fnmut_env_f64` rows hold it in every
    rlib x bin cell at O0-O3. Measured 2026-10-08 on aarch64-apple-darwin and
    x86_64-apple-darwin under Rosetta (`targo --unverified`, no proof claim):
    the first run had `env_f64` / `env_f32` WRONG on x86-64 in both cells with
    a bridge-built binary, exit 0 against LLVM's 7 at every level (16 cells),
    while AArch64 agreed. The binary copied the returned environment into its
    slot with an integer-typed store of the float value
    (`copy_memory_aggregate_call_result`), which the x86-64 selector encoded as
    a store of an unrelated general register (the slot's own address). The
    copy now stores a float lane at its own type (`slot_lane_value_ty`), the
    x86-64 selector refuses a store whose value lives in the other register
    file (`store_source_for_type`), and every cell of those rows agrees on both
    targets. Not re-measured on Linux AArch64.
  - Under `-Cpanic=unwind`, any `Box<dyn Fn>` call that has a cleanup edge is
    `[TCG-MIR-UNSUPPORTED]` ("Box<dyn Fn> blanket call with cleanup unwind edge
    (EH active) not yet lowered") at O0, O1 and Os: an owned box in the frame
    that drops it (`let b = make(k); b(x)`), a BORROWED box called in a frame
    that holds any other value with a destructor, and calls while iterating a
    `Vec<Box<dyn Fn>>`. They compile and match at O2 and O3, and under
    `-Cpanic=abort`. The borrowed `Box<dyn Fn>` that matches above is called
    in a frame with nothing to drop. This refusal is not specific to float
    pairs.
- Over-aligned scalar HOMES (fixed on x86-64 2026-09-28; not introduced by the
  lane): every stack home the bridge gives an over-aligned single-scalar newtype
  (the same layout test admits a single-field union; not measured, because a
  borrowed over-aligned union local fails closed before and after with `memory
  aggregate construct without layout`) — the temporary behind a `&a` call argument
  (a local, or the callee's copy of a by-value parameter), a local's scalar cell
  (all cells are allocated in one place; measured for a raw-borrowed and a
  closure-captured local), and the data half of `&a as &dyn Trait` — used to be an
  `Alloca` of the scalar, so `&a` was 8 mod 16 and the home 8 bytes where rustc's
  value is 16 (measured before: a probe flagging misaligned `&A16` addresses 8 =
  none for LLVM x LLVM, 13 / 10 / 15 in the cells with a bridge side; an LLVM
  `-O2` callee whose `movaps` loads the promised 16 aligned bytes SIGSEGV'd on a
  bridge local). Each home now has rustc's size and alignment with the scalar at
  offset 0 (`padded_scalar_home_extent`, over-allocated and rounded up past the
  16-byte stack alignment like the sub-lane's argument copy; `m145` `w1_*_home_*`
  rows, `padded_scalar_home_alignment` fixture). Still open (not measured): a
  SCALARIZED over-aligned MULTI-field aggregate materialized for a `&T` call
  argument or a `&dyn` data pointer is an `Alloca` of the bridge's field tuple at
  its natural alignment. The September 30 scalar-cell repairs record the
  padded home's actual rustc extent. Each admitted scalar-cell field projection
  selects the container's only field occupying storage, at offset zero, and
  ends at the exact allocated scalar type, size and alignment
  (`checked_scalar_cell_projection`). Zero-sized siblings do not count as fields
  occupying storage; selecting a zero-sized field still refuses in this scalar
  access path. The cell must have exclusive ownership, and every projection
  step must retain the checked storage or allocated-home extent and alignment.
  This closes the former `[TCG-SCALAR-CELL-LAYOUT]` refusal for a celled padded
  local's `a.a` and for the existing `ZstLead((), u64)` field-1 store without
  replacing its allocation. The unchanged `m145` matrix passes on AArch64 Linux
  at O0–O3, including the O0 dynamic-method home; the earlier failed campaign
  remains separately recorded in the
  consolidation audit.
  The separate closure-wrapper projection helper retains its narrower
  one-declared-field rule. Earlier pointer-projection and mutable-reference
  field-write refusals (`(*p).a`: `Place projection`; `r.a = v`: `assignment
  destination projection is not scalar-bindable`) remain separate recorded
  boundaries, not measurements of these repairs.
- Over-aligned C-ABI ARGUMENTS on AArch64 ELF (lowered 2026-10-14, decision
  record LD-28). AAPCS64 places a composite of at most 16 bytes by its
  NATURAL alignment, that of its most-aligned member; a `#[repr(C,
  align(N))]` attribute does not count, and rustc's Linux `FnAbi` agrees
  (`unadjusted_abi_align`). So `#[repr(C, align(16))] struct { u64, u64 }`
  (likewise `{ u64 }`, `{ u32 }`, `{ u8 }`, `{ u32, u32, u32 }`, `{ u32, Oa4 }`)
  is cast to `[2 x i64]`: two consecutive registers from any NGRN (x1:x2 after
  one integer) and an 8-aligned stack slot. The bridge declared the value's
  16-aligned `I128` slot (a single-scalar newtype: the scalar), which
  trust-cg's classifier starts on an even register and in a 16-aligned stack
  slot, DarwinPCS's reading. Measured by the L06-P9 review on `6d57acba4`:
  silent wrong values in both mixed pairings at O0-O3 (`take(u64, Al16, u64)`
  read `p1` from x2:x3). From round 10 (`check_signature_placement`) to
  `395954590` the declarations were refused by name instead, at an odd NGRN
  or an NSAA of 8 mod 16 and, for the scalar newtypes, at every position (on
  `395954590` the bridge refused 11 of the 14 callee functions of the
  `overaligned_c_arguments` fixture). They are now declared as rustc's two
  `I64` units
  (`aapcs64_unadjusted_block_plan` for a memory slot, `Aapcs64ScalarBlock` for
  a padded scalar) and match LLVM in all four rlib x bin pairings at O0-O3:
  `overaligned_c_arguments` in the required `aarch64_c_fnabi_aggregate_linux`
  target (x1/x3/x5, the stack with one register left and at NSAA 8, the
  padded newtypes, a result, a C `fn` pointer and a C callback) and the
  `overalign` family of the Linux cross-backend runner
  ([record](reports/perf/2026-10-14-linux-cross-backend-abi/README.md)). Still
  REFUSED BY NAME on Linux and listed in that runner's table: an over-aligned
  value rustc casts to `i128` (a repr(C) struct around a 16-aligned member) or
  to one narrow integer (`#[repr(C, align(2))] struct { u8 }`, `align(8) { u16
  }`, Rust-ABI `#[repr(align(4))] struct { u16 }`) while the bridge declares
  its scalar (`[TCG-ARG-ABI]`); over-aligned HFAs (`[TCG-AAPCS64-HFA]`);
  32- and 64-aligned values; and the over-aligned results listed there. Darwin
  keeps the adjusted alignment (`i128`) and is unchanged; it was not measured
  for this change. The two-unit declaration and the "match LLVM" above hold
  for non-variadic signatures only. As a FIXED argument of a C-variadic
  function the declaration is not taken (the variadic aggregate scope refuses
  its carrier), and until 2026-10-15 the whole-signature check skipped
  C-variadic signatures: a trust-cg caller of an LLVM-built variadic function
  passed `#[repr(C, align(16))] { u64 }`, `{ u32 }`, `{ u8 }` and the repr(C)
  wrapper around a 16-aligned member in the scalar's register, a silent wrong
  value or a crash at O0-O3 (found by the L06-P9 re-review, on `395954590`'s
  backend as well); `{ u64 }`, `{ u8 }` and the wrapper were also wrong
  through a C-variadic `fn` pointer called with no anonymous argument (found
  by the next review; measured on that backend). The check now judges
  every Linux AArch64 direct variadic call whole, anonymous arguments
  included, and every C-variadic `fn` pointer signature on its fixed
  arguments (decision record LD-29), and those fixed arguments are REFUSED BY
  NAME on a trust-cg caller (`[TCG-ARG-ABI]`; a `{ u64, u64 }` composite by
  the aggregate scope, `[TCG-AGGREGATE-ABI-SCOPE]`), pinned by the
  `overaligned_c_arguments` refusal fixture and the cross-backend runner's
  `varargs` rows.
- Collection representation (source repair, 2026-09-30): default-Global
  Vec/String headers use rustc's actual 24-byte, alignment-8 image,
  `{cap,ptr,len}`, checked through the real nested fields and allocator
  identity. Bare values, references and Box payloads share that image through
  storage, calls, returns and drop. Earlier synthetic pointer-to-slot values
  caused mixed-backend SIGSEGVs and wrong reference reads (September 27–28);
  those witnesses remain part of the audit. Qualification covers native
  AArch64 Linux and explicitly measured shapes. Collection-containing
  aggregates, drop-needing elements and other targets remain separate open
  work. BTreeMap/HashMap keep their synthetic slot representation, licensed by
  provenance since 2026-10-01 (`[TCG-FOREIGN-MAP]`): a map method, field read
  or drop applies only to a map value this function's own constructor built,
  and a slot-modeled map crossing a code boundary (a call to code compiled
  elsewhere, a `fn` pointer, a vtable) is refused, so a map LLVM-compiled code
  built is never read as a slot. Since 2026-10-03 a map constructor is
  recognized by crate identity (an inherent function of the real
  `BTreeMap`/`HashMap`/hashbrown map), an unsizing of a map-holding value to a
  trait object anywhere in the crate is a boundary, upstream drop glue over a
  map kind this crate builds refuses, and an `Entry` is served only from a
  live record of the `entry()` call that made it (`[TCG-MAP-ENTRY-USE]`
  otherwise). Since 2026-10-04 that record follows its local through loops
  and joins: every record made on a local is also stored in a per-local
  record cell, so a loop header or join whose incoming records differ reads
  the record of the path taken (`e = b.entry(..)` at the bottom of a loop,
  `if c { a.entry(1) } else { b.entry(2) }`, now matching LLVM); a loop whose
  back edge rebinds the local to anything but such an entry refuses; a
  record moves only into a value that provably is that entry or wraps it as
  its only field (a tuple of two entries refuses), and a variant read
  through such a wrapper (`match w.0` for `struct W(Entry<..>)`) is served
  from the map, while the drop glue of a wrapper that has any (a `Drop`
  impl) refuses; and every read of a local that may hold an intercepted
  entry refuses unless a live record serves it (`[TCG-FOREIGN-MAP]`: a join
  of an own and a foreign entry, a raw pointer taken to the entry local). A
  cast, raw-pointer build (`slice::from_raw_parts`) or union read that turns
  a value able to carry a slot-modeled map into a type that cannot (`as
  usize`, `.cast::<u8>()`, `ptr::addr`, `transmute`), or forges one from such
  a type (`*(buf.as_mut_ptr() as *mut &HashMap<..>) = &h`, and the element
  pointer `Vec`/`VecDeque` make of their `u8` buffer), refuses in every
  function the crate lowers; std's own `Box::new` and `<Box as Drop>::drop`
  for `Global` are exempt, since they only allocate and free the box. The
  round-2 review's four open classes (60 of 552 cells of its 138-program
  corpus), the forged-pointer, byte-slice and `Vec<&HashMap>` escapes and
  the two wrapper classes found since no longer build a wrong value: across
  the 28 corpora that change re-ran (599 programs, 2,396 cells at O0–O3, 20
  cells where LLVM itself fails excluded) no cell builds and disagrees with
  LLVM, where 205 did before it (59 of them now match, 146 refuse; 59 cells
  that refused before now match). 33 cells that matched before now refuse:
  26 are joins of an own and a foreign entry and 4 a loop whose back edge
  brings a foreign entry, where the binary before it reads memory the
  intercepted `entry()` never wrote, or the first entry's record, whenever
  the other path is taken (they matched because the run took the foreign
  branch, or the stale bytes or the stale record gave the right variant;
  the same shape with another key is wrong before it), and 3 are a raw
  pointer taken to an entry local at -O1..-O3, whose writes through the
  pointer no record can follow. Still open:
  the boundary walk does not see through `PhantomData` (a `Vec`'s elements),
  which only the forging check stands in for, and an upstream crate this
  bridge compiled is treated as LLVM code. The map model compares raw key
  lanes and runs no user code, so it serves only key/value types none of whose
  std-called trait methods it would skip: no drop glue in `K` or `V`; a key
  `Ord` (BTreeMap) or `PartialEq` + `Hash` (HashMap) that is primitive,
  `PhantomData`, or a builtin derive over such fields; std's `RandomState`
  hasher; a lookup `&Q` with `Q == K`; and, for `or_default`, a primitive or
  builtin-derived `Default` with no default field value over such fields (the
  zero lane). A builtin derive is an `#[automatically_derived]` impl whose
  span is a rustc builtin derive macro's expansion, in the crate or upstream;
  the attribute alone is ungated and is not trusted. A map with integer lanes
  outside that set refuses as `[TCG-MAP-MODEL-TRAIT]`. Before, a hand-written
  key `Ord`/`Eq`/`Hash`, value `Default`, `Drop` key or value, or user
  `BuildHasher` compiled and diverged from LLVM at every level, and so did,
  until 2026-10-04, an upstream hand-written impl carrying
  `#[automatically_derived]` and a derived `Default` with a default field
  value. Refused although std's behavior for them equals the model's (a
  fail-closed loss): core's hand-written impls (`NonZero` keys, `Reverse` keys
  in a BTreeMap), every hasher but `RandomState` (std's
  `BuildHasherDefault<DefaultHasher>` too), and a default field value that is
  zero. `bool` keys and values are not integer lanes and stay unmodeled.
  Evidence: `tests/map_model_user_trait_differential_aarch64.rs`. The
  real std/sysroot audit records the
  broader graph's required roots; standalone collection success does not
  establish full std support.
  The 2026-10-04 current sysroot/header checkpoint
  repairs receiver-based Vec routing to require the actual impl owner, and
  String aggregate construction to copy its real Vec<u8> header instead of
  substituting an empty header for a parameter without scalar state. Native
  AArch64 Linux controls check O0–O3 mixed LLVM/CG calls, buffer identity,
  capacity, contents and one observed free per drop. The unchanged full library
  graph and native consumer matrix still fail; collection-containing String
  images, Unicode case conversion and bounded Vec drains retain their separate
  refusals. Certificates-off execution supplies no proof credit.
  Both `vec![value; count]` paths (`lower_vec_from_elem` for a scalar element,
  `lower_vec_from_elem_image` for a struct element) used to allocate
  `max(count, 1)` elements, so an empty result reported capacity 1 where LLVM
  reports 0 (candidate 9d: both CG empty `Vec<Pair>` cases at O0/O3;
  re-measured 2026-10-03 on Darwin AArch64 with a bridge-built `make`: the
  struct program exits 15 against LLVM's 117 and the scalar program 223
  against LLVM's 74, at O0 and O3). FIXED 2026-10-03: the buffer holds exactly
  `count` elements through `emit_collection_resize` (the alignment's dangling
  pointer and no allocator call for zero bytes), and the struct prototype
  lives in a stack slot of the element's extent and alignment instead of heap
  element 0 (`tests/vec_from_elem_capacity_aarch64.rs`: both programs, all
  sixteen backend x opt-level cells agree with LLVM). Both share the
  constructors' byte-bound capacity guard and null-handler guard, which
  `real_program_runtime_aarch64`'s from_elem capacity-overflow, byte-wrap,
  struct-overflow and allocation-failure rows execute natively.
- Owning-iterator representation (source repair, 2026-10-05): the bridge's
  `vec::Drain<T>` (a no-drop element it intercepts, over the Global allocator;
  another allocator's Drain is std's code throughout) is std's own state at
  rustc's offsets (`VecDrainLayout`, read through `layout_of`; a layout it
  cannot match refuses as `[TCG-VEC-DRAIN-LAYOUT]`). `Vec::drain` writes std's
  five words and, as std does, shortens the Vec to the range start before the
  Drain exists; `next` advances `iter.ptr`; the identity `into_iter` copies
  all five words; and the drop of a Drain local, like the `<Drain as
  Drop>::drop` call in rustc's `drop_glue::<Drain<T>>`, applies std's
  transition (memmove the kept tail back, restore the length). A Drain built
  on either side of a bridge/LLVM boundary is therefore valid on the other.
  The earlier private four-word cursor read and wrote the wrong words there
  (hunt UP2-T1-DRAIN-PRIVATE-LAYOUT-AT-STD-BOUNDARY and
  UP2-T1-DRAIN-DEFERRED-TRUNCATION on c8b07006b: out-of-bounds memmoves,
  lengths past the capacity, drained elements restored, a leaked Drain leaving
  a moved-out element in the Vec, and an undefined shared drop glue at O0).
  Across that hunt's 122 probe programs with a recorded baseline (1,247
  cells, a bridge library and an LLVM driver, O0–O3), all 455 wrong,
  crashing or unlinkable cells now match LLVM, 117 refused cells now match,
  no matching cell changed, and 409 still refuse by name;
  `tests/vec_drain_std_layout_differential.rs` pins both directions and a
  custom-allocator Drain (wrong on c8b07006b: its drop was intercepted over
  std's state) at O0–O3.
  A bounded-end range (`..b`, `a..b`, `a..=b`) built by the bridge, a Drain
  adapter chain and a droppable element still refuse, as does any other call
  whose first argument is a Drain or a pointer to one
  (`[TCG-OWNING-ITER-METHOD]`: `mem::forget`, `ptr::drop_in_place` and a
  crate-local function taking a Drain where the MIR inliner leaves the call,
  `Box<dyn Iterator>` over a Drain at every level). The same root cause, a
  private state where std has its own, was measured in three other
  intercepts on c8b07006b (a bridge library and an LLVM driver), and each
  now keeps std's state as well. The slice stride iterators (`windows`,
  `chunks`, `chunks_exact`, `rchunks`, `rchunks_exact`) kept a private
  `{ptr, end, n}` cursor (returned to or passed from LLVM code:
  SIGBUS/SIGSEGV or a wrong value at O1, an undefined shared generic at O0,
  `[TCG-STRIDE-ITER-INLINE]` at O2/O3); they now hold std's fields at the
  `slice_stride_iter_layout` offsets (`[TCG-STRIDE-ITER-LAYOUT]` when that
  certificate fails), and the Drain fixer's stride-boundary probe matches
  LLVM in all 24 cells. `StepBy` kept a synthetic state (wrong values both
  ways at O0); it now holds core's `StepBy::new` state and is still
  O0-only (`[TCG-STEPBY-OPT-LEVEL]` above). A bounded `flat_map` returned
  as `impl Iterator` kept a private encoding (wrong values at O0/O1); it
  now holds std's `FlattenCompat` layout (hunt clusters
  R2T-STEPBY-PACKED-STATE-AT-BOUNDARY and
  R2T-FLATMAP-PRIVATE-ENCODING-ESCAPE).
- Dead bodies and generic instances a bridge-built library would export
  (2026-10-02). A std body the bridge classifies as DEAD because it replaces
  every call site it lowers with an intercepted operation — the
  iterator-reduction internals (`SpecTake::spec_fold`, `Chain::try_fold`, ...)
  and the intercepted collections' alloc/drop glue (`drop_glue::<Vec<T>>`, ...)
  — becomes a trapping stub in a library when it does not lower, and an
  unlowerable non-local body nothing in the crate references is dropped. The
  classification sees only this crate's call sites. Measured on origin/main
  6a57e8ab9 (proofs-off lane, LLVM caller over a bridge rlib): under
  `-Zshare-generics` (rustc's default at `-Copt-level=0`, `1`, `s` and `z`, and
  for every `#[inline(never)]` generic) rustc lists the instances a library
  instantiates in its metadata and a downstream crate links them instead of
  instantiating its own, so an `-O1` caller's own
  `a.iter().chain(a.iter()).take(5).count()` linked the library's stubbed
  `Chain::try_fold` (SIGTRAP), an `-O3` caller built with
  `-Zshare-generics=yes` reached the `-O0` library's stubbed
  `SpecTake::spec_fold` the same way (SIGTRAP), and an `-O0`/`-O1` caller
  dropping its own `vec::IntoIter<u32>` failed to link on the library's DROPPED
  `drop_glue::<vec::IntoIter<u32>>` / `<IntoIter<u32> as Drop>::drop` (closed,
  but no binary for a correct program); and a library `static` holding
  `drop_in_place::<Vec<u32>>` as a fn pointer named the dead-heap-glue stub
  (SIGTRAP at `-O0`..`-O3` when the caller dropped its own `Vec` through it),
  because a library's reference graph held only its functions' references.
  Re-measured on origin/main 6b108b81d (2026-10-05, same lane): the static
  still trapped at `-O0`..`-O3`, the `-O1` caller's own chain/take/count
  still trapped, and the `-O0`/`-O1` owning-iterator callers still failed to
  link.
  Now: where Trust lets a codegen backend provide queries (`-Ztrust-verify=off`
  without `-Ztrust-ir-lower` or a Trust test monitor; verification is on by
  default), the bridge provides an empty `exported_generic_symbols` for its
  crate (`withheld_exported_generic_symbols`), so a downstream crate
  instantiates its own copy, as at `-Copt-level=2`/`3`; a library's static
  relocations join its reference graph, so
  `[TCG-HEAP-GLUE-STUB-REACHABLE]` refuses the static's stub; and where
  rustc's list stands (verification, `-Ztrust-ir-lower`, a Trust test
  monitor: Trust stops a compile whose backend replaced that provider), a
  dead body rustc exports is refused by name (`[TCG-DEAD-BODY-EXPORTED]`)
  instead of stubbed. The repros
  (`tests/dead_body_trap_stub_differential.rs`) match LLVM in the proofs-off
  lane except the static, which is refused. Still open in the canonical lanes:
  an exported body the bridge DROPS (the owning-iterator glue above, or an
  `-O1` library's `LocalKey::with` for the `RandomState` key cell that a
  caller's own `HashMap::new` links) still fails the downstream link closed
  rather than being refused in the library.

**Linux allocation integration check (2026-10-04).** On the installed
`ae9c2c1d` Trust package, all nine allocation-model tests pass after the
scalar-owner field-address repair: 640 of 712 rows match LLVM, and 72 iterator
rows retain the fixture's declared refusals. The null-allocation fixture's
120 rows now execute at O0–O3 with abort/unwind strategies. Its `Rc::new<u64>`
raw borrow of a nested zero-sized `Global` field uses the scalar owner's
checked rustc layout and storage, shared with references and other field
projections. The unchanged small reproducer also runs successfully in all
eight configurations. The
historical integration record
retains the original eight passing tests, strict failed ninth test and
artifact identities. The
repair record
adds sixteen native field-address runs against an independent LLVM observer,
including function-item fields, aligned one-past addresses and a callback
rewriting the pointer field. Each run requires forty actual address
observations; a constant-success producer fails that count. Certificates and
frontend verification remain off. The 72 required iterator refusals and
broader Linux qualification remain open; no completion row or proof authority
is closed by these native diagnostics.

The subsequent constant Chain payload repair
materializes compiler-folded iterator images through the checked CTFE byte and
relocation path, preserving direct `Some` tags and niche pointer payloads.
Its separate strict O0–O3 abort/unwind test passes 64 rows, including exact
allocation/free sizes, capacity and independent LLVM observation of the
produced chain. Two native outputs with the required observer count omitted
are rejected even though their values and allocation output remain correct.
The original fixture's 72 optimized StepBy refusal rows remain required work;
this constructor repair supplies no full std, proof or platform closure.
The full ten-test allocation target passes at this checkpoint: 704 native
LLVM matches, 72 declared refusals and zero unexpected refusals over 776 rows.

**`vec![x; n]` and slice-sort models against the user code std runs in them
(2026-10-04).** Measured on Darwin AArch64 (Trust pack 9192, `no-proof-certs`,
bridge against LLVM, -O0..-O3) by
`tests/clone_sort_user_trait_differential_aarch64.rs`. Each first-round finding
row built a diverging binary at origin/main 33eefbf58 (or another gate refused
it at O2/O3); each second-round item below was measured at the first fix,
529ace6eb, where it built a diverging binary or (the derived-`Copy` element)
refused a program 33eefbf58 matched. Every finding row now builds-and-matches
or refuses by name; the control rows match LLVM before and after; the
evidence-boundary rows pin a refusal this entry names.

- `vec![x; n]` of a struct or tuple element broadcast `x`'s image and never
  called its `Clone` (a counting `clone` that adds 1: `r=11100` against LLVM's
  `r=12202`; a `clone` that panics on its second call never panicked), also for
  a field-wise derived `Clone` that reaches a hand-written field `clone`. The
  image lowering now requires `clone_is_bitwise_copy` or
  `clone_body_copies_self` (the resolved `clone` is exactly `*self` and calls
  nothing: a non-generic type deriving both `Clone` and `Copy`, whose derived
  clone never calls a field's `clone`, or a hand-written `*self`) and otherwise
  refuses with `[TCG-FROM-ELEM-CLONE]`. Second round: 529ace6eb's field-wise
  check alone refused a derived-`Copy` element whose field has a hand-written
  `clone` std never calls, which 33eefbf58 compiled and matched; it keeps the
  model again (`clones=0`, as LLVM). A tuple is not such a type: core's tuple
  clone shim calls each field's `clone` even for a `Copy` tuple (LLVM ran a
  counting field `clone` three times for `vec![(In(5), 6u32); 4]`), so that
  element refuses. Field-wise derived, `Copy` and tuple-of-primitive elements
  and every primitive scalar element keep the model. Not lowered either way:
  std's own `SpecFromElem::from_elem` body, which the bridge refuses at O0..O3
  when the intercept steps aside, so a hand-written `Clone` element is
  refused, not run.
- `<[u64]>::sort` / `sort_unstable` (and `usize`) put values `>= 2^63` first
  at O0/O1: the `__trustcg_vec_sort_*` helper compared with a signed `Sgt`
  after a zero-extension that is a no-op at 64 bits. Unsigned elements now
  compare with `Ugt` (the fix the FIXED 2026-10-08 entry above records). At
  O2/O3 MIR inlining exposes core's stable `driftsort_main`, which stays
  refused (`[TCG-MIR-UNSUPPORTED]`); `sort_unstable`'s `heapsort` compiles.
- The stable `sort_by_key` model replaces std's comparator
  `|a, b| f(a).lt(&f(b))` (two key calls per comparison, the insertee read from
  a stack copy) with one call per comparison plus one per insertee, on the
  element in place. With a key that counts its calls the count differed (14
  against 11; 458 against 414 for 40 elements), and with a key that reads its
  own count the sorted result differed (`6143289` against `4631829`), so call
  pattern is not the only observable difference. The model now admits only a
  key whose optimized MIR, followed through its direct callees
  (`sort_key_closure_is_pure`), writes nothing outside its locals, turns
  no address into a value by a form the check recognises (a cast from a pointer
  to a non-pointer, a transmute from a non-numeric type, a binary operation on
  pointers, a thread-local reference, a union field, a pointer cast or
  raw-pointer aggregate reading memory that may hold an address at another
  type), and can fail in at most one way: under `panic=abort`, one kept
  overflow or division check with a constant message, when every key call
  terminates (a check in a `#[track_caller]` callee, such as core's operator
  impls on references, reports the call that reached it, so it counts once per
  calling chain). Any other `sort_by_key` key refuses with `[TCG-SORT-KEY-EFFECT]`. Second round: 529ace6eb admitted any
  number of such checks, arguing that every algorithm keys every element, so
  the same panic is reached in any order; that holds for one site only. With
  two (a subtraction that underflows and a multiplication that overflows, or
  two divisions by zero with overflow checks off) the site reached first
  depends on the call order: LLVM reported the multiplication (`:8:39`), the
  model the subtraction (`:8:62`), at O0..O3 at both commits. One check in a
  `#[track_caller]` callee reached from two calls is two sites (it diverged
  the same way at 529ace6eb); reached from one call it keeps the model. A key reading its
  argument's address, sorting by whether it lies in the slice, built and
  diverged (`h=123579` against `h=271359`): through a union at O0..O3 at both
  commits, and at 529ace6eb through a pointer cast over a local array holding
  the argument (O1..O3) and through `ptr::from_raw_parts` over that array's
  data pointer (O2/O3; the other levels refused another construct). These
  forms now refuse at every level. EVIDENCE BOUNDARY: std's stable sort body is
  not an alternative for `sort_by_key` (with the intercept stepped aside the
  bridge refused `driftsort_main` at every level O0..O3 at `33eefbf58`), so a
  refused `sort_by_key` key is not run. Every `sort_unstable_by_key` takes
  std's ordinary body instead, without emitting the replacement model:
  `unstable_by_key_counter` (a key counting its calls) compiles and matches
  LLVM at O0..O3. Refused although std would run them,
  measured: an argsort key with a bounds check (`|&i| scores[i]`: its message
  names the index, so which out-of-range element is reached first is
  observable), at every level; any key that keeps an overflow or division
  check under `panic=unwind` (the default debug profile: `-Copt-level=0`,
  overflow checks on, unwinding), because the model has no unwind guard: a
  panic out of a key call after a shift would leave the insertee only in the
  model's scratch slot, where std's sort guards write it back (read from both
  sources, not measured); and, under `panic=abort` with overflow checks on, a
  key with two kept checks even where one cannot fire for the slice at hand:
  `(*x - base).abs()` (the subtraction and `abs`'s negation; it matched at
  529ace6eb because no element overflows) at every level, and `x / 3 + 1` on
  `&u32` at O0/O1, where the division's check sits behind a call to core's
  `<&u32 as Div<u32>>::div` whose constant divisor the walk does not see (at
  O2/O3 it is inlined, proved never to fire, and the key keeps the model).
  The check also refuses what it cannot see through (a call through a pointer,
  an unlisted intrinsic, an atomic, an allocation) even when it is in fact
  pure.
- `sort_unstable_by_key` over more than 20 elements: std's ipnsort may order
  distinct elements with equal keys differently from the model's stable order
  (40 elements keyed by `x / 100`, at O0..O3). Every unstable key sort now
  takes std's own body, as the FIXED 2026-10-08 entry above records
  (`unstable_by_key_ties` matches LLVM at O0..O3 that way). Second round:
  529ace6eb did not count the argument's entry value, so a key that reassigns
  its argument (`|mut x: &u64| { if *x >= 100 { x = &BIG; } *x }`) passed as
  `*x` and sorted its ties in the stable order (`h=10277673255144864164`
  against LLVM's `h=10033734573842138824`, O0..O3, also at 33eefbf58); such a
  key now steps aside to std's body.
- `sort_by_cached_key` was routed into the per-comparison model: 17 key calls
  for 6 elements where std documents at most one per element, a key reading
  its own count sorted wrong, and std's one `(key, index)` allocation never
  happened (a counting allocator: LLVM `allocs=2 sizes=48080 aligns=408`,
  bridge `allocs=0`). The merged replacement model repaired those small
  examples but used quadratic insertion sorting and needed a separate
  allocation-capacity and unwind contract. The integration removes it:
  every cached key sort takes std's actual body, using the general compiler
  argument-ABI and aggregate-iterator lowering. This retains the library's
  algorithm, key-call sequence, allocation and cleanup code rather than
  substituting another algorithm. Ordinary-body lowering can still refuse
  unsupported constructs; a source route is not proof or performance credit.
- Not changed, measured: the plain `sort` and stable `sort_by_key` models
  allocate nothing, where std's stable sort above 20 elements takes its scratch
  buffer from a 4 KiB stack array when it fits and from the global allocator
  otherwise (`driftsort_main`). A counting allocator around a 2000-element
  `u32` `sort()` and `sort_by_key(|x| *x)` saw one allocation each under LLVM
  and none under the bridge at O0/O1, with the same sorted result; at O2/O3
  the bridge refuses (`[TCG-MIR-UNSUPPORTED]`). A program that observes its
  allocator can tell; no model here reproduces std's scratch allocation.

**Iterator drives: the item a by-reference payload borrows when it unwinds
(2026-10-09).** Measured on Darwin AArch64 (Trust pack 9192,
`no-proof-certs`, bridge against LLVM, -O0..-O3, abort and unwind) by
`tests/iter_chain_unwind_item_differential_aarch64.rs`. Over a `Range` or
slice source whose `map` yields an item with a user `Drop`, a drive stores the
item and calls a by-reference payload on it: a `find` predicate, a `filter` /
`take_while` / `skip_while` predicate, an `inspect` closure. At origin/main
b53f9641f a payload that unwound left that item undropped (`log: ... 203`
against LLVM's `log: ... 203 3`; 71 of the 95 unwind `Match` cells of that
file's held-item test, the others being the `find` rows, `filter_fold` and
`inspect_count` at O2/O3 where std's own closures hold the item), a
destructor panicking during that unwind exited 101 where LLVM aborts, and an
`extern "C"` frame skipped the drop LLVM prints before its abort. Each such
call now unwinds into a drive-owned pad that drops the item as a cleanup-path
drop and continues at the call's own unwind action; a held item whose drop
the drive does not lower (a tuple carrying one, a struct dropped through a
field) refuses with `[TCG-ITER-DISCARD-DROP]`, and a body without EH lowering
(the `disable-unwind` knob) with `[TCG-ITER-UNWIND-DROP]`, which the file
pins per site. By-value payloads (`any`, `all`, `position`, `fold`,
`for_each`) already dropped their item and are controls.

The same drives handed an interior-mutable item (`C(Cell<u32>)`, `!Freeze`)
kept the image they stored before the payload ran: a `filter` predicate that
wrote `c.0.set(c.0.get() + 10)` left LLVM's `log: 11 12 13 14 15 103` as
`log: 1 2 3 4 5 103` (O0..O3), `find` returned the unwritten item (O0/O1),
`min_by` / `max_by_key` kept it (O0/O1), and `take_while` / `skip_while`
yielded it (O2/O3). A drive now reloads such an item from the slot the
payload received; a tuple item with an interior-mutable component refuses
with `[TCG-ITER-INTERIOR-MUT-ITEM]`.

A value a terminal carries across the drive was not dropped when an adapter
closure unwound, where std's frame drops it (measured with the held-item pad
in place, 3bbbfe2bb): a `fold` over a `D` accumulator (O0/O1: LLVM
`log: 1 50 2 51 3 53`, bridge `... 51 3`), `reduce` (O0..O3: `2 1 3` against
`2 1`) and the result `last` keeps (O0/O1: `1 3 2` against `1 3`). Such a
terminal, holding a value that needs drop across a `map`, `filter`,
`filter_map`, `take_while`, `skip_while`, `scan`, `map_while`, `inspect` or
`flat_map` closure, now refuses under `panic=unwind` with
`[TCG-ITER-UNWIND-CARRY]`, which also withdraws such a drive that never
unwinds (a `fold(D(50), ..)` over `map` and `filter` matched LLVM at O0/O1
before).

The `Vec` a `collect` builds over a source that owns nothing (a `Range`, a
slice) was not freed when a payload unwound, where std's `from_iter` frees it:
at dcf9d45e5, 24 of the 36 unwind cells of that file's collect test left its
buffer allocated (O0..O3: `live=7` against LLVM's `live=6`, for a by-value
`map` closure as for a `filter` predicate, also when no item needs drop, and
from a frame with no cleanup of its own). The collect now owns a pad that
frees the `Vec` (a held item's pad drops the item first and continues into
it), as it already did over an owning `vec::IntoIter`; all 72 cells match,
and a body without EH lowering refuses with `[TCG-COLLECT-UNWIND-RELEASE]`.
Every `[TCG-MIR-UNSUPPORTED]` cell of that file is now pinned by the reason
the bridge gives for it.

**Historical AArch64 argument-lane qualification (2026-09-28).** The
argument and return refusals described in that dated lane applied on Apple and
ELF (its closure and `rust-call` refusals are gone since round 10, below); the
current collection-image qualification is described above. One predicate,
`rust_abi_indirect_lane_target`, scopes the lane, the padded scalar homes and
the scalar argument / return refusals, so they cannot cover different targets.
rustc's Rust ABI states the same `Indirect { on_stack: false }` pointer
there, and AAPCS64 places it like any pointer (the next X register, else an
8-byte stack slot) — where trust-cg's classifier places the declared `Ptr`.
Measured on an AArch64 Darwin host with the `m145` matrix run natively (its test
and `tests/tools/m145_xback.py` now build for the host's architecture): before,
213 of 460 rlib x bin cells at O0/O2 disagreed with LLVM x LLVM (SIGSEGV /
SIGBUS, or wrong values — `T12` by value 6 / SIGBUS against 34); after, every
