  `pic`, a default-visibility definition through the GOT and the PLT.
  trust-ir has no such fact, so the importer drops the keyword and refuses
  by name what makes the two objects differ, reading the relocation model a
  caller compiles under (`import_text_for_compile`; the
  `trust-cg-ws2-import` driver passes the one it compiles with, `static`).
  A `dso_local` declaration for the linker (a data or function declaration,
  an `available_externally` global or function) whose address the module's
  code takes is refused under `pie` and `pic`, for any target but AArch64
  ELF, and with no model known (`import_text`, `import_text_for_target`):
  measured by the third round's repair (O0-O3; GNU ld, gold and LLD), in all
  48 shared-object configurations of the four forms the import's object
  linked and an `LD_PRELOAD` interposer took its read (1005 for the
  definition's 12), while llc's linked under gold alone and read 12, and in
  24 of 48 PIE configurations GNU ld refused llc's object, or gold's PIE of
  llc's function-address forms died with `SIGILL`, where the import's
  linked and ran. For an AArch64 ELF compile under `static` it is admitted
  (since the fifth round): a `static` object goes into a non-PIE
  executable, and rustc's `-C relocation-model=static` output reading an
  `extern` static, which the fourth verifier round found refused although
  its import equalled llc's in 48 of 48 executable runs, ran equal in 96 of
  96. The two objects differ where the symbol has two addresses in the
  link: the one the static link gives the executable's non-PIC references
  (a copy relocation for data, a canonical PLT entry for a function), which
  llc's PC-relative object takes, and the one the dynamic linker binds GOT
  slots to, which the import's takes; and where no linker may give the
  executable that address, llc's object does not link. Measured in the
  sixth and seventh rounds (a data read, write, address and offset, a
  function's address and a call; three C drivers, one naming neither
  symbol, one taking `&s` and `f` itself `-fno-pic`, one `-fPIE`; the
  definitions in the executable, `-no-pie` and `-static`, or in a shared
  library, plain, under an interposer, linked `-Bsymbolic` or
  `-Bsymbolic-functions`, and with protected definitions; O0-O3, GNU ld,
  gold and LLD; the native row
  `imported_static_dso_local_declarations_run_like_llc`), the two printed
  alike in 148 of 252 links and not in 104. With a `-Bsymbolic` library,
  which keeps its own references, llc's program writes the executable's
  copy of `s` that the library does not read (and takes the executable's
  address of `f`), where the import's has one `s` unless `-fno-pic` code in
  the executable names it too (28 links; in the 4 under gold with that code
  only the address of `f` differs). With a `-Bsymbolic-functions` library
  (Ubuntu's default for its packages), which keeps its own references to
  its functions, llc's address of `f` is the executable's PLT entry and the
  library's its own, where the import's is the library's (28 links; alike
  where `-fno-pic` code names `f` under GNU ld and LLD, whose PLT entry the
  import's GOT slot then reads too; the sixth verifier round counted 32 of
  36 for this, describing the same 28). Under gold, which exports no
  canonical PLT entry, llc's address of a library's `f` is the executable's
  and `-fno-pic` code's, the import's the library's and `-fPIE` code's (24
  links). With protected definitions in the library, which no linker lets a
  copy relocation or canonical PLT entry move into the executable, llc's
  object links under none of GNU ld, gold and LLD, where the import's links
  and names the library's symbols (24 links; with the driver naming them
  `-fno-pic` neither links). In each of those links llc's own program gives
  the symbol two addresses or does not link, and refusing the declaration
  under `static` would refuse that producer output in every link (253 texts
  of the sixth round's recount); LD-31's 2026-10-15 amendments have the
  ruling. The
  cost of the refusal with no model known is that static-model producer
  output (rustc `-C relocation-model=static`, clang `-fno-pic`, which mark
  every external declaration `dso_local`) is refused for a caller that does
  not state the model, when its code addresses an external variable or
  function. A direct call of such a declaration (`CALL26`), a pointer to it
  in an initializer (`R_AARCH64_ABS64`) and one nothing addresses are
  written as llc writes them and stay admitted. A `dso_local` definition
  (default visibility, not local) that the module references (an address,
  a call, an initializer's pointer) is refused under a known `pic`: llc
  binds those references locally (an `.L<name>$local` alias for an
  `external` one, PC-relative for a `weak` or ODR one), and in a shared
  library an interposer took every reference of the import and none of
  llc's in all 12 gold runs of the fifth round, where GNU ld and LLD refused
  llc's library for the `weak` one. Under `static` and PIE its forms are
  llc's (96 of 96 executable configurations equal in the third round), and
  with no model known it stays admitted, with that `pic` difference when
  such a module is compiled `pic` into a shared object: refusing it there
  would refuse modules like the in-tree `intmm_*_clang_o0.ll` fixtures,
  written by clang for a PIE (`PIE Level` 2), which mark every definition
  `dso_local` (under a stated `pic`, two of them are refused). The
  references are read from the imported module: every definition's code,
  and every initializer. An `available_externally` body, which llc's
  object never contains (it calls the function) and the AOT compile may
  splice into a caller at O1-O3, is read apart (since the seventh round): a
  `dso_local` declaration it addresses is refused by name where the
  backend may splice the body and the definition the body copies may be in
  a shared library, `static` for AArch64 ELF included. That definition,
  compiled by llc from the same text, reads the symbol PC-relative, which
  in a shared library gold links binds it inside the library (GNU ld and
  LLD refuse that reference there), while the splice reads it through the
  GOT: an `LD_PRELOAD` interposer took the import's spliced read at O1-O3
  (1005) and not llc's program's (12). The sixth verifier round measured it
  for a default body under `static`, `pie` and with no model known, which
  the sixth round admitted on the ground that the spliced code is that of
  the twin without `dso_local` (byte-identical objects; but the twin's
  copied definition reads `s` through the GOT too, and its programs ran
  alike); the sixth round had measured it for a hidden body under `pic`.
  So the refusal covers a default body under `static` and `pie`, a hidden
  or protected body under `pic` (a default one the backend withholds
  there), every body with no model known, and, for a target other than
  AArch64 ELF (not measured), every body the backend may splice. A hidden
  or protected body under `static` and `pie` stays admitted for AArch64
  ELF: its definition binds in the executable (llc's program does not link
  with it in a shared library, under GNU ld, gold and LLD), where both
  programs read the executable's one `s`, interposed or not (the seventh
  round: 12 of 12 links alike per model and visibility). With a library
  linked `-Bsymbolic` the module and its twin without `dso_local` both
  differ from llc's (the library keeps its own `s`), which is the splice's
  one-definition premise (the JIT and inliner paragraph). The
  definitions rule under `pic` counts the bodies the backend splices there
  (a hidden one's call of a `dso_local` definition). A
  hidden or protected declaration keeps the backend's GOT form where llc's
  is PC-relative, as before (the IFUNC reason in the relocation-model
  paragraph above).

  The compile target is read by `src/triple.rs`, as LLVM's `Triple` reads
  it, for the listed-declaration rule and the `\01` label reader alike
  (since the port onto L02-P15). The second round's reader split a triple
  at every `-` and named only a Linux OS or an `elf` environment ELF, so
  the five-component `aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu-macho`, which llc writes
  as Mach-O with an `N_NO_DEAD_STRIP` `_fd`, admitted a listed function
  declaration, and `aarch64-linux-gnu`, which llc writes as ELF, refused
  one. Other ELF operating systems (`aarch64-unknown-freebsd`,
  `aarch64-unknown-none`) are admitted, as llc writes them as ELF, and a
  triple naming an Apple OS with an `-elf` ending reads no `\01` label.
  The fourth verifier round found the reader's Darwin OS names `tvos`,
  `watchos`, `bridgeos`, `driverkit` and `visionos`, and its `win32`
  spelling of Windows, decided by no test (dropping them passed the
  importer suite, and nine triples llc writes as Mach-O or COFF then
  admitted a listed declaration); `triple.rs`'s test, the importer's and
  the floor row now name each, as llc 22.1.2 writes them (measured).
  `symbol_linkage_elf` gained a host-neutral row for the `dso_local` rules
  (the refused spellings with no model, under `pie` and `pic`, for x86-64
  and Mach-O, and admitted with the backend's GOT form for AArch64 ELF
  under `static`; the definitions refused under `pic`; the
  `available_externally` body counted where its splice may bind otherwise,
  for AArch64 ELF, x86-64 and Mach-O since the seventh round, its admitted
  objects identical to the twin's without `dso_local`; since the sixth
  round, a declaration after 300 globals and `static` with no known target
  refused by name), the
  listed-declaration row the triples the readers tell apart and the `\01`
  label decision, the mergeable row every name of its exemption list and
  eleven names one character away (the third verifier round's mutants
  dropping `.sbss*` or the exact `.bss` from the list passed every test
  before), and, in the fifth round, the native rows
  `imported_static_dso_local_declarations_run_like_llc` and
  `imported_integer_literals_run_like_llc` and the host-neutral
  `integer_literals_are_read_at_their_type_width`. The fourth round's
  recount (2,257 texts at its own tree, O0 and O2, PIE) found the 1,368
  objects both its base and head compiled byte-identical, as were the
  1,920 objects of the second round's fuzz modules, the verifier's 64
  compiled sweep modules, the 708 relocation-matrix objects that stayed
  admitted, and the 372 imported objects of the earlier rounds' 33 llc
  differential cases. The fifth and sixth rounds' recounts are in LD-31
  and LD-32.

  Integer literals (LD-32). The importer reads an integer literal as LLVM
  reads it for its type, its bits at the type's width (`LLParser`'s
  `APSInt::extOrTrunc`), spelled in the range of its signed carrier: `i64
  18076885954311749632` is the `i64` -369858119397801984, bits
  `0xFADE000000000000`, and `i32 4294967295` is -1. Written as its decimal
  value, that `i64` literal lay in the interval `[0xFADE << 48, 0xFADF <<
  48)` the lowering adapter decodes as a module global's address (the
  stub encoding the importer and the rustc bridge share), and the fourth
  verifier round compiled `ret i64 18076885954311749632` to `@g`'s address
  where llc's object returns `0xfade000000000000` (at `e8ae736f6`); at
  395954590 trust-ir's codegen admission refused that spelling instead
  (`const type mismatch`), while `ret ptr 18076885954311749632`, which
  LLVM's parser rejects, still compiled to `@g`'s address, an array GEP
  index `i32 4294967295` folded to 32 GiB forward where llc's object goes
  one element back, and a struct GEP's outer index alike to 64 GiB forward
  (its executable faulted). The fifth verifier round found the reading
  incomplete: an `i1` GEP index was read +1 where LLVM sign-extends it to
  -1 (constant `1` or `true` on the array, struct and constant-expression
  paths, and a computed one, which the importer zero-extended: one element
  forward where llc's object goes one back), and switch cases, scalar
  initializers and `i1` literals other than 0 and 1 were refused although
  llc reads them; the sixth round's transplant differential at that head
  also found an `i1 -1` aggregate field stored as 255, an `i1 3` switch case
  never taken and `alloca i8, i8 %n` with 200 killed by `SIGSEGV` (its count
  sign-extended). The sixth verifier round found the reading still short of
  that: an integer array initializer's literal outside its type's ranges
  (`[2 x i8] [i8 300, i8 1]`, which llc stores as 44 and 1), `alloca i8, i8
  -56` (200 elements to llc; refused as a negative count where `i8 200`
  imported) and GEP offsets folded past 2^64 (`i64 2305843009213693953`
  elements of 8 bytes, 8 bytes forward to llc; compiled to a constant
  trust-ir refused) were refused, and an `i1 false` GEP index and an `i1
  true` `alloca` count were pinned by no row (a mutant reading the index as
  true compiled to `p - 8` where llc's object returns `p`). Now every
  integer literal is its low bits at its type's width, as LLVM's parser
  reads it (llc 22.1.2: `ret i8 300` is 44, `ret i1 2` is 0), wherever it
  becomes a constant: an operand (an instruction's, a call's, a `phi`'s, a
  vector lane's; an `i1` one a `bool`), a GEP index (sign-extended, `i1`
  included; a computed index too), a switch case (an `i1` one as its low
  bit), a scalar global's initializer, an aggregate field (an `i1` one as
  its low bit) and an integer array's element, and an `alloca` count
  (zero-extended whatever its sign; a computed count and a `memset.pattern`
  count too); a folded GEP offset is summed modulo 2^64, as llc folds it,
  and spelled signed. Still read as written, and refused when out of range
  (none of them wrong code; llc 22.1.2 reads the first two): a struct field
  index of a GEP instruction (`i32 4294967297`, field 1 to llc), a vector
  lane index (`i8 258`, lane 2 to llc) and a `shufflevector` mask element,
  and a literal outside `[-2^127, 2^127)`; an `i128` `alloca` count of 2^64
  elements or more and an aggregate `alloca` of 2^64 bytes or more are
  refused by name (no stack object is that large). An integer literal for
  `ptr` is refused by name, and any top-level `i64` constant still in the
  interval is refused by name. The interval stays reserved at the trust-ir level for
  producers: no constant this importer writes from a module's text lies in
  it. The sixth round's 30 literal units ran equal to llc at O0-O3 (120 of
  120), where the previous head refused 18 and printed a wrong value in 9;
  its recount (19,666 texts) has no text going from imported to refused
  and every earlier differential case it newly compiles printing llc's
  output (94 of 94 runs); LD-32's 2026-10-15 amendment has the counts.
  Of the fifth round's 49 mutants (the
  `dso_local` amendment, the literal reading and the triple names), 48 are
  killed, each by a `symbol_linkage_elf` row except two that fail to
  compile and whose behavioural twins the row kills; the one survivor
  removes only the interval guard, which no input reaches while the
  reading holds (report);
  the sixth round's mutants are in its
  report,
  and the seventh round's, with its llc differential and recount, in
  its own.
  The third closure audit (at `e0474f6ce`) found that no test read the
  visibility the importer writes for a global defined by an array, string,
  zero-fill, struct or pointer initializer (its mutant S13, which writes
  `default` there, passed every importer floor target while a `pic` library
  built from its objects exported hidden and protected data and let an
  `LD_PRELOAD` interposer rebind the library's reads). The importer's
  behaviour was correct; `symbol_linkage_elf` now states the linkage and
  visibility of every initializer shape under every admitted linkage and
  visibility, in trust-ir and in the object, and runs hidden, protected,
  weak and ODR data of eight shapes against an `LD_PRELOAD` interposer
  beside gcc and llc twins (LD-85).
  Attributes on a global, an
  attribute group or an inline string attribute, are refused by name,
  among them clang's `#pragma clang section` attributes (`"bss-section"`,
  `"data-section"`, `"rodata-section"`, `"relro-section"`), from which
  LLVM's object writers take the global's section; before, they were
  dropped on a global without an `align` clause and on one whose attribute
  group follows a metadata attachment, the form LLVM prints for a
  `clang -g` global (`, align 8, !dbg !0 #0`). The `code_model` and
  sanitizer clauses are refused by name too.

  Before any line is read, the importer lexes the whole module as LLVM's
  lexer does, in two passes, and refuses by name what the rest of the
  importer, which reads one line at a time, would read differently. The
  first reads strings, comments and address spaces: a string runs to the
  next quote, across lines, and a `;` comment ends at a newline or a
  carriage return. It refuses a string holding a raw newline or carriage
  return ("a string spanning lines is not read by this importer"), a
  string never closed, a carriage return inside a `;` comment with text
  after it, and a C-style block comment (`/* ... */`, which LLVM 22 reads
  as whitespace). Before, a metadata string continued on a line beginning
  `;"` made the importer read as code the lines of a block comment that
  LLVM skips, so it built a different function than llc (the base did the
  same). Every address space other than the default one is refused by name
  at the same check, outside strings and comments, wherever the module
  spells it: on a global, on a function (its `addrspace(N)` clause), on a
  call (`call addrspace(1) ...`) and in any type (a parameter, argument or
  return type, a loaded, stored or GEP pointer type, a constant such as
  `ptr addrspace(257) null`, a cast target). The check covers glued,
  spaced and tab-separated clauses and every operand other than one or
  more `0` digits (`01` is address space 1; negative, out-of-range and
  symbolic `"P"` spaces are refused too). It follows LLVM's lexer: an
  integer type `iN`, a numbered ID (`%0`, `@0`, `#0`, `!0`) or an integer
  literal ends at the first non-digit, so `i8addrspace(270)*` and
  `%0addrspace(270)*` are clauses and are refused, while `%v1addrspace` is
  a name. A clause word that ends its line, whose operand LLVM would read
  from the next line, is refused by name, since the importer reads a clause
  only on one line. Before this check, a quote or `;` inside a block
  comment hid an address space (`ptr /*"*/ addrspace(270)` imported as a
  64-bit pointer, as at the base). Before, the importer dropped the clause
  wherever it read the position and imported the pointer as an ordinary
  64-bit one. LLVM's AArch64 data layouts make `addrspace(270)` a 32-bit
  pointer (`p270:32:32`), yet a stack argument of that type was placed like
  a 64-bit pointer (an `i32` after it on the stack went 8 bytes on instead
  of 4 on `aarch64-apple-darwin`). `addrspace(0)` is admitted in every
  spelling (`addrspace ( 0 )`, `addrspace(00)`, `i8addrspace(0)*`), though
  an operand position that did not parse it before still does not.

  The second pass (`crates/trust-cg-llvm-import/src/lexical.rs`) splits
  every token as `LLLexer.cpp` does (a keyword ends at the first byte that
  is not a letter, digit or `_`, an `iN` type at the first non-digit after
  the `i`) and refuses by name:
  - whitespace LLVM reads that the line reader does not split on, outside
    strings and comments: a NUL byte, and a carriage return that ends no
    line. Every other control byte and every non-ASCII byte there is a
    lexer error in LLVM and is refused too. A tab reads as a space. Before,
    a NUL glued to a keyword (`hidden\0`, `internal\0`, `linkonce_odr\0`)
    was read as an unknown word and skipped, so a hidden or internal
    function was exported and interposable and a `linkonce_odr` one strong,
    and `addrspace\0(1)` passed the address-space check; a tab dropped a
    global's `align\t32`;
  - two tokens LLVM splits but the line reader would read as one: a
    keyword, number, name or string glued to a following string, name,
    number, keyword or `[`/`{`/`<`/`!` (`section"x"`, `prologue[...]`,
    `partition"p"`, `ptr@g`, `i64-1`, `global[2 x i8]`), except `c"..."`
    and a glued `addrspace`, which the first pass reads. Before, a glued
    `section` was dropped and a glued `prologue` was admitted, so the
    function returned 1 where llc's returned the prologue's 42;
  - a second top-level entity on a line (`attributes #0 = { nounwind }
    declare hidden i64 @dh()` dropped the declaration, whose call then
    stated `external` + `default`), and an entity continued on a later
    line;
  - a function header continued on a later line (only its `{` may start
    the next line, alone), `define` alone on its line or at the end of the
    module included (the first version of this pass panicked there), a
    body that starts on its header line, and a closing `}` that shares its
    line;
  - a second instruction on a line (two stores on one line imported as the
    first: 1 where llc returns 2), a block label sharing its line, and an
    instruction continued on a later line, except a `switch` case list. An
    opcode word in operand position (a constant-expression operator before
    its `(`, an `atomicrmw` operation, the `call` of `tail call`) is not a
    second instruction. An instruction whose brackets do not balance is
    refused too;
  - a numbered ID (`%01`, `@00`, `#00`, `!00`, `^00`, a label `00:`) or an
    integer type (`i064`) spelled with a leading zero: LLVM reads it by the
    value of its digits, the importer matched it by spelling. A function
    marked `#00` lost the `sspstrong` of the group `#0` defines, so its
    buffer overflow ended in SIGBUS where llc's build aborts (stack
    smashing detected), and `i064` returned nothing;
  - a metadata attachment, on a global, a function or an instruction, of a
    kind llc's code generator or object writer reads: `!associated`
    (`SHF_LINK_ORDER`), `!exclude` (`SHF_EXCLUDE`), `!section_prefix`
    (`.data.hot.`), `!absolute_symbol`, `!func_sanitize` (signature words
    before the function), `!kcfi_type`, `!pcsections`, `!implicit.ref` and,
    since the second repair of L02-P15, `!stack-protector` (llc's stack
    protector builds no canary for an alloca marked `!{i32 0}`, which the
    importer's `ssp` policy protects; the attachment was dropped).
    The importer reads no metadata: an `!exclude` global linked from the
    imported object where llc's excluded section is discarded, and
    `!func_sanitize` lost its words;
  - every calling-convention keyword other than `ccc` and `fastcc`, on a
    definition, a declaration or a call, `cc N` included: the importer
    lowers every function and call with the C convention, so an imported
    `preserve_nonecc` callee returned 1 to an llc caller expecting 5.
    `fastcc` is read as C on AArch64 and x86-64: LLVM lowers it like C
    there unless `-tailcallopt` is given, which no object path here
    passes. The differential below calls
    twelve-argument `fastcc` functions each way between llc and imported
    AArch64 objects; the x86-64 System V leg rests on LLVM's calling
    convention tables (`CC_X86_64` has no `Fast` case) and is not executed.
    On RISC-V it is not C: `CC_RISCV_FastCC` passes integer arguments 9 to
    12 in `x28`-`x31` and floating-point ones in more registers (LLVM
    22.1.2's `RISCVCallingConv.cpp`; LLVM 18.1.3's llc, a STOCK EXCEPTION,
    added a ten-argument `fastcc` function's last two from `t2` and `t3`),
    so `fastcc` anywhere is refused by name for a RISC-V compile target and
    when no target is known (the sixth verifier round of L02-P15; before,
    only the backend's refusal of more than eight arguments kept it out,
    and a `fastcc` function of eight or fewer integer arguments, which
    `CC_RISCV_FastCC` places as C does, is now refused too: a stated
    over-refusal).

  The header readers then read each token as LLVM splits it and refuse one
  they do not know by name instead of skipping it. Before a function's
  name they admit symbol keywords, `ccc`/`fastcc`, return attributes
  (`inreg` is refused) and the return type, which is read where it stands,
  the last token before the name (with any `addrspace(0)` after it, and
  `i8 addrspace(0)*` as a pointer), and must be `void` or a type the
  importer reads. A type it did not read used to be skipped for an earlier
  token, so a declaration returning `{ i64, i64, i64 }`, `[9 x i64]` or
  `%S` returned `void`; a call that dropped such a result passed no result
  buffer, and the program crashed (SIGSEGV) where llc's ran. Such a
  declaration is now skipped as unmodeled when nothing calls it, and a
  definition or call is refused. After its parameter list they admit
  `section`, `comdat`, `unnamed_addr`, `addrspace(0)`, metadata
  attachments (but the kinds above), `align N` up to 4 (AArch64 functions
  are whole words on word boundaries; x86-64 functions start on 32- or
  64-byte boundaries unless both `TCG_NO_X86_JCC_ALIGN` and
  `TCG_NO_X86_LOOP_HEAD_ALIGN` are set), `personality ptr @f` (LLVM emits
  no personality for a function without a landing pad, and the importer
  refuses `invoke` and `landingpad`), and the function attributes below.
  They refuse `partition`, `prefix`, `prologue`, `gc`, a larger `align` (it
  was dropped) and an SEH personality. A call's prefix is read the same
  way: fast-math flags, `ccc`/`fastcc`, return attributes (`inreg`
  refused), address spaces, the return type (a call read
  `{ i64, i64, i64 }` as its last `i64`) and an explicit function type;
  after its arguments only function attributes are read, and an operand
  bundle is refused by name (`clang.arc.attachedcall` made llc call the
  retain function after the call; the import retained nothing; `kcfi`,
  `ptrauth` and `deopt` are refused alike, while `llvm.assume`'s bundles
  are dropped with the call, as llc drops them). A global's clauses are
  read token by token after its initializer, its metadata attachments
  among them (a global's line used to be cut at its first `, !`, so a
  `section`, `align` or `comdat` after an attachment was dropped), so a
  string in the initializer is no clause (`c"section "` was read as a
  section name and refused) and a `section` written with two spaces is read
  (it was dropped). A function header is no longer cut at its last `{`, so
  a struct return type or a `!{...}` attachment reaches the readers. An
  attribute string runs to the next quote, as in LLVM: a backslash before
  the quote used to hide the rest of the group, `sspstrong` included, and
  the function lost its stack guard.

  A function attribute, inline or in an attribute group that a
  definition, a declaration or a call uses, is read only when it changes
  nothing the importer builds (`crates/trust-cg-llvm-import/src/attributes.rs`);
  every other one is refused by name. Read: facts about the function and
  permissions or restrictions on optimization (`memory`, `nounwind`,
  `noinline`, `optnone`, `cold`, `noreturn`, ...), sanitizer markers (the
  instrumentation is an `opt` pass), profiling markers, `nocf_check`,
  `nonlazybind`, `uwtable`, `ssp`/`sspstrong`/`sspreq` (which the importer
  reads), and an allowlist of string attributes: floating-point
  permissions, `target-cpu` and `tune-cpu` naming a processor LLVM 22
  defines for the compile target's architecture (but `thunderx3t110`;
  both below),
  `frame-pointer` (frame records
  serve stack walkers only), `stack-protector-buffer-size` of 8 (the
  importer's `ssp` threshold), `probe-stack` (`inline-asm` or Apple's
  `__chkstk_darwin`), `stack-probe-size` from 4096 to 2^63 - 1,
  `use-soft-float`/`sign-return-address` when off, and `target-features`
  whose every entry enables an instruction-set extension (or is `-fmv`)
  and implies no mode (but `+thunderx3t110`, below; on a RISC-V triple a
  definition's processor and features are also read for the calling
  convention they select, below),
  each key and value read as LLVM decodes it (L02-P15, below). Refused: `naked`,
  `alignstack`, `returns_twice` (`setjmp`; the backend keeps nothing safe
  across a second return), `strictfp`, `null_pointer_is_valid`,
  `noimplicitfloat`, `noredzone`, `safestack`, `shadowcallstack`,
  `sanitize_memtag`, `speculative_load_hardening`, `fn_ret_thunk_extern`,
  `hybrid_patchable`, `presplitcoroutine`, `nobuiltin` and the string
  attributes `no-builtins` and `no-builtin-<name>` (llc keeps a call they
  mark as a call of the named function, where this importer's backend
  reads a call of `memcpy` or `memset` by its name; below), a target
  feature that is a mode
  (`+strict-align`, `+reserve-x18`, `+call-saved-x9`, retpoline and
  speculation hardening, `+soft-float`, ...), implies one or disables one
  (`-neon`), a
  `target-cpu` or `tune-cpu` that names a processor whose LLVM 22 features
  imply such a mode or one LLVM 22 does not define for the compile target's
  architecture, and every string attribute the allowlist does not
  name, among them clang
  `-pg`'s `"instrument-function-entry-inlined"="mcount"` (llc called
  `mcount`; the import did not), `"patchable-function-entry"`,
  `"fentry-call"`, `"trap-func-name"` and `"zero-call-used-regs"`. A group
  no function or call uses refuses nothing. The read list rests on LLVM's
  documented meaning of each attribute and on an AArch64 and x86-64 llc
  survey of one function compiled with and without each one; it is a
  review, not a proof that llc builds the same program.

  `target-cpu` sets a processor's feature list and tuning list, and
  `tune-cpu` its tuning list; llc builds code for every feature they imply,
  so a processor is not only a source of added instructions (this entry
  listed both keys as changing nothing the importer builds, and
  `attributes.rs` said a processor's features only add instructions). Of LLVM
  22.1.2's processor definitions for the importer's three architectures
  (AArch64, x86 and RISC-V: 99, 131 and 51 names with aliases, read with
  `llvm-tblgen --dump-json` and closed under the features each implies),
  only `thunderx3t110` implies a feature the importer refuses as a
  `+feature`: its tuning list holds `strict-align`, so for it, as either
  key, llc 22.1.2 loads an `align 1` `i64` byte by byte on AArch64 Linux and
  Apple, where each of the other 98 AArch64 names (llc's list, and
  `apple-latest`, which it does not print) gives one `ldr`. The importer
  admitted it and built one `ldr` (pre-existing from L02-P13; the third
  verifier round of L02-P15); the two run alike
  where unaligned access is allowed, as in Linux user space, and differ only
  where alignment checking is on, the case `+strict-align` is refused for.
  It is now refused by name, matched exactly as LLVM matches a processor
  name; every other processor LLVM 22 defines implies instruction-set
  extensions and tuning. A name LLVM 22 does not define is not the generic
  processor (this entry used to say llc only ignores it; below). The x86
  and RISC-V names were read from LLVM's tables only (this
  host's llc has no RISC-V target, and no x86 program runs here).
  A `+feature` is closed under `Implies` the same way (llc sets every
  feature it implies), and `+thunderx3t110`, the tuning feature behind that
  processor, sets `strict-align`: llc 22.1.2 loads an unaligned `i64` byte by
  byte for `"target-features"="+thunderx3t110"` on Linux and Apple, which
  the third repair of L02-P15 read (the fourth verifier round; a sweep of
  all 349 AArch64 feature names through llc found byte loads for it and
  `+strict-align` only). Every feature and processor whose closure holds a
  feature refused as a `+feature` is now refused by name, and both tables
  are derived rather than listed by hand: a committed extract of LLVM
  22.1.2's AArch64, RISC-V and x86 feature and processor tables
  (`crates/trust-cg-llvm-import/tests/fixtures/llvm22_subtarget_features.json`:
  349, 348 and 199 features; 99, 51 and 131 processor names with aliases;
  written from `llvm-tblgen --dump-json` by
  `scripts/extract_llvm_subtarget_features.py`) is closed under `Implies` by
  the unit test `mode_implying_tables_are_the_closure_of_llvms_tables`,
  which requires the importer's two tables to equal the derivation (each
  holds `thunderx3t110` only), requires both readers to refuse each entry,
  and checks that no feature but `fmv` sets `fmv`, so `-fmv`, the one
  `-feature` read, clears nothing else (llc clears a feature together with
  every feature that implies it). The extract is LLVM's source of record
  here, not an llc run: a new LLVM needs the script rerun.

  A `target-cpu` or `tune-cpu` is read only when it names a processor LLVM
  22 defines for the compile target's architecture (the caller's triple,
  else the module's `target triple`), matched exactly (case and every
  byte, as llc's lookup matches it): for `aarch64` or `arm64` one of
  AArch64's 99 names (82 processors and 17 aliases, which its subtarget
  resolves), for a RISC-V triple one of RISC-V's 51, for an x86 triple one
  of x86's 131, and in each case the empty name, which those subtargets
  read as `generic`. With no target known only a name all three define is
  read (`generic`, and the empty name); on any other architecture
  (`arm64e`, `aarch64_be` and `aarch64_32` among them) none is. Every other
  name is refused by name (`attributes::ProcessorTable`; the three name
  tables are derived from the extract above by
  `processor_name_tables_are_llvms`). Until the second closure audit of
  L02-P15 (2026-10-23) the importer read every name but `thunderx3t110`, on
  the premise (this entry, `attributes.rs`, ruling LD-04) that llc builds a
  name it does not define for the generic processor. It does not: llc
  22.1.2 ignores such a name (with a warning) and sets none of a
  processor's features, so on AArch64 it builds the function without
  `fp-armv8` or `neon`, with the soft-float calling convention (a `double`
  argument in `x0`, floating-point arithmetic in library calls such as
  `__adddf3`), where the import builds the hard-float AAPCS, and a program
  mixing the two objects computes otherwise. llc 22.1.2 did so for
  `native`, `armv8-a`, case variants (`Cortex-A57`, `GENERIC`), a name
  with a leading or trailing space or a trailing NUL, typos, `help`, and
  each of the 180 x86 and RISC-V names AArch64 does not define; it kept
  the hard-float convention for each of the 99 AArch64 names, whose
  features all imply `fp-armv8` and `neon`
  (`reports/2026-10-23-l02p15-target-cpu/cc_probe.py` reruns the sweep).
  Functions under `generic`, `cortex-a72`, `neoverse-v2` and `apple-m1`
  run equal to llc's object at O0-O3 (`symbol_linkage_elf`). An undefined
  `tune-cpu` changes only tuning (llc 22.1.2 kept the hard-float
  convention for four), so refusing it is a stated over-refusal, kept for
  one rule over both keys (LD-95). Still read:
  names LLVM defines for which llc builds no program for a 64-bit target
  (llc 22.1.2 stops with "64-bit code requested on a subtarget that
  doesn't support it!" for `i386` on x86-64; on a 64-bit RISC-V triple
  LLVM's source rejects a processor without `64bit` unless a feature adds
  it, not run here).

  On RISC-V, `e`, `d` and `f` are not only instruction-set extensions: llc
  22 builds each function with the calling convention its own processor
  and features select (`RISCVABI::computeTargetABI`; with no `target-abi`,
  a module flag the importer refuses, `RISCVISAInfo::computeDefaultABI`
  gives `lp64e` with `e`, otherwise `lp64d` with `d`, `lp64f` with `f`, and
  the soft-float `lp64` with neither, `generic-rv64` holding none), while
  the importer's backend builds `lp64d` (pre-existing; the fifth verifier
  round of L02-P15). All but `lp64e` pass integers in `a0`-`a7`
  (`RISCVCallingConv.cpp`) and differ where a floating-point value is
  passed. For a RISC-V compile target (the target the importer is given,
  `import_text_for_target`, which the driver passes and which takes the
  place of the module's `target triple` as llc's `-mtriple` does, or else
  the module's triple) a definition is therefore refused
  when its processor and features (inline and through its groups, every
  value stated) select `lp64e`, or select no `d` while its text or a named
  type of the module names a floating-point or vector type (anywhere: an
  over-refusal where no such value crosses a call boundary), and every
  definition for a 32-bit RISC-V target is refused; a declaration and
  `"tune-cpu"` are not read for it. The features implying `d` (16), `e`
  (`e` alone) and `f` (42, the 16 among them) and the 29 processors
  implying `64bit` (with whether each implies `d`) are derived from the
  same extract by
  `riscv_calling_convention_tables_are_the_closure_of_llvms_tables`, which
  also checks that no processor implies `e`, no 64-bit processor `f`
  without `d`, no tuning list `e`, `d`, `f` or a width, and no feature
  implying `e` or `f` is named in LLVM's AArch64 or x86 table. This rests on
  LLVM 22.1.2's source and its TargetParser library: the Trust llc here
  has no RISC-V target. LLVM 18.1.3's llc (a STOCK EXCEPTION, the only
  RISC-V llc on this host) put the seventh and eighth `i64` arguments on
  the stack for `+e` and passed a `double` in `fa0` for `+d`, `+v` and
  `"target-cpu"="sifive-u74"` but in `a0` (calling `__adddf3`) with no
  feature, `+f` or `sifive-s51`. LLVM 22 builds `lp64e` for `+e` too: its
  `RISCVISAInfo::updateImplication` erases the `i` every 64-bit processor
  implies when `e` is set, before `checkDependency` would reject the pair
  (LLVM 22.1.2's TargetParser library, linked into a scratch program, gave
  `lp64e` for `+i,+e` and `+i,+e,+d`, `lp64f` for `+i,+f`, `+i,+zfh` and
  `+i,+zve32f`, and `lp64d` for `+i,+d` and `+i,+v`, and LLVM's own
  `rv64e.ll` test runs `llc -mtriple=riscv64 -mattr=+e` and loads the
  seventh argument from the stack); the fifth repair's statement that
  llc 22 rejects `e` beside `i` was false (sixth verifier round of
  L02-P15), while its refusal stands. The backend's own RISC-V instruction
  selection refuses floating-point parameters ("RISC-V minimal ISel ... type
  F64 is not a single-GPR ABI slot") and passed the eighth `i64` in `a7`;
  no RISC-V program ran here.

  The rule read only the module's `target triple`, so a module stating
  none, compiled with `--target riscv64-unknown-linux-gnu` (llc's
  `-mtriple=riscv64`), admitted `+e`: the backend's object read the
  seventh and eighth `i64` arguments from `a6`/`a7` where LLVM 18.1.3's
  llc loads them from the stack (pre-existing; sixth verifier round of
  L02-P15; object level). It now reads the compile target; a module with
  a RISC-V triple compiled for AArch64 is no longer refused for `+e`, a
  feature llc ignores there with a warning. When no target is known (no
  triple stated or given: the library's `import_text` on such a module),
  a definition that states a feature selecting a RISC-V convention (one
  implying `e` or `f`) is read as for 64-bit RISC-V, the one RISC-V width
  the backend builds, and `fastcc` is refused (above); a definition
  stating none is admitted, though for a RISC-V target llc would build it
  with the soft-float `lp64`: a caller that compiles such a module for
  RISC-V passes that target, as the driver does, and is then refused where
  the conventions differ.

  Not covered: the instruction readers still match their operands' text
  with spelled patterns, so punctuation spacing LLVM's printer does not
  produce (`,ptr` for `, ptr`) is left to each reader, and an
  instruction's tokens are checked only as the pass above checks them; an
  instruction's metadata attachments are dropped unread (only the kinds
  listed above are refused); `musttail call` is refused by name (it
  guarantees a tail call the backend does not), while `tail` and `notail`
  are hints; `probe-stack` is read on every
  target although only AArch64 frames are probed (x86-64 and RISC-V
  frames are not, as recorded with AArch64 frame lowering); and
  `dso_local` and `unnamed_addr` are dropped (trust-ir has neither fact),
  except where the L02-P13 paragraph refuses them by name (a `dso_local`
  declaration whose address the module's code takes, unless the caller
  states an AArch64 ELF compile under `static`; a referenced `dso_local`
  definition under a stated `pic`; a mergeable `unnamed_addr` constant in a
  named section), with the differences that paragraph states (a `dso_local`
  definition compiled `pic` with no model stated, equal `unnamed_addr`
  constants in implicit sections).

  Evidence (L02-P13): the unit tests in
  `crates/trust-cg-llvm-import/src/parser.rs` (the 46 mutants of this
  repair's decisions, the 37 of the first version and the 5 a review found
  surviving it are all killed); a recount of every module the importer's
  test suite imports on this Linux host (1000 texts, with the in-tree
  `.ll` files): the 610 the suite shares with the first version's 620
  keep that version's verdicts and imported modules (341 import, 269 are
  refused; against the base, that version changed only 25 modules'
  linkage or retention), and of the 390 texts this repair's tests add or
  change, 90 the first version imported and 4 it panicked on are
  refused; 1,086 more texts
  (`opt -S` and `opt -O2 -S` prints of the first version's corpus and 58
  rustc modules) change no verdict and no imported module; 66,880
  structural and insertion mutants of these texts import or are refused
  without a panic (the first version panicked on 469); and an llc
  differential on AArch64 Linux over 156 generated spellings of these
  shapes, each compiled by the importer and by llc 22.1.2 and linked with
  one C driver through GNU ld 2.42, gold 1.16 and LLD 22.1.6 at O0-O3
  (static and PIE executables, and `pic` shared objects run plain and under
  `LD_PRELOAD`; 1332 compared configurations): every module is equal to
  llc (52) or refused by name (104). The first version differed from llc
  on 21 of the 38 spellings added for this repair and panicked on one; the
  base differed on 40 of the first 118.

  Names, strings and metadata are read as LLVM decodes them (L02-P15). LLVM
  decodes the `\XX` and `\\` escapes of every quoted name, metadata name and
  string before it reads it (`UnEscapeLexed`); the importer has one decoder
  with the same rules (`lexical::decode_escapes`). Before any reader runs,
  every quoted name and metadata name is rewritten to the one spelling its
  decoded name has (`lexical::canonicalize`): `@"f\6Fo"`, `@"foo"` and
  `@foo` are one symbol (the importer used to keep the quotes and escapes in
  the symbol it wrote, so a C caller of `foo` did not link), `%"x"` and `%x`
  one value, `@"llvm.memset.p0.i64"` the intrinsic, and `!\65xclude` the
  `!exclude` kind, refused like its plain spelling (llc's section was
  `SHF_EXCLUDE`; the imported one linked; the other seven kinds listed above
  alike). A name that is no plain name after decoding keeps a quoted
  spelling with every byte outside `[-a-zA-Z$._0-9]` escaped, so `%"a b"`
  and `%"a\20b"` are one value and `%"a,b"` passes a call's comma-splitting
  reader as one (it failed to parse before). Such a symbol name (`@"a b"`,
  `@"012"`) is carried only for an internal or private definition, whose
  name stays inside the object; any other is refused by name (the importer
  wrote the quoted spelling into the symbol table, where llc writes the
  decoded bytes). A name that decodes to a NUL byte (LLVM rejects it) and an
  empty quoted name are refused. A `\01` asm label is read, as the Mach-O C
  name (`@"\01_foo"` as `foo`), only in a module whose `target triple` names
  an Apple OS; otherwise it is refused by name: on ELF, llc writes the name
  after `\01` verbatim (`_foo`), where the importer's reading gave `foo`. A
  label whose name after `\01_` holds a byte outside `[-a-zA-Z$._0-9]`
  (`@"\01_a b"`, `@"\01_caf\C3\A9"`) names a symbol that is no plain name
  and follows the rule above: it is carried, in its quoted spelling, only for
  an internal or private definition. The second repair of this row wrote
  the canonical escapes into the Mach-O symbol table (`_a\20b`,
  `_caf\C3\A9`) where llc writes the decoded bytes (`_a b`, `_café`), for a
  definition, a global and a called declaration (the third verifier round;
  the base wrote `_g v` for `@"\01_g v"` and, already wrong, `_caf\C3\A9`).
  Such a label and the plain `@"a b"` are one Mach-O symbol, `_a b`, and
  are refused together like any label and plain name that meet. LLVM's
  Mangler writes a `\01` name verbatim without the `\01`, and any other
  non-private name after the prefix `_`, so `@"\01_S"` and `@"S"` are one
  symbol whatever `S` is; the third repair quoted the name after `\01_` only
  when it held an escape, so `@"\01_1x"` was read as `1x` and the plain
  `@"1x"` as `"1x"`, and with an internal `@"1x"` and a called declaration
  of `@"\01_1x"` llc bound the call to the local function while the
  importer left an undefined `_1x` (both defined, llc rejected the module
  and the importer imported it; the fourth verifier round). The name after
  `\01_` is now read exactly as the plain `@"S"` is (plain when `S` is a
  plain LLVM name, otherwise quoted: `"1x"`, `""`), so the two compare
  equal and are refused together, and a label that is no plain name, one
  starting with a digit or empty included, is carried only for an internal
  or private definition: an external `@"\01_1x"` or `@"\01_"`, whose symbol
  the third repair wrote as llc does, is now refused. A private plain name
  and a label of the same name are refused together too, although llc keeps
  them apart (a private plain name gets a private prefix: llc 22.1.2
  wrote the private function `@"1x"` as `l_1x`).

  A numbered symbol (`@0`, `define i64 @1()`) is carried by its number,
  which the importer writes as the symbol (`0`, `_0`), where LLVM's Mangler
  names it `__unnamed_N` (`___unnamed_N` on Mach-O), numbering the unnamed
  symbols in the order llc first names them; an object defining an external
  `@0` and one reading it linked and ran when one tool built both, and
  failed to link when llc built one of them (pre-existing; the fourth
  verifier round). Such a symbol is now carried only for an internal or
  private definition, and a module that has one is refused when another
  symbol's name holds `__unnamed_` (llc may give the numbered one that name:
  it bound a call of a declared `@__unnamed_1` to an internal `@0`, where
  the importer called the external function). That check matches the
  substring, so it also refuses a name llc keeps apart
  (`@.L__unnamed_1` beside a private `@0` on Mach-O).

  Outside an Apple triple, llc names every private symbol after `.L`, not
  only a numbered one: LLVM's ELF private prefix (`.LX` for a private
  `@X`), which its MC layer reads, in any symbol name, as an assembler
  temporary. The importer wrote a private `@foo` as a local `foo` and a
  declared `@.Lfoo` as an undefined `.Lfoo`, so llc bound a call of
  `@.Lfoo` to the private function (14) where the importer's build called a
  peer's `.Lfoo` (107) or did not link, and a load of `@.Lg` beside a
  private `@g` printed 22 and 1011 (pre-existing; the fifth verifier round
  of L02-P15); llc also rejects an undefined `.L` reference, an internal
  `@.Lfoo` beside a private `@foo` and an external `@.Lfunc_end0`, which the
  importer imported, and leaves an external `.L` definition out of its
  symbol table unless its own object refers to it. Unless the compile
  target's object format is Mach-O (below; "outside an Apple triple" in the
  fifth repair), a symbol that is not private is now refused under a `.L`
  name (decoded:
  `@"\2ELg"` is `@.Lg`), function or global, defined (internal included) or
  declared; this also refuses an external `.L` definition its own object
  calls and an internal one alone, which ran equal. A private symbol's `.L`
  name meets no other (llc writes a private `@.Lx` as `.L.Lx`); the fifth
  repair's statement that a private symbol keeps any name was false for a
  name the importer gives a call it writes in place of an intrinsic
  (below). On Mach-O, llc writes a
  private `@foo` as `l_foo` (or `L_foo`) and every name the importer admits
  after `_`, so such names are read there.

  Every rule that depends on the target reads it as llc does: the triple
  the importer is given (`import_text_for_target`; the driver passes the
  triple of the target it compiles for, resolved as the compiler resolves
  an architecture-only spec), which takes the place of the module's
  `target triple` as llc's `-mtriple` does, or else the module's triple (an
  empty one names none), read by one function as LLVM 22.1.2's `Triple`
  reads it (`src/triple.rs`: `parseArch`, `parseOS`, the format a last
  component's ending names, `-elf`, `-macho`, `-coff` and the rest, and
  `getDefaultFormat`; no normalization, which llc gives `-mtriple` alone
  and which changes nothing in the triples the driver passes). The `.L`
  rule and the `\01` label rule read its object format: Mach-O, where
  before they read the Apple OS alone, so with
  `arm64-apple-macosx14.0.0-elf`, for which llc writes ELF, the importer
  admitted a declared `@.Lfoo` beside a private `@foo` (llc's build printed
  14, the importer's 107 against a peer defining `.Lfoo`) and carried
  `@"\01_bar"` as `bar` (llc's object calls `_bar`: 5 and 9 against a C
  peer defining both), and a module stating an Apple triple compiled for
  Linux did the same (pre-existing; the sixth verifier round of L02-P15;
  O0-O3, GNU ld, gold and LLD). Both are refused now, and a module stating
  no triple, or Linux, compiled for `aarch64-apple-darwin` reads its labels
  and `.L` names as Mach-O ones (llc's and the importer's objects have the
  same non-local symbols). The RISC-V rules read its architecture (above).
  The reading was compared with LLVM 22.1.2's own `Triple` (the
  TargetParser library of the Trust LLVM build, linked into a scratch
  program) over 78,128 generated triples: every parsed architecture name,
  ARM, Thumb, AArch64 and BPF spellings through LLVM's special parsers,
  every OS prefix the default reads, version suffixes, format endings and
  one to five components; the object format and the RISC-V width agree on
  every one. When no target is known (the library's `import_text` on a
  module stating none), the object format is taken for not Mach-O.

  llc lowers an intrinsic the importer writes as a call
  (`@llvm.sin.f64` and the other libm intrinsics of `libm_intrinsic_symbol`,
  as `sin`, `sinf`, `pow`, ...; `@llvm.experimental.memset.pattern.*` as
  `memset_patternN`) to a call of the external symbol, outside the
  module's symbols, while it names a private `@sin` after its private
  prefix (`.Lsin` on ELF, `l_sin` on Mach-O). The importer's call reached
  the module's private definition: llc's builds printed sin(0.5) = 0.479,
  pow(2, 10) = 1024 and sinf(0.5) = 0.479 where the importer's printed 42,
  and a private `@memset_pattern16` beside a pattern fill wrote 99 where
  llc's loop filled 7s (pre-existing; the sixth verifier round of L02-P15;
  AArch64 Linux, O0-O3, GNU ld, gold and LLD; on Mach-O llc's object for
  `pow` calls `_pow` and the importer's none). The sixth repair refused a
  private function or global so named, but a Mach-O `\01_sin` label, and
  admitted an internal `@sin`, stating that llc binds its libcall to it as
  the importer does (both printed 42 for a lone `@llvm.sin.f64`). That
  holds only where llc lowers the intrinsic to a call of `sin` alone: at O2
  llc 22.1.2 merges `@llvm.sin.f64` and `@llvm.cos.f64` of one operand into
  a call of `sincos` (an internal `@sincos` received it: llc's build
  printed 42, the importer's sin + cos 1.357; beside an internal `@sin`
  llc's object calls libm's `sincos`), and the stated reason for refusing
  a private `@memset_pattern16` was false: llc 22.1.2 calls the module's
  own private `memset_pattern16` on Mach-O and expands a loop on Linux,
  calling nothing (pre-existing; the seventh verifier round of L02-P15).
  Such a definition is now refused whatever its linkage, a `\01_sin` label
  included, with the library names llc's code generator calls or replaces
  on its own (below).

  llc 22.1.2's code generator gives library functions meaning on its own
  for AArch64 (read in its source, and run at O0 and O2 for Linux and
  Darwin triples with the object's relocations read): it forms calls the
  module does not make, `sincos`/`sincosf` (GNU) or
  `__sincos_stret`/`__sincosf_stret` (Darwin) for a `sin` and a `cos` of
  one operand at O2 (also for `memory(none)` calls of a module's own
  external `sin` and of `cos`), `cbrt`/`cbrtf` for `pow(x, 1/3)` with
  `nnan ninf nsz afn`, `bzero` for a zero fill on Darwin (O0 too),
  `memset_pattern16` for a constant pattern fill on Darwin (the module's
  function of that name, whatever its linkage), and at O1-O3 the plain
  function of a fortified call whose object size is unknown (`strcpy` for
  `__strcpy_chk`, `memcpy` for `__mempcpy_chk`, `memccpy` for
  `__memccpy_chk`), and `MergeICmps` forms `memcmp` (source read; a probe
  of ten comparisons formed none); and it lowers a call of a function that
  is not module-local named `fabs`, `copysign`, `sqrt`, `sin`, `cos`,
  `memcmp`, `bcmp`, `mempcpy`, `ldexp` or `exp10` to other code (`fsqrt`
  for a `memory(none)` call of a module's own external `sqrt` at O2,
  `memcpy` for `mempcpy`, an SVE `fscale` for `ldexp` where the function's
  features or processor give SVE, a call of `__exp10` for `exp10` on
  Darwin). The importer calls exactly the functions the module calls
  (false for a constant-count `memcpy` or `memset`; corrected 2026-10-23,
  below), so a module definition under such a name ran otherwise: the internal
  `@sincos` above. A module defining a function or global under one of
  these names (`LLC_LIBRARY_NAMES`, with the `f` and `l` forms, for either
  target), whatever its linkage, is refused by name, as is one defining a
  name the importer gives a call it writes in place of an intrinsic the
  module calls (`exp` beside `@llvm.exp.f64`, `memset_pattern4` beside an
  `i32` pattern fill on Darwin). An `available_externally` body and a
  declaration are admitted. This over-refuses definitions llc's lowering
  does not reach (an internal `sqrt`, which `visitCall` skips; `bzero` on
  Linux; an internal or external `@exp` beside `@llvm.exp.f64`, whose
  libcall llc binds to it as the importer does) and definitions that
  behave as the library function (a module's own standard `memcpy` or
  `memset`: the `nobuiltin` loops of L02-P13's second verifier round,
  which ran equal). Not covered: a definition of such a name in another
  object of the link, and other targets' llc (x86-64, RISC-V), whose
  libcalls were not enumerated.

  The closure audit of 2026-10-16 found four classes the list above
  missed, each admitted and each running otherwise than llc's build at
  O1-O3 (AArch64 Linux, GNU ld, gold and LLD, static and PIE; Darwin by
  reading the objects): a module's own fortified function (`__strcpy_chk`
  writing `X` gave 88 in the import, llc's `strcpy` 97; an internal
  `__memcpy_chk` 7 against `memcpy`'s 42; 15 names, external and
  internal); `ldexp`/`ldexpf` under SVE (the module's 42 against llc's
  `fscale` of 1.5 * 2^3 = 12, under `+sve`, `+sve2`, `+sve2p1` or
  `"target-cpu"="neoverse-v2"`); `exp10`/`exp10f` on Darwin (llc's object
  called libSystem's `___exp10`, the import's ran the module's body, and
  llc's call reached a module's own `__exp10` where the import's did not);
  and compiler-runtime helpers (with a module's own `__udivti3` returning
  42, `udiv i128 100, 3` gave 42 in the import, 33 in llc's build, which
  divides by a constant inline; a module's own `__floattidf` 70 against
  100). All four are now refused by name, whatever the definition's
  linkage, on every target: the 18 fortified functions LLVM 22.1.2's
  `TargetLibraryInfo.td` names, `ldexp`, `ldexpf`, `ldexpl`, `exp10`,
  `exp10f` and `exp10l` (the features and the OS are not read), all in
  `LLC_LIBRARY_NAMES`, and every name LLVM 22.1.2's `RuntimeLibcalls.td`
  lists in the member list of `AArch64SystemLibrary`, whatever the
  availability predicate it is listed under (602 names:
  `crates/trust-cg-llvm-import/src/llvm_runtime_libcalls.rs`, which a
  unit test requires to equal the names a committed `llvm-tblgen
  --dump-json` extract reaches, `scripts/extract_llvm_library_names.py`).
  That table holds the libm and libc names llc calls for an operation
  (`fmod` for `frem`, `floor`, `pow`, `exp`, `tan`, `memcpy`, ...), the
  integer and floating-point helpers (`__udivti3`, `__floattidf`,
  `__addtf3`, ...), the outline atomics, the SME routines,
  `__stack_chk_fail` and `__stack_chk_guard`, `_Unwind_Resume`, names
  LLVM lists only for Darwin (`bzero`, `__exp10`, `memset_pattern4`,
  `memset_pattern8`), Windows (`__chkstk`), OpenBSD (`__guard_local`) or
  an SjLj exception model, and `malloc`, `calloc` and `free`, which LLVM
  lists for its middle end and the LTO symbol table and llc's code
  generator never calls. Each is refused as a function or a global
  definition; a declaration is admitted. Stated over-refusals: every
  definition llc's own call would reach as the import's does (a module's
  own `floor` or `fmod` that ran equal at the audit's base, a custom
  `malloc`), `ldexp` without SVE and `exp10` off Darwin. Not covered, as
  above: a definition in another object of the link, and other targets'
  libcalls (the table is AArch64's).

  Corrected 2026-10-23 (third closure audit of L02-P15, at `9a237122b`):
  the importer's build does not call exactly the functions the module
  calls. Its backend reads a call of a declared `memcpy`, `memmove` or
  `memset` with a constant count as a bulk-memory operation and may
  expand it into loads and stores, calling nothing, where llc 22.1.2 keeps
  the call. (Corrected again the same day, below: the reader on AArch64 is
  trust-cg-lower's adapter, not `trust-cg-irmid`'s memory-call pass, which
  runs on the wasm32 profile only, and it reads a call of any count.)
  Measured on AArch64 Linux at O0-O3: a plain 8-byte `memcpy`
  and a plain 16-byte zero `memset` left no reference to the function in
  the import's object, while llc's object called it (`bl memcpy`,
  `bl memset`); a 4-byte `memmove` was called by both. The audit's skeptic
  read llc as expanding these calls too; it did not in these probes.
  LLVM's LangRef lets a plain call of a C99 library name be read as the
  library function, so this is a difference LLVM allows, seen only by a
  `memcpy` or `memset` that does more than copy or fill (a counting one in
  another object printed 0 calls in the import against llc's 1: 0 of 24
  configurations equal, O0-O3; GNU ld, gold and LLD; static and PIE). It is
  stated, not refused. The keyword `nobuiltin` and the string attributes
  `"no-builtins"` and `"no-builtin-<name>"` withdraw that licence: LLVM
  reads a call carrying `nobuiltin`, or of a function declared with it, as
  no call of the library function, and `TargetLibraryInfo` reads none of
  a function's calls (`no-builtins`, with any value or none) or none of
  its calls of the named function (`no-builtin-<name>`) as one, and llc
  keeps them as calls. The importer read the three as only restricting
  llc, so a freestanding module's own `memcpy` or `memset` was not called
  where llc's object calls it (the audit's `r1_nobuiltin_memcpy` and
  `r5_memset`, 0 of 24 configurations equal each). Each is now refused by
  name wherever a function attribute is read (a definition's or
  declaration's own, a call's own, and an attribute group one of them
  uses; any key that starts with `no-builtin-`; keys read after LLVM's
  escapes). Not read for them: a call the importer drops (`llvm.assume`,
  `llvm.lifetime.*`, `llvm.dbg.*`, ...), and a group no function or call
  uses. `builtin` is still read. Over-refused: every module built with
  `-ffreestanding`/`-fno-builtin` or from a Rust `#![no_builtins]` crate
  (they carry `"no-builtins"` on every function), whatever it calls, and a
  restriction on an intrinsic declaration, whose attributes LLVM's parser
  replaces.

  Corrected again 2026-10-23 (the L02-P15 LD-74 re-check at `ff895a9be`):
  the backend read those calls by the callee's NAME alone. trust-cg-lower's
  adapter lowered any call of a non-module-local `memcpy`, `memmove` or
  `memset` (any count, not only a constant one) as the bulk-memory
  operation and defined its result as the destination, whatever the
  declaration said; the irmid memory-call pass named above runs only on the
  wasm32 profile. LLVM reads a declaration with another prototype as an
  ordinary function (its `TargetLibraryInfo` checks the prototype) and llc
  calls it, so the re-check's `n1_memcpy_ints` (`i64 @memcpy(i64, i64,
  i64)`, defined in another object) crashed where llc's build printed
  `r=348`, `n2_memset_ret_count` (`memset` returning its count) printed the
  destination address, and 8 of a 16-module family of other prototypes
  (a `void`, `i32` or integer result, a 32- or 128-bit count, a variadic or
  `fastcc` declaration) ran otherwise. Now (LD-100) a
  call is the routine only when its callee is declared with C's prototype
  on these LP64 targets and C's convention: `memcpy`/`memmove`
  `(ptr, ptr, size_t) -> ptr`, `memset` `(ptr, int, size_t) -> ptr`, a
  pointer a thin data pointer, `int` 32 bits and `size_t` 64 bits of either
  signedness, not variadic. Any other declaration is an ordinary call of
  the symbol, as llc builds it; a `fastcc` declaration of the three names,
  which this importer reads as C, is refused by name. An LLVM intrinsic name
  the adapter reads (`llvm.mem*`, `llvm.bitreverse.*`, `llvm.objectsize.*`,
  `llvm.fma.*`/`llvm.fmuladd.*`, `llvm.aarch64.crc32*`) declared at another
  type than its name states is refused by name. The verifier's fsym scan
  reads the same decision, and AArch64 SROA's memcpy-fill rewrite reads
  only the `bl memcpy` instruction selection makes for a bulk-memory
  operation (`InstFlags::LIBRARY_ROUTINE_CALL`), not any call so named.
  The difference stated above (a C-prototype call with a constant count may
  be expanded where llc 22.1.2 calls) is unchanged. Not covered: the
  AArch64 vectorizer still reads a `bl calloc` as C's `calloc` by its name
  alone (a source `calloc` declared otherwise is not told apart), and other
  targets' runs (the differential ran on AArch64 Linux only); both are
  LD-100's stated residuals.

  Corrected once more 2026-10-23 (the re-check at `f95ca7609`): the gate
  read the signature the importer gave the callee, and the importer did not
  always take it from the module's own header. An unprototyped `declare ptr
  @memcpy(...)` called as `ptr (ptr, ptr, i64)` was signed from the call
  (OD-56), so the gate saw C's prototype and the copy was expanded where
  LLVM reads a variadic function, not the library's, and llc calls it (the
  re-check's `u1`, `u3b`, `u6` and `u7` ran otherwise in 24 of 24
  configurations); a header of these names this importer does not model
  (`declare fp128 @memcpy(ptr, ptr, i64)`) was skipped and signed by its
  call the same way. The importer now refuses by name, for `memcpy`,
  `memmove` and `memset` (the names come from the adapter's
  `classify_adapter_named_call`): an unprototyped `(...)` header (also on
  an intrinsic name the adapter reads), an unmodeled header, a call with no
  header (LLVM refuses that module too), and a Mach-O `\01_` label naming
  one, which LLVM reads as an ordinary function and this importer carried
  under the plain name (LD-100 rule 8). Stated
  over-refusals: such modules that llc builds alike, among them an
  unprototyped `memcpy`, `memmove` or `memset` whose calls the backend
  happened to keep (five of the re-check's probes), and an uncalled
  unprototyped intrinsic declaration.

  Corrected a third time 2026-10-23 (the re-check at `f37c48df9`): the
  importer compared a direct call's own function type with its callee's
  only for the fixed/variadic split of a variadic or unprototyped callee,
  never its result or parameter types. A call through a cast, `%c = call
  i64 @memcpy(ptr, ptr, i64 8)` against C's `declare ptr @memcpy(ptr, ptr,
  i64)` (clang emits it for a call through a function cast; also other
  results, a tail call, `memset` returning `i64`), was read by the backend
  as the routine and expanded, where LLVM reads a call whose type is not
  its callee's as no call of the declared function and llc calls the
  symbol (34 of the re-check's probes printed other data in 24 of 24
  configurations each). An ordinary callee had the defect in kind where no
  reader types the result: `double g(void)` called as `i64 ()`, its result
  passed to `printf`, printed another value (0 of 24). Every direct call
  the importer keeps as a call of its callee, an intrinsic the backend
  lowers included, is now refused by name when its stated type, result and
  parameters, is not its callee's signature (the header's, or for an
  unprototyped header or none, the first call's)
  (LD-100 rule 9). Stated
  over-refusals: every call through a cast llc builds as a call, among
  them 182 of the re-check's probes that ran alike (or, `l_strlen_callty`,
  differed only in a static link's call count, as its control does).

  Corrected a fourth time 2026-10-24 (rule 9's verifier): the calls the
  importer writes itself in place of an intrinsic were typed by the
  module's own function of the symbol they call. Beside `declare i64
  @sin(double)`, `@llvm.sin.f64`, which the importer calls as `sin`, read
  its result from `x0` where llc, lowering the intrinsic to a call of `sin`
  at `double (double)` whatever the module declares, reads `d0` (0 of 24
  configurations equal for 13 of the 16 libm families with an `i64` header,
  12 of 24 for `sinh` and `cosh`, and 0 of 24 for `sin` with an `i32` or
  `ptr` header and `sinf` with an `i32` one). Such a call is now recorded at the
  intrinsic's type and refused by name when the symbol's final signature is
  another (LD-100 rule 10); so is a libm intrinsic call stating another
  type than the intrinsic's (llc refuses it), and, on Darwin, a
  `memset_patternN` declared otherwise beside a pattern fill. Stated
  over-refusals: such modules whose results happened to read alike (12 of
  the differential's probes ran alike in 24 of 24, among them a variadic
  `declare double @sin(double, ...)`), and an unprototyped header of the
  symbol before the intrinsic's call (refused before, by the backend).
  Still admitted where llc refuses (no wrong code against an llc build):
  an intrinsic the importer rewrites to operations (`fabs`, `sqrt`,
  min/max, ...) whose declaration states another type than its own
  (`declare double @llvm.fabs.f64(float)` called at `double`); it reads no
  signature.

  Corrected a fifth time 2026-10-24 (the fifth re-check at `848a8638d`):
  instruction selection keys a callee's hidden return buffer (`sret`) by
  the symbol's name, and read that fact for its own calls of the same name
  too. With `declare void @memcpy(ptr sret(%S), ptr, i64)` called once in
  a function (an ordinary call since LD-100), the selector's own `memcpy`
  call for an `@llvm.memcpy` in that function passed the destination in
  `x8`, the source in `x0` and the count in `x1`, and the import died with
  signal 11 where llc's build, which calls the routine at C's convention
  whatever the module declares, copied (0 of 24 configurations equal for
  `memcpy` at a run-time count, 40 and 64 bytes, and `memmove` and `memset`
  at a run-time count, 8, 40 and 64). A direct call of a function named like
  any routine the backend calls on its own, declared with a hidden return
  buffer, is now refused by name by AArch64 instruction selection (LD-100
  rule 11; x86-64 places such a pointer in C's first argument register and
  still lowers it, not run). Stated over-refusals:
  such a call where the backend makes no call of the routine in the same
  function, or makes it without reading the fact (an `sret` `__divti3`
  beside an `i128` division), which llc builds as a call: 9 probes that ran
  alike in 24 of 24 configurations (an 8-byte `memcpy` expanded inline, the
  three routines called only from another function, the four i128
  division helpers, and an earlier round's `memcpy` declared `sret(i8)`).
  The importer also gave a call's result the fresh-allocation facts
  (`NoAlias`, `Aligned(16)`) of `malloc`, `calloc`, `aligned_alloc` or
  `reallocarray` by name whatever the prototype; it now gives them only at
  C's prototype.

  Corrected a sixth time 2026-10-24 (rule 11's verifier and the sixth
  re-check at `f8e524bc9`): the importer respells a direct call of an
  `extern_weak` function as an indirect call through its address (the one
  call trust-ir admits for a weak declaration), which keeps the signature
  and convention but none of the function's attributes. Declared with a
  hidden return buffer (`declare extern_weak void @fill_s(ptr sret(%S),
  ptr, i64)`), the buffer went in `x0` instead of `x8` and every argument
  one register later, where llc applies the declaration's `sret` (12
  probes, 0 of 24 configurations equal: SIGSEGV or other data), and a
  runtime routine's name so declared got past rule 11. Declared
  `extern_weak`, an intrinsic the backend lowers by name
  (`@llvm.memcpy.p0.p0.i64`, `@llvm.fma.f64`, ...) became a call of an
  undefined weak symbol so named, which faulted where llc lowers the
  intrinsic (found by the repair's sweep). Both calls are now refused by
  name at import, as is a weak callee with any other placement fact the
  indirect call does not carry (`byval`, a stated extension or pass mode;
  the importer writes none) (LD-100 rule 12). Stated over-refusals: such a
  call llc builds alike, among them one never executed or guarded by a
  null test that skips it, and every such call on x86-64, where the buffer
  takes C's first argument register either way (read, not run).

  The importer read a function's blocks only from their labels. LLVM starts
  a new block at an instruction that follows a terminator, numbered like an
  unnamed value when it has no label, and llc builds such a module; the
  importer appended the instruction to the terminated block, and the IR
  validator then refused the module ("MidBlockTerminator"). Such an
  instruction is now refused by name when it is read (2026-10-23). A
  `uselistorder` directive in that place, which LLVM reads after the last
  block, keeps its own refusal.

  `@llvm.experimental.memset.pattern.*` is
  now lowered (to libSystem's `memset_patternN`) only for a macOS, iOS,
  tvOS or watchOS target, the OSes LLVM's `TargetLibraryInfo` gives
  `memset_pattern16`; for any other target, or none known, llc expands a
  loop and the intrinsic is refused by name (on Linux the importer's
  object referred to a `memset_pattern16` glibc does not define). The
  version bounds LLVM also reads (macOS 10.5, iOS 3.0) are not read.

  LLVM reads an overloaded intrinsic's types from its function type and
  renames it to match (`Intrinsic::remangleIntrinsicFunction`; a call of
  an undeclared one is declared from the call's type), so `declare double
  @llvm.sin.f32(double)` is `@llvm.sin.f64` to llc. The importer read the
  libm function from the name's suffix and passed `llvm.bitreverse.i32`,
  `llvm.objectsize.i32.p0` and `llvm.fma.f64` to the adapter, which reads
  them by name: llc's builds printed sin(0.5) = 0.479426 and powf(3, 2) =
  9 for `@llvm.sin.f32` declared `double (double)` and `@llvm.pow.f64`
  declared `float (float, float)`, the importer's 0.5 (`sinf`) and 0 (`pow`
  with float arguments) (pre-existing; the seventh verifier round of
  L02-P15). An overloaded intrinsic the importer reads is now admitted, at
  a declaration and at a call, only under the name LLVM gives its type
  (and an elementwise vector one only under its element type's suffix):
  a name with other suffixes is refused by name, which over-refuses the
  mis-suffixed `memcpy`, `fma` and `fmuladd` calls that ran equal and a
  name with extra suffixes or none, all of which LLVM renames. A
  declaration the signature reader passes over (one stating a vector type)
  was not checked, so `declare <4 x float> @llvm.sin.v2f64(<4 x float>)`
  beside a call of `@llvm.sin.v2f64` with `<2 x double>` was admitted and
  ran (94), where LLVM renames the declaration `@llvm.sin.v4f32` and its
  verifier rejects the call ("Intrinsic called with incompatible
  signature"; the closure audit of 2026-10-16). Such a declaration of an
  intrinsic the importer reads, or of a family its vector expander reads
  (the elementwise ones, named by their result, and the
  `llvm.vector.reduce.*` folds, named by their vector operand), is now
  refused unless its name is the one LLVM gives its declared types (`v4f32`
  for `<4 x float>`), and so is a reduction call whose name is not the one
  its operand's type gives; a call whose types differ from its
  declaration's is therefore refused at one of the two. This over-refuses
  mis-suffixed reduction calls, which LLVM renames (the audit's seven, five
  with no declaration and two beside a declaration under the same name whose
  types agree with the call, ran equal at its base), and a mis-named
  declaration no call uses. A unit test requires the table of overloaded intrinsics the
  importer reads to equal those of LLVM 22.1.2's `Intrinsics.td` (a
  committed extract) that its call classifiers read under some suffixes,
  each with LLVM's overloaded types, so the deletion of any entry fails
  it. The
  adapter answers the one `@llvm.objectsize.i64.p0` form it lowers (`min`
  false, `nullunknown` true, not `dynamic`) with -1, where llc 22.1.2
  evaluates a size it can determine: for a 16-byte global its build
  printed 16 at O0-O3 and the importer's -1 (pre-existing; this repair's
  differential control). LangRef allows it ("The maximum size may be any
  size greater than or equal to the actual object size (including -1 if
  unknown)"), but a program printing or branching on the value runs
  otherwise than llc's build, and a fortified check llc's build fails
  passes.

  LLVM reads an intrinsic, and its reserved `llvm.` globals, by the IR
  name (`Function::isIntrinsic`), which for a Mach-O `\01` label starts
  with the `\01` byte: `@"\01_llvm.assume"` is the ordinary function
  `_llvm.assume` to llc 22, which calls it. The importer carries a label by
  the name after `\01_` and read that name as the intrinsic: it dropped a
  call of `\01_llvm.assume`, lowered `\01_llvm.memcpy.p0.p0.i64` inline,
  called libm's `_sin` for `\01_llvm.sin.f64` (also where the module
  defined it), and exempted `declare void @"\01_llvm.assume"(i1)` with the
  signing key alone, which llc rejects (pre-existing, the exemption from the
  fourth repair; the fifth verifier round). Such a label is now refused by
  name wherever it appears, a global such as `@"\01_llvm.used"` included,
  and the exemption reads the IR name. The calls the importer drops (the
  list above), and those it lowers as `memcpy`, `memmove` and `memset`, are
  now matched as `Intrinsic::lookupIntrinsicID` matches a name (the name
  exactly, or for an overloaded intrinsic the name, `.` and a type suffix,
  each read from LLVM 22.1.2's `Intrinsics.td`), where they were matched by
  prefix: `@llvm.assumex`, `@llvm.sideeffect.x`, `@llvm.dbg.custom`,
  `@llvm.prefetchx` and `@llvm.memcpyx`, which llc 22.1.2 calls as ordinary
  external functions, were dropped or lowered as `memcpy` (against a C peer
  defining `llvm.assumex`, `llvm.sideeffect.x` and `llvm.memcpyx`, llc's
  builds printed 100, 1000 and a changed copy, the importer's 0, 0 and a
  plain one), and the distinct
  `@llvm.memcpy.inline.p0.p0.i64`, which llc expands without a call, was
  lowered as `memcpy` (for 4096 bytes the importer's object called
  `memcpy`). Each is now refused by name as an `llvm.` call without a
  lowering, as are `llvm.memset.inline` and the `.element.unordered.atomic`
  forms (refused before by the volatile-flag reader).
  Every reader of a string's content decodes it the same way: an attribute's
  key and value (`"target-features"="+v8a\2C+call-saved-x9"` is two
  features, and the mode feature is refused: before, the imported callee
  clobbered x9, which the llc-built caller relied on, in 24 of 24
  configurations), a section name, the `#pragma clang section` keys, the
  module's triple and metadata strings.

  Named metadata and module flags are read or refused by name
  (`crates/trust-cg-llvm-import/src/metadata.rs`), from a survey of the names
  LLVM 22's parser, auto-upgrade, code generator and object writers read
  (`getNamedMetadata`, `getModuleFlag` and the `Module` accessors over it).
  `!llvm.module.flags` is read flag by flag. `!llvm.ident`,
  `!llvm.commandline` and `!llvm.dbg.cu` are records llc builds no code from,
  read once every operand is the node LLVM's verifier checks for there (a
  node holding one string, which it requires; a `!DICompileUnit`, which it
  checks as debug information: llc 22 drops invalid debug information with a
  warning, "ignoring invalid debug info", and builds the code, and the
  importer refuses it); the debug-information records are not otherwise
  validated. Refused: `!llvm.dependent-libraries` (llc's
  `.deplibs` made LLD link libm; the imported object did not) and
  `!llvm.linker.options` with an operand (with none, llc writes an empty
  `.deplibs` or `.linker-options` section on ELF, which no linker acts on,
  gold copying the empty `.deplibs` into the executable, and nothing on
  Mach-O; these are read), `!llvm.stats`, `!llvm.pseudo_probe_desc`, the
  offloading lists, `!llvm.errno.tbaa`, the debugify lists,
  `!nvvm.annotations` (which LLVM's parser upgrades into attributes and
  calling conventions), `!hipe.literals`, `!wasm.custom_sections`, the
  Objective-C ARC marker, any other name in the `llvm.dbg.` namespace (which
  llc 22 drops with the debug information, warning that it is invalid) and
  any other name in the `llvm.` namespace; any other name is one llc does
  not read. A module flag is read only when it changes nothing the importer
  builds: `wchar_size`, `PIC Level`, `PIE Level`, `uwtable`,
  `frame-pointer`, the DWARF versions, `RtLibUseGOT` (the same runtime
  functions, called through the GOT), `SDK Version`, the profile summaries,
  `Code Model` small, branch protection (`branch-target-enforcement`,
  `sign-return-address`, `-all`, `-with-bkey`, `guarded-control-stack`,
  `branch-protection-pauth-lr`) at 0, `probe-stack` `inline-asm`,
  `stack-probe-size` from 4096 to 2^63 - 1 (below), and `ptrauth-elf-got` and
  `ptrauth-sign-personality` at 0 (llc's three readers of them act only on 1;
  clang 22 writes them only when on). `PIC Level` does change llc 22's
  AArch64 build of an `ssp` function, though not the importer's: at level 0,
  as without the flag, llc addresses `__stack_chk_guard` PC-relative, and at
  any other level through the GOT, as the importer's backend always does. In
  the differential below, llc's object at level 0 or without the flag did
  not link into a GNU ld PIE or a GNU ld or LLD shared object ("recompile
  with -fPIC"), where the imported one linked and ran; every other run was
  equal. Later clang (upstream clang at 2f8eb5b4be, 2026-07-31, and at
  least since 2026-07-24, the oldest commit of the shallow clone read: the
