  emission predates 2f8eb5b4be, which the second repair of this row named
  as its origin) writes
  `ptrauth-elf-got`, `ptrauth-init-fini` and
  `ptrauth-init-fini-address-discrimination` at 0 on every AArch64 ELF
  module, and on AArch64 Linux also `ptrauth-sign-personality` at 0 and the
  `aarch64-elf-pauthabi-platform`/`-version` pair (platform `0x10000002`,
  version 0 without pointer authentication). Such a module is refused: the
  two `ptrauth-init-fini` flags are keys this importer does not read (llc 22
  reads neither), and llc 22 writes the pauthabi pair, a version of 0
  included, into a `.note.gnu.property` pointer-authentication property and
  the `.ARM.attributes` build attributes, which the importer's objects lack.
  Reading `ptrauth-elf-got` and `ptrauth-sign-personality` at 0 therefore
  admits no module later clang writes for AArch64 ELF (the second verifier
  round of this row found the earlier wording, that later clang writes both
  at 0 on every AArch64 Linux module, silent on the flags it writes with
  them).
  Every other flag is refused by name, among them the `stack-protector-guard`
  flags (llc read the canary from `sp_el0` and trapped where the imported
  build read `__stack_chk_guard`), branch protection on (llc writes the GNU
  property note and, for a value of 1 under an ARM or AArch64 `target triple`,
  LLVM's parser gives every definition the attribute), x86 CET
  (`cf-protection-*`, which llc reads by presence), KCFI,
  `override-stack-alignment`, the other pointer-authentication flags and these
  two at any other value, a code model other than small, and every key the
  list does not name. A flag's integer is read as LLVM's `iN` constant, the
  literal truncated to `N` bits (`i8 255` is -1, `i1 2` is 0), and its
  behavior as LLVM's parser upgrades it (`PIC Level` from error or max to min,
  `PIE Level` from error to max, branch protection from error to min); an
  integer spelled in LLVM's `u0x`/`s0x` hexadecimal, which LLVM reads like
  any other (llc 22 accepts `!{i32 u0x1, !"wchar_size", i32 4}`), is refused
  by name, as a spelling this importer does not read. A flag
  LLVM's verifier then rejects (a behavior outside 1-8, a key listed twice, a
  value its behavior does not admit, a `require` flag) is refused: `!{i32 1,
  !"PIC Level", i32 -1}`, `!{i32 7, !"PIC Level", i32 -1}` and `!{i32 8, !"PIC
  Level", i8 255}` imported before the first repair of this row, where llc
  rejects them. So are a numbered metadata node defined twice, a use of one
  never defined, and a `!DICompileUnit`, a `!DIAssignID` or a defining
  `!DISubprogram` written without `distinct` (LLVM's parser rejects each; a
  non-distinct `!DICompileUnit` in `!llvm.dbg.cu` imported before that
  repair). A `!DISubprogram`'s `spFlags` is read as LLVM's parser reads it:
  `|`-separated `DISPFlag` names and unsigned 32-bit integers, decimal or
  `u0x` hexadecimal, any with the definition bit (8) making it a definition
  (the first repair read only decimal integers and the name, and imported
  `spFlags: u0x8` and `DISPFlagLocalToUnit | u0x8` without `distinct`, which
  llc rejects); an `spFlags` LLVM's parser rejects (a negative or `s0x`
  integer, one above 32 bits, an unknown name or `DISPFlagZero`, an empty
  piece) is refused, `distinct` or not. So are an `isDefinition` other than
  `true` or `false` (LLVM's parser reads it as a boolean, "expected 'true'
  or 'false'") and a `distinct` anywhere but right after the `=` of a
  numbered node's definition, the one place LLVM's parser reads it (inside
  another node, as in `unit: distinct !DICompileUnit(...)`, it rejects it:
  "expected metadata operand"); the importer took a distinct `isDefinition:
  0` and such an inline compile unit before the third repair of this row,
  where llc rejects both. So is a `!DISubprogram` that writes
  `isDefinition` or `spFlags` twice (LLVM's parser: "field 'X' cannot be
  specified more than once"), which the importer read by the first one
  before the fourth repair.

  Boolean string attributes follow LLVM 22's reading of each: the
  floating-point permissions, `disable-tail-calls` and `use-soft-float` are
  read by value and `nooutline` by presence, each only restricting llc;
  `no-builtins` is read by presence too, and with every
  `no-builtin-<name>` is refused (above: it does not only restrict llc,
  because this importer's backend reads a call of a library function by
  its name); `"branch-target-enforcement"` is read by presence
  (`AArch64FunctionInfo`), so llc builds BTI landing pads for `"false"` too
  (only under an ARM or AArch64 `target triple` does LLVM's parser first
  drop a `"false"` one), and it is refused in every form. Attribute values
  LLVM's verifier rejects are refused: a `target-features` entry that is
  empty or does not start with `+`/`-` (the value is no longer trimmed), a
  `frame-pointer`, `denormal-fp-math`, `warn-stack-size` or
  `sign-return-address-key` value it does not read, an empty
  `alloc-variant-zeroed`, and a `sign-return-address-key` without a
  `sign-return-address` among one function's or call's attributes, inline
  or through its group (LLVM's verifier checks them together:
  "'sign-return-address-key' present without `sign-return-address`"; the
  key alone imported before the third repair of this row). LLVM's verifier
  checks every call, so a call the importer drops (`llvm.assume`,
  `llvm.lifetime.*`, `llvm.dbg.*`, ...) is read for these checks alone
  (inline and through its group; an operand bundle is skipped): the key
  without its scope and a `sign-return-address` other than `none`, `all`
  or `non-leaf` or a key other than `a_key` or `b_key` are refused there,
  and nothing else of it is read (the third repair read none of a dropped
  call's attributes and imported such calls, which llc rejects; fourth
  verifier round). A declaration whose IR name starts with `llvm.` (a
  Mach-O `\01_llvm.` label is none, and is refused) is not
  checked for the key alone: LLVM's parser replaces an intrinsic
  declaration's attributes with the intrinsic's own, so llc accepts it
  (the third repair refused it). The importer carries no table of LLVM's
  intrinsics, so a name LLVM does not define (`@llvm.foo`, or a quoted
  `@"llvm.a b"` whose signature the importer does not model, which skips
  the declaration before the quoted-name rule reads it) or a type that
  does not match the intrinsic (`@llvm.assume(i64)`), whose attributes LLVM
  keeps and rejects with the key alone, imports. The name is read as LLVM
  decodes it: LLVM reads an overloaded intrinsic by its name and a `.`,
  whatever follows, then remangles the name and replaces the attributes, so
  llc 22.1.2 accepts the key alone on `declare <4 x double>
  @"llvm.fmuladd.a b"(<4 x double>, <4 x double>, <4 x double>)` (it prints
  `@llvm.fmuladd.v4f64`), which imports, while the same exemption read
  from the spelled, quoted name refused it; a quoted one whose signature
  is modelled, such as `@"llvm.memcpy.s_struct.a bs"(ptr, ptr, i64, i1)`,
  is registered and refused by the quoted-name rule, though llc accepts it
  too (sixth verifier round of L02-P15, which found the fifth repair's
  claim that such a declaration is refused either way false); and the allowlist still
  reads an intrinsic declaration's attributes, so a value it refuses there
  (`"sign-return-address-key"="c_key"`) is refused although LLVM discards
  it. `probe-stack`
  is read only as `inline-asm` or
  Apple's `__chkstk_darwin` (llc on AArch64 aborts on any other value; on
  x86-64 it calls the named function), and `stack-probe-size` only as a
  plain decimal (LLVM reads `010000` as octal) from 4096 to 2^63 - 1. LLVM
  22's `AArch64FunctionInfo` reads the interval, attribute or module flag, as
  a `uint64_t` (the flag through `getZExtValue`, which asserts that the
  value needs at most 64 bits, so `i128 8192` reads as 8192; the second
  repair of this row said it asserted on a constant wider than 64 bits) and
  asserts it is positive as an `int64_t`. The
  importer's AArch64 frames are probed at most 4096 bytes apart, at least as
  often as llc's at any interval it reads as positive. At or above 2^63 a
  release llc goes on with the negative size: with
  `"probe-stack"="inline-asm"` and a 300000-byte frame, llc 22.1.2's build
  crashed (SIGSEGV) in all 24 configurations of the differential where the
  imported one printed what it should, at 2^64 - 4096 (the attribute
  `"18446744073709547520"`; the flag `i64 -4096`, `i64 18446744073709547520`
  or an `i128` whose low 64 bits are -4096) and at 2^64 - 1 (`i64 -1`); at
  2^63 it ran. The first repair of this row read the flag unsigned at its
  width and so admitted `i64 -4096` and `i64 -1`, which the row's first
  version refused as negative literals; the positive spellings and the
  attribute were admitted from the row's first version. The flag and the
  attribute now
  share one predicate (`attributes::stack_probe_interval_read`), and a flag
  is read at its width, unsigned (`i16 61440` is 61440, `i32 -4096` is
  4294963200, both read). Upstream llc 22 aborts on
  `__chkstk_darwin` too ("Unsupported stack probing method"); Apple's LLVM,
  which writes it on every Darwin function, calls it for frames over a page,
  the probing the importer's AArch64 frames do. This is the one spelling the
  importer admits where upstream llc refuses the module.

  Literals are read as LLVM's lexer and parser read them: a floating-point
  constant is a decimal with its `.` or a `0x` bit pattern with an uppercase
  type tag (an integer literal for a floating-point type, `inf` and `nan` are
  refused), a `0xH` literal is only a `half`, and the value must fit its type
  exactly (`float 0.1` and `float 0x3FB999999999999A` imported as the nearest
  float, where llc rejects them); a `half` NaN keeps its sign and payload in
  either spelling (until the first repair of this row, every `0xH` NaN was
  read as a positive quiet NaN: `ret half 0xHFE00` returned `0x7e00` where
  llc's build returns `0xfe00`, on `aarch64-apple-darwin` and on Linux with
  the FP16 profile; the default Linux profile refuses every `half` constant at
  instruction selection); a signaling NaN narrowed to `half` or `float`, in
  either spelling, is refused (the importer carries it as a double, whose
  narrowing would quiet it); `0x...` is no integer (LLVM reads it as a
  floating-point bit pattern); `true`, `false` and `null` are no
  floating-point constants; and a global defined in section `llvm.metadata`,
  which llc does not emit, is refused. The importer is not an LLVM validator:
  other text LLVM's parser or verifier rejects may still import.

  Whether an object path spells a carried fact is the backend's decision:
  - On `aarch64-apple-darwin`, an imported hidden `external` function
    definition is a private extern (`N_SECT | N_EXT | N_PEXT`, the binding
    llc writes), the one function visibility fact the Mach-O object path
    spells. Imported protected functions, hidden functions of any other
    linkage, hidden declarations, function sections and `extern_weak`
    references are refused by name.
  - On `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` (`static` only), imported hidden or
    protected functions, definitions and declarations, and `extern_weak`
    references, functions and globals, are refused by the adapter.
    Hidden globals are emitted `HIDDEN`, and `weak`, `weak_odr`, `linkonce`
    and `linkonce_odr` functions and globals `STB_WEAK` in the shared
    `.text` or data section with no COMDAT group, as llc emits them without
    a `comdat` clause. A self-keyed COMDAT the importer admits (for the
    AArch64 ELF path, which groups it) is not grouped on x86-64, where llc
    groups it.

  Before L02-P13 these refused shapes compiled as exported,
  default-visibility, strong symbols on both targets. A function's address
  used before the line that declares or defines it is still refused
  ("address-of undeclared global"), so clang's order, which prints
  declarations last, does not import an `if (&weak_fn)` test; the native
  evidence declares the weak function first. trust-ir admits a call of an
  `extern_weak` function only through its address, so a direct call of one
  is imported as an indirect call. Until the L06-P15 fix lands (AArch64
  indirect calls store only the low half of a stack-passed 128-bit
  integer), such a call is refused by name when a 128-bit integer argument
  may be passed on the stack under the AArch64 conventions: each earlier
  pointer or integer argument (`i1` to `i64`) counts as one general-purpose
  register, `half`/`float`/`double` as none and each 128-bit integer as an
  even-aligned pair. The check runs at import, before a target is chosen,
  so it refuses that shape for every target. A call of a variadic
  `extern_weak` function is refused because no indirect variadic call is
  lowered. Before L02-P13 both shapes compiled, as a strong reference to
  the weak function. So is (LD-100 rule 12, every target) a call of an
  `extern_weak` function declared with a hidden return buffer (`sret`),
  which the indirect call does not carry, or with any other placement fact
  of a trust-ir slot the indirect call does not read (`byval`, a stated
  extension or pass mode), and of one named like an LLVM intrinsic, whose
  call would reach an undefined symbol so named. Argument and result
  extensions (`zeroext`, `signext`) are carried by the signature the
  indirect call keeps. The native evidence (`tests/symbol_linkage_elf.rs`) is
  AArch64 Linux execution with GNU ld, gold and LLD, against gcc/g++ twins
  (that host has no clang) and against the same LLVM text compiled by llc.
  The test finds llc through `TCG_LLC`, the first `llc` in an absolute
  `PATH` entry, or the sysroot of the compiler that builds it
  (`<sysroot>/lib/rustlib/aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu/bin/llc`, where a Trust
  package ships one with its other LLVM tools). The llc must be an
  executable file reporting the same LLVM major version as that compiler,
  and the test prints which it used. The Linux floor requires one for this
  target (`TCG_REQUIRE_LLC`), and its preflight refuses to run without one,
  so its only lane, the Trust package's `targo --unverified`, runs the llc
  twins with the package's own llc (LLVM 22.1.2). The retired stock 1.97.1
  lane (owner directive 2026-09-28) ran them with rustup's `llvm-tools`
  component (LLVM 22.1.6). A missing llc is refused with its remedy: a
  Trust package that ships its LLVM tools at `lib/rustlib/<host>/bin/llc`,
  or `TCG_LLC` naming an llc of the compiler's LLVM major version. It is not
  a linker or loader proof.
- The LLVM IR importer reads the parameter attributes that change the call
  ABI and ignores the rest (`noalias`, `align`, `nonnull`, `writable`,
  `dead_on_unwind`, ... only permit optimizations). `sret` on a `define` or
  `declare` parameter, or on the first call of an undeclared callee, is
  carried as trust-ir `ParamAttrs::sret` on the callee, which the backend
  lowers through X8 (L01-P11; before, the buffer went in X0 and a call
  returning a large struct crashed). Refused by name, since trust-ir has no
  spelling for them: a direct call whose own `sret` disagrees with its
  callee's (LLVM lowers the buffer when either says so), a declaration and a
  definition that disagree, an indirect call with an `sret` argument (a
  `CallIndirect` carries no parameter attributes), two `sret` parameters or a
  non-`ptr` one, and `byval`, `byref`, `inreg`, `inalloca`, `preallocated`,
  `nest`, `swiftself`, `swifterror` and `swiftasync` wherever they appear
  (a declaration with one is refused even where its signature would
  otherwise skip it, because LLVM applies a callee's attributes to calls
  that do not repeat them). So x86-64 System V IR that passes an aggregate
  `byval` does not import. The native evidence (`tests/sret_abi_e2e.rs`) is
  macOS AArch64 only: clang's IR of C sret definitions and sret callers of C
  callees at -O0..-O3, compiled by trust-cg and linked by ld64 with a
  clang-compiled driver, prints what the all-clang build prints; the Linux
  GNU ld, gold and LLD legs the ledger row names have not been run.
  `zeroext` and `signext` on an `i8` or `i16` parameter, argument or return
  value (DarwinPCS makes the caller extend an argument and the callee its
  return value, and a clang-compiled peer reads the register without
  re-extending) are carried as the signedness of the call edge's trust-ir
  type: a `zeroext` edge is `U8`/`U16`, which the backend zero-extends, and a
  `signext` or unstated one `I8`/`I16`, with a `Bitcast` between the edge
  type and the body's signless one at the definition's entry, before `ret`
  and at each call (L01-P11; before, every narrow edge was sign-extended, so
  an imported caller passed `(unsigned char)255` to a clang callee as -1 and
  an imported `unsigned char` function returned 200 to a clang caller as
  -56). `zeroext i1` is trust-ir `Bool` (0 or 1). Refused by name: `signext
  i1` (true as all ones), either attribute on a narrow variadic argument, and
  a call or a header whose extension disagrees with the callee's edge type
  (LLVM extends when the call site or the callee says so; trust-ir states it
  once, on the callee). On `i32` and wider both are no-ops on AArch64 and are
  not carried. `tests/int_ext_abi_e2e.rs` runs clang's -O0..-O3 IR of a C
  callee unit and a C caller unit through trust-cg, each linked by ld64 with
  the other unit built by clang and by trust-cg, against the all-clang build
  on macOS AArch64; its `_Bool` rows run at -O1..-O3 only, because clang's
  -O0 IR reloads a `_Bool` through `trunc i8 to i1`, which the backend
  refuses (`CastOp::Trunc` from `I8` to `Bool`).
- The importer decodes string tokens (`c"..."` initializers, `section`
  names) as LLVM's `UnEscapeLexed` does: `\\` is one backslash and is
  recognized before a hex escape, `\XX` is one byte, and any other
  backslash is itself (L02-P14; before, `\\` stayed two bytes, so
  `c"a\\\00"` imported as four bytes where LLVM reads three). A
  `c"..."` whose decoded length is not its declared `[N x i8]` length is
  refused by name ("a c-string whose decoded length differs from its
  declared array type"), as LLVM's parser rejects it, and a section name
  whose bytes are not UTF-8 is refused. `tests/c_string_escapes_e2e.rs`
  compares an escape corpus (every rule, every byte value) against clang
  reading the same `.ll`, linked by ld64 on macOS AArch64.
- At O1 only, AArch64 ELF refuses some calls with nine or more pointer
  arguments computed from a symbol's address, some of them passed on the
  stack: object emission reports that a fixup `Page21` addresses the
  callee or the global PC-relatively where only its GOT slot is correct
  (for example "fixup Page21 addresses `wf`, a weak undefined symbol,
  PC-relatively"). It fails closed; O0, O2 and O3 compile the same shapes.
  Since L02-P13 imports a direct call of an `extern_weak` function as an
  indirect call, a null-guarded call of one whose pointer arguments are
  GEPs of an external global is refused at O1 from nine arguments under
  `static`, `pie` and `pic`. The base compiled that call, as a strong
  direct call, under `pic` with up to ten such arguments and under
  `static` and `pie` at every count measured (up to twelve). Under `pic`
  at O1 the base already refused calls of this kind with more arguments
  ("fixup Page21 addresses `gvals`, an undefined symbol, PC-relatively"):
  a call through a function address loaded from memory from ten pointer
  arguments, and a direct call or a call through a function-pointer
  parameter from eleven. With nine it compiled all three.
- The LLVM-import driver's two-pass AOT PGO path supports only AArch64 at O2
  or O3. Its GEN and USE requests for another target or optimization level
  fail closed. The driver also rejects non-mode `TCG_*` and `TRUST_CG_*`
  controls so hidden compilation settings cannot disagree between GEN and USE.
- The low-level AArch64 `Pipeline` profile sink also supports O0; this does
  not broaden the import driver's policy. Insertion plans IDs, instructions
  and metadata before mutation and refuses poisoned/conflicting metadata.
  Returned insertion errors preserve that phase's inputs, not earlier work
  in a pipeline or batch. The scaled load/store offset limits a module to
  4,096 counters. Profile-generation batches prepare in input order; ordinary
  batches remain parallel. Callers must provide the counter globals/runtime.
  Counts wrap at u64 exhaustion and non-atomic increments can lose updates
  under concurrent execution; they are performance guidance, not proof.
- The v3 `.sites` sidecar carries a compatibility digest over the imported
  input, published producer/schema identity, target, optimization/CEGIS
  settings, and a stable digest of the bytes read from the path returned by
  `current_exe`. That executable digest is non-cryptographic and the path can
  be replaced around the lookup/read; it is a compatibility discriminator, not
  proof of the running process image or a security boundary. A separate
  checksum covers the ordered site rows and detects accidental corruption or
  reordering, but it is also non-cryptographic and can be recomputed.
- The AOT PGO runtime writes a headerless array of little-endian `u64` counters.
  It permits one same-path writer, rejects symlink targets and any process that
  forks after setup, and fails closed on requested-output setup, write, close,
  or rename errors. Startup truncation makes ordinary abnormal exits fail the
  raw-length check, while a normal non-forking run installs its complete dump
  by atomic rename. Neither the sidecar checksums nor the raw file authenticate
  an unrelated, deliberately reconstructed same-length pair, so each
  `.sites`/`.raw` pair must be managed as one generation and treated only as
  performance guidance, never correctness or security authority.
- This document makes no aggregate compiler-performance claim.
- On `aarch64-apple-darwin` the certificates-on bridge compiles none of the
  18 benchmark programs at `01fc13b13`: proof promotion refuses every one with
  `[TCG-PROOF-465]` (ledger `L07-P2`), as it refuses the compile-time canary
  and the determinism sentinel's program. The first Darwin arm64 ledger row
  therefore records 0% coverage and no runtime, compile, size or memory ratio.
  Ratios for the emitted code exist only in a `no-proof-certs` diagnostic
  lane, which is never evidence. In that lane `scale_gate.py` measured 12x LLVM
  compile time and 25x peak RSS (9.45 GB) on its 33,605-line crate, growing
  roughly quadratically
  ([campaign](reports/perf/2026-09-28-darwin-aarch64-campaign/README.md)).
  That growth came from the pre-RA scheduler's call-barrier edges and from
  register-allocation scans over every call site, which scaled with the
  number of calls in one basic block. With those removed, the same lane read
  1.50x time and 1.45x memory at 33,605 lines, under a load of 8 to 12
  ([L14-P6](reports/perf/2026-09-28-darwin-scaling-l14p6/README.md)).
  Scaling is still measured only with proofs off. Main's `becb4b9df` removed
  `ProvenanceMap::record_merge`'s scan of the whole trust-ir-to-machine map on
  every CSE merge, and the linear scan now reads the registers its active
  intervals hold from an index instead of walking the active set
  ([L14-P6 residuals](reports/perf/2026-09-29-darwin-cold-start-and-loops-l14p5p6/README.md)). With both, store/load pairs through a pointer
  grow 4.5x and then 4.9x instructions per 4x step (256 to 4,096 pairs), and
  pairs into a stack tuple 6.4x and then 5.0x (500 to 8,000 pairs, 18.5 G
  instead of 28.8 G at 8,000). The first stack-tuple step crosses the
  512-field SROA limit, below which the tuple lives in registers. A function
  of many loops still grows faster than linearly. neon-fill, loop-unswitch,
  LICM and post-RA coalescing no longer redo whole-function work per loop,
  so compile-scaling's 120-loop crate costs 1.69x LLVM's CPU instead of
  2.09x, and the CLI compiles its 480-loop trust-ir in 52.8 G instead of
  101.1 G instructions. The remaining terms are the allocation stage and the
  allocation validator's value-flow fixpoint, about 3.3x and 3.8x per
  doubling of the loop count, and, for a chain of 1,024 fill loops, per-loop
  whole-function work in the vectorizer, `loop_latch_layout`, dominator-tree
  recomputation and the final layout check (15.6x from 256 to 1,024 loops).
  Since 2026-10-01 the loop-state contract answers a recognition sweep's
  liveness questions from one index of the function (it walked the rest of
  the function once per loop), and the dominator tree and the latch driver's
  indexes are dense arrays: the `loops` trust-ir at 120 and 240 loops
  compiles in 4.21 G and 13.18 G instructions instead of 5.94 G and 20.00 G
  (3.1x per doubling, was 3.4x). The loop-latch-layout driver still
  re-derives the dominator tree, loop analysis and vreg-use index after every
  rotated loop (59 ms of the 120-loop function's 280 ms), and the validator's
  value flow and the post-RA spill-slot frame net still grow with the values
  live across loops.
  A census of every blocking row of the corpus and the scale crates (1,324 of
  1,345 functions refused, 46,250 rows) found 416 pair-memory rows, 12,920
  rows with only sampled evidence and 32,913 registry-name rows; 32,685 of the
  last are now uncertified instruction-derived obligations, so the wall is the
  same size and no additional function compiles
  (census). At
  `main` `9bd719584` (46,768 rows, under the Formal-only bound-memory rule)
  the 912 memory rows keep their classes on this host, as checker-identity
  misses that also carry the memory-effect clause; no function changes status
  (report).
  A re-measure at `80b0e03aa` confirms this. Its evidence row is again 0 of 18,
  all refused with `[TCG-PROOF-465]`, and the canary and sentinel still fail
  closed. In the `no-proof-certs` lane, which is not evidence, the runtime
  geomean is 0.950x LLVM `-O3` (worst 1.113x), warm compile 1.23x `-O2`, cold
  3.9x and compiler peak RSS 1.20x. `scale_gate.py` reads 1.26x time and 1.46x
  peak RSS at 33,605 lines on a shared, intermittently loaded host
  ([re-measure](reports/perf/2026-09-29-darwin-aarch64-remeasure/README.md)).
  Per program, in cycles over 21 interleaved rounds of the same lane
  (re-measured 2026-10-07, not evidence), `main` `a7ce025ee` reads 1.022x LLVM
  `-O3` and the runtime-parity branch 0.918x; `p6_branch_match` is still slower
  than LLVM (1.015x, mispredicted dispatch), five programs are at parity, and
  emitted-code size is 1.0201x, below `main`'s 1.0233x but above the 1.0x bound
  ([record](reports/perf/2026-10-01-darwin-runtime-per-program/README.md)).
  Warm compiles now replay their stored certificates on a background thread
  while the front end runs, and probe the solver once per crate instead of
  once per function (2026-10-01, `CHANGELOG.md` L14-P5/L14-P6): in the same
  lane the warm corpus reads 1.05x LLVM `-O2` wall at load 21 to 32 (1.34x
  for the base it was measured against), not yet at or below 1.00x. The
  remaining critical path of a small crate is the refinement lane's
  per-obligation solver and checker re-resolution and precondition query
  (about 6 ms on `p3_gcd`) and the backend's CGU compiles; the replays still
  cost CPU (the corpus's CPU, child processes included, is 1.59x LLVM's), and
  the three custody digests (299 MB of SHA-256 per warm compile) stay off the
  critical path. compile-scaling's 120-loop crate reads 1.64x LLVM's CPU
  (10.31 G instructions against 6.26 G) and `scale_gate` xlarge 1.80x
  (64.1 G against 30.8 G).
  A requalification at `efc47d3bc` (2026-10-14, `main` `2dde71362` plus the
  larger-corpus harness) appended a third evidence row, again 0 of 18 with
  every program refused `[TCG-PROOF-465]`; 11 of the 18 refusals happened
  under load and are labeled NONDET-CANDIDATE in the row. In the
  `no-proof-certs` lane (not evidence) the corpus reads 0.926x LLVM `-O3`
  wall and 0.916x in cycles (`p6_branch_match` still slower), warm compile
  1.03x `-O2` wall but 1.185x in compiler instructions retired and 1.52x in
  CPU including child processes, cold compile 3.37x, emitted code 1.016x
  and compiler peak RSS 1.22x; `scale_gate.py` reads 1.14x time and 1.23x
  peak RSS at 33,605 lines, proofs off
  ([requalification](reports/perf/2026-10-14-darwin-aarch64-requalification/README.md)).
  Beyond the 18 programs, the versioned 62-row corpus of
  `benchmarks/real-corpus/` (real-program guests, crates.io crates from the
  Trust compiler's `Cargo.lock`, `library/core` at the driver's revision,
  the scaling ladders) completes none of the 57 rows that give the backend
  code to compile in the production lane (56 refused `[TCG-PROOF-465]`,
  `core` at `-O0` past 3,600 s); its only completion is a crate whose LLVM
  object holds no code, and for four more such crates the bridge exits 0
  without writing an object, which the harness now scores as ERROR. With
  certificates off, 16 rows still meet lowering gaps
  (`[TCG-COLLECTION-IMAGE]`, `[TCG-POINTEE-LANES]`, untyped MIR shapes), and
  the bridge's library objects hold 1.4x to 76x LLVM's code bytes; `core`
  at `-O0` compiles at 8.4x LLVM's wall time. That run is not evidence (rows
  ran under load), and its 27 crates are a hand-picked sample of the 189
  that meet the corpus's selection rule on this host.
- Size and memory accounting (gates.json version 3, ledger `L14-P10`):
  emitted-code size counts the code and read-only data bytes of the linked
  image that the linker's own map attributes to the objects the compile
  produced, after dead stripping. It includes the standard-library generics
  the crate instantiates and excludes the program's writable data, zero fill
  and unwind tables. Only the Apple `ld -map` reader has run against real
  links. The GNU `ld -Map` reader is exercised by a synthetic map only and has
  not yet run on a Linux host; any other linker's map is a missing reading,
  which makes a row ineligible. Peak RSS is the median of five samples per
  lane through the same per-process sampler, so the floor caveat below still
  applies. In the `no-proof-certs` lane on `aarch64-apple-darwin`, which is
  not evidence, emitted-code size reads 1.147x LLVM `-O3` (linked file size
  1.0006x) and compiler peak RSS 1.109x LLVM `-O2` after the backend's object
  compile moved out of rustc's type context and two eager type renderings
  stopped computing rustc's visible-path map (1.188x before, with identical
  emitted bytes;
  [report](reports/perf/2026-09-29-darwin-l14p10-size-memory/README.md)).
  Emitted-code size then fell to 0.951x LLVM `-O3` (2026-09-30, same lane, not
  evidence; worst program 1.602x, `p4_matmul`), mostly by removing a fixed
  runtime-entry cost and default loop-head padding; 12 of the 18 programs are
  still larger than LLVM's, and the remaining excess is attributed in the
  [size report](reports/perf/2026-09-30-darwin-emitted-size/README.md).
  Of the remaining compiler-RSS excess of about 15 MiB on a small program, about 6 MiB is
  loading and binding the 109 MiB backend dylib (a front-end-only
  `--emit=metadata` compile with and without it). The rest is not attributed
  by a retained measurement. The backend's code working set is a candidate,
  not a measured share: compiling `p1_xorshift` executes about 5.5 MiB of
  backend code, while the LLVM lane touches its own `librustc_driver` code
  instead.
- A compile that populates a fresh cache root (every compile of
  `run.py --cold`) writes a new AY private copy, and on macOS the first start
  of that new executable waits for Gatekeeper's XProtect scan of the whole
  file: 0.68 to 0.92 s for the 91 MB Trust 9192 AY on an M4 Max in 27 of
  40 cold samples (0.68 to 0.75 s in 22), and 1.0 to 3.2 s in the other 13
  on a host shared with other builds, against 8 ms for a later start. One
  read of the AY now both admits it and writes the copy, and a suspended
  spawn, checked to be stopped and killed before its first instruction,
  starts the scan as soon as this process has published the copy, about 80
  to 95 ms after the process starts. A candidate that is not the admitted
  AY is refused from that read, but is first streamed into a temporary
  under the cache root, which is removed. The first start
  still waits for the scan, and a small crate's first solve waits for most
  of it (before its solver deadline starts, not inside it). With a fresh
  certificate store every obligation is also discharged live, one after
  another under the bridge's default one-worker proof policy, which costs
  about 250 ms more than the warm replays on `p3_gcd`.
  These two, not per-process set-up, are most of the Darwin cold/warm compile
  gap ([attribution](reports/perf/2026-09-29-darwin-cold-start-and-loops-l14p5p6/README.md)). The scan is a host policy cost of the private
  copy the AY identity rule requires; it is paid once per cache root and AY
  build.
- SAT-Comp and microbenchmark measurements apply only to the documented
  binaries, inputs, hosts, resource envelopes, and checker results. They do not
  imply end-to-end superiority over LLVM, Cranelift, or production SAT solvers.
- Open: an unusable independent proof checker is not always reported. When
  trust-cg-verify probes a Clean candidate, it prints the `verification is
  DEGRADED` banner only for capability defects. These are a missing
  `carcara-verify` or `ay-smt` feature and a rejected control proof
  (`CheckerDefect::cacheable` in `obligation_cert_store.rs`). A candidate
  that cannot be executed, whose identity changes during the probe, or whose
  control-proof probe times out is dropped with only a trace. When no other
  candidate is usable, the backend runs without an independent checker.
  Solver UNSAT verdicts are then not promoted and the certificate store is
  inert, and nothing reports it. The beat-llvm harness narrows this: it
  stamps each Clean candidate with a digest, runs `clean --version`, and
  marks a run with no candidate that executes as not evidence. That probe
  shows only that the file executes and answers `--version` with exit 0 and
  some output. Any program that does so passes it, including a script or an
  unrelated binary. Whether a candidate can check proofs is reported only by
  the backend's DEGRADED banner. So a checker that executes but whose
  control-proof probe times out inside a compile is not detected.
- On Linux the portable peak-RSS sampler reports at least the resident set
  of its own Python wrapper, which exec inherits (about 13.7 MB on the
  AArch64 host). Most beat-llvm programs peak below that, so their
  comparisons are unresolved and gate R1 reads unmeasured there.

See [`metrics-contract.md`](metrics-contract.md) for the evidence required to
publish a new performance comparison.

## Distribution and compatibility

- The 0.x releases are source-workspace releases, not a crates.io package set.
- It builds against exact revisions of companion Trust repositories. Those
  revisions must be present in the public release graph for an anonymous clone
  to build.
- The root workspace pins the Trust toolchain (`channel = "trust"`) in
  `rust-toolchain.toml` and builds with an installed Trust package's `targo`;
  the optional rustc backend is a separate workspace with the same pin. The
  public build therefore needs a Trust package, which is not distributed with
  the snapshot. Root-workspace checks do not cover the separate bridge or
  cargo-fuzz workspace.
  The cargo-fuzz targets execute only in the Linux AArch64 fuzz lane
  (`scripts/run_linux_fuzz_lane.py`), a stock-toolchain exception because Trust
  ships no AddressSanitizer runtime, `rust-lld` or cargo-fuzz. It needs
  cargo-fuzz and the pinned stock `nightly-2026-08-06`, and links the
  AddressSanitizer build with that nightly's `rust-lld` (GNU ld 2.42 cannot
  link it). Its pass is budgeted
  testing at fixed seeds from an empty corpus, not coverage or absence-of-bugs
  evidence. About a quarter of its JIT-differential scalar rows have no
  interpreter value and compare only the optimization levels with each other.
  The lane is not part of the public release checks. There is no Darwin fuzz
  lane, and the csmith/yarpgen drivers remain unavailable.
- The Rust library APIs, proof schemas, diagnostics, and text/debug formats are
  not stable yet.
- There are no official prebuilt binaries or package-manager distributions.
- The main soundness gate is deliberately local and cross-repository. This
  repository does not currently use GitHub Actions as a substitute for that
  pinned constellation check.

## Trusted base

The opt-in `core-byte-replay` API checks a canonical Clean ByteV1 Store/Return
invocation against an independently reconstructed whole-memory claim. It
quantifies over initial bytes; caller allocation rows, address and stored word
are concrete inputs. The result is model-specific strict rooted kernel evidence;
no independent micro cross-check is performed. It is not a source-to-machine proof or
compiler publication authority. A separate retained-writer regression now
kernel-checks all 51 captured instructions, including typed reference carriers
and Copy, universally over positive caller addresses, five canonical 64-bit
words, allocation histories, initial bytes, cursors and host states under the
actual ByteV1 entry ownership, range and live-access premises. A checked
retirement lemma proves that every original allocation row survives root
return. Two applications also check concrete allocation histories, including
the last valid 40-byte output range. These premises do not prove Rust reference validity, frontend
adequacy, native caller ownership, private-stack/ABI refinement or composed
native correctness. The [zero-storage leaf qualification](reports/perf/2026-09-20-linux-zero-storage-leaves/README.md)
now compiles and executes the actual O1 writer with backend proof checks enabled;
the [installed follow-up](reports/perf/2026-09-20-linux-zero-storage-install/README.md)
also preserves the existing arithmetic proof exports. Its unverified development
frontend and finite native controls do not discharge those semantic gaps. The
[bounded-guard frame extension](reports/perf/2026-09-20-zero-storage-bounds/README.md)
now also compiles and executes the O0 writer and fixed-array bounds programs.
The [direct integer branch repair](reports/perf/2026-09-20-direct-integer-branches/README.md)
now compiles and executes the dominated conditional stores at O0/O1, while
unwinding programs retain missing STP/LDP frame proofs. Generic CSet and precise
CMP proof binding remain separate obligations.
The [emitted-layout frame repair](reports/perf/2026-09-20-emitted-frame-effects/README.md)
now admits the masked-index unwind source at O2/O3 after its unreachable panic
block is removed. It excludes retained dead arena effects when computing the
frame. This is not general unwinding support: O0/O1 and genuinely live unwind
frames still require separate proofs.
The [current installed package](reports/perf/2026-09-20-ground-projection-install/README.md)
also includes canonical allocation references, direct global-address leaves and
the complete Linux regression repairs.
All 246 preflight commands pass before activation, including eighteen admitted
Rust compilation cases, the existing arithmetic proof exports and the additional
i128/narrow-argument ABI fixture. The masked
unwind cases pass at O2/O3; the sixteen earlier cases pass at O0/O1. The activated
launcher also passes proof export, native link and execution.
The [frameless byte checker](reports/perf/2026-09-20-frameless-output-bytes/README.md)
now binds the O1 writer's original TrustIR, adapter LIR and actual emitted bytes,
with independent replay of conditional byte-map equality. Its Rust decoder and
trace interpretation remain unproved, caller validity remains a premise, and
the checker grants no new production authority.
See the caller-memory replay.

Depending on the selected path, the trusted base includes Rust and C compiler
toolchains, trust-cg implementation code not covered by a complete theorem,
the trust-ir semantic encoding, solver/bit-blaster code, proof serializers,
object/linker/runtime behavior, target specifications, and hardware or emulator
oracles. Independently replayed certificates reduce the trusted base only for
the exact claim and artifact the checker accepted.

[`SOUNDNESS_CHECK.md`](SOUNDNESS_CHECK.md) documents the repository's pinned
cross-project gate and separately reported solver-capacity pending work. Treat
that as an engineering soundness program, not as a claim that all residual
trust has been eliminated.

## Reporting a limitation or wrong-code bug

Open an [issue](https://github.com/alabsystems/trust-cg/issues) with:

- the trust-cg revision and `trust-cg --version` output;
- host and requested target triples;
- optimization level, input format, and relevant environment controls;
- the smallest input that reproduces the problem;
- expected and actual behavior; and
- `--trace --metrics` output when available.

For a suspected miscompilation, preserve the original input and independent
oracle result. Do not reduce away the behavior that distinguishes them.
